top10_weekly.title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
top10_weekly.abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

top10_weekly.title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation.
top10_weekly.abstract: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scaper, ttc5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that scaper and ttc5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MT organizing centers (MTOCs). SCAPER is also instructive, as its overexpression raises γ-tubulin levels at nucleation sites and increases MT density. SCAPER, TTC5, and γ-tubulin are dispensable for developmental axon growth but play essential roles during regeneration, where SCAPER recruits γ-tubulin to a growth-cone-localized MTOC to orient MT nucleation. Last, SCAPER is required for activity-dependent MT nucleation in rat hippocampal neurons, suggesting a conserved role. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and MT nucleation.

top10_weekly.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
top10_weekly.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

top10_weekly.title: Bioinformatic investigation of convergent proteins and cellular functions downstream of autism-associated genes.
top10_weekly.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder affects 1 in 31 people yet exhibits remarkable genetic heterogeneity with over 1000 genes identified in autistic populations producing convergent neurobiological phenotypes through not yet understood mechanisms. Here, we employed systems-level network analysis to test if diverse autism risk genes converge onto common cellular vulnerabilities across brain cell types. Using 1238 autism-associated genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) database, we stratified genes by cell-type-specific expression patterns and constructed protein-protein interaction networks to map functional clusters and identify critical connector proteins. Through permutation-based statistical analysis, we identified convergent downstream proteins targets, representing molecular vulnerabilities where multiple autism-associated protein pathways converge for miscoordination of cellular function. Network analysis revealed cell-type-specific vulnerability signatures: SYN1 in inhibitory neurons, GRIN/DLG/CAMK2 proteins in excitatory neurons, GRIA2A/DLG4/GRIN2 in oligodendrocyte precursor cells, ACTL6B in oligodendrocytes, and ARHGAP/DOCK proteins in astrocytes. Remarkably, these computationally predicted targets have been independently validated in human genetics and autism research, demonstrating that network-based convergent vulnerability analysis successfully identifies critical nodes where diverse genetic insults disrupt coordinated cellular responses. This framework provides a molecular basis for understanding autism pathophysiology and identifies promising targets for intervention in the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders.

top10_weekly.title: Tubulin polyglutamylation modulates Golgi morphodynamics and neurite branching during neuronal morphogenesis.
top10_weekly.abstract: Neurons establish functional networks through morphological remodeling during neuronal differentiation. Microtubule polyglutamylation is a key microtubule post-translational modification that is highly enriched during this process and plays an important role in differentiation. However, how remodeling of organelle features such as morphology, distribution and interactions depends on tubulin polyglutamylation during neuronal differentiation remains unclear. Here, we employed multispectral imaging combined with quantitative three-dimensional organelle analysis to comprehensively profile eight organelles simultaneously in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. We discovered that depletion of tubulin polyglutamylation induces pronounced alterations in somatic Golgi morphology and associated organelle interactions. In addition, Golgi-derived compartments in proximal neurites exhibited altered morphology and dynamics, namely, decreased anterograde transport together with less efficient movement. These changes were accompanied by increased neurite branching and tortuosity. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for tubulin polyglutamylation in coordinating organelle organization with neurite architecture, providing a mechanistic link between tubulin post-translational modifications, Golgi morphology, dynamics and neuronal morphogenesis.

top10_weekly.title: Two functionally distinct amyloid-β intermediates link aggregation pathways to pathology in Alzheimer's disease.
top10_weekly.abstract: Neurotoxic intermediates formed during amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation are thought to drive Alzheimer's disease, yet their rarity and transient nature have obscured their identity and formation pathways in the human brain. Here, we combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify Aβ intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them. Applying this framework to recombinant Aβ42, an Alzheimer's knock-in mouse model and human Alzheimer's brain tissue, we find two functionally distinct intermediate populations present across all systems. They form through separate aggregation routes and differ in their neurotoxicity, abundance and susceptibility to inhibition. Both damage neurons and glia, but only one converts into plaques. Suppressing these intermediates pharmacologically in mice reduces plaque burden, attenuates astrogliosis and improves cognition. Our findings connect model systems with human pathology and identify intermediate formation pathways as actionable therapeutic targets across protein-misfolding disorders.

top10_weekly.title: AKT is necessary for neuronal hypertrophy and epilepsy caused by Pten knockout.
top10_weekly.abstract: Phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is a key negative regulator of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Mutations in PTEN are highly implicated in autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, congenital hydrocephaly and macrocephaly. While the conditional genetic knockout of Pten in murine neurons results in hypertrophy, increased migration, excitatory synaptogenesis, hyperexcitability and epileptiform activity, the specific downstream signalling mediators of these pathologies remain to be fully elucidated. Using retroviral-mediated genetic manipulation of individual neurons within the Cre-lox recombination system, we have analysed pathway outputs in response to the manipulation of various genes using immunohistochemistry, confocal microscopy and extensive morphological analyses, alongside whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology and 120-h video-EEG monitoring for seizure assessment. Here, we demonstrate that signalling through AKT is necessary for the development of neuronal overgrowth, increased excitatory synapse formation, excessive migration and hyperexcitability fuelled by the loss of PTEN function. Notably, the concurrent deletion of Akt1 and Akt3 isoforms was sufficient to effectively rescue hypertrophic neuronal morphology and physiology. These findings establish AKT as the essential mediator through which PTEN deficiency manifests, providing a transformative therapeutic target to correct the morphological and functional defects central to PTEN-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

top10_weekly.title: Integrated Multi-omics Reveals Molecular Signatures of Rett Syndrome, Informing Future Biomarker Discovery.
top10_weekly.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. Despite numerous clinical trials being conducted, there are limited disease-modifying options available for individuals with RTT. This paucity of effective treatments can in part be attributed to the lack of clinically useful biomarkers that can objectively assess treatment response. Moreover, diagnosis of RTT continues to be clinical, when clinical manifestations are apparent, precluding early therapeutic approaches. Thus, clinical biomarkers of disease stage could improve diagnosis and enable real-time monitoring of response to treatment, providing the earliest possible indications of therapeutic efficacy. Given MeCP2's role as a key regulator of gene transcription, we used an untargeted omics approach to evaluate transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolic profiles in blood from individuals with RTT (n = 9) and age- and sex-matched controls (n = 8). In addition to characterising differential expression at each omic layer, to understand the shared biology and coordinated molecular signals across all omic datasets, we used the unsupervised machine learning framework Multi-Omics Factor Analysis version 2 (MOFA2). The individual omic data consisted of a robust upregulation of genes involved in ribosomal structure and translation together with a downregulation in vesicle trafficking genes. An upregulation in ribosomal machinery and mitochondrial function together with a concomitant downregulation of critical epigenetic regulators, immune-signalling molecules, and cytoskeletal structural anchors was observed in the proteomics, which was supported by the phosphoproteomics. Notably, plasma metabolomics pointed towards alterations in energy substrates and lipid/cholesterol handling, suggesting systemic downstream consequences of primary intracellular disturbances. The integrated MOFA2 data supported the individual omic data revealing a central disease axis principally shaped by the proteome and transcriptome and supported by the metabolome and phosphoproteome, identifying potential biomarkers, including latent biological processes that distinguish RTT from controls (Latent Factor 1) and correlates of clinical severity (Latent Factor 2). Overall, our data reveal a distinctive 'disease state' molecular signature that distinguishes individuals with RTT from controls, where the findings in RTT blood cells are consistent with previously reported altered translational and mitochondrial function and disrupted chromatin regulation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and metabolic signalling. Our integrated multi-omics analyses revealed that PBMC's LTN1, ATRX, CHD8, SPTB, DMTN, PRF1, CD40LG, and PTPRCAP and plasma glutamate are the most promising disease-state (complementary diagnostic) candidate biomarkers while sphingomyelin, RTN3, and MMP1 appear to be the most suitable biomarkers of disease severity. Here, we demonstrate that blood from individuals with RTT reflects the molecular systemic consequences of MeCP2 dysfunction.

top10_weekly.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
top10_weekly.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

top10_weekly.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism.
top10_weekly.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1-3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this 'female protective effect' (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

primary.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
primary.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

primary.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
primary.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

primary.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. best.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
best.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

best.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
best.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

best.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
best.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: Bioinformatic investigation of convergent proteins and cellular functions downstream of autism-associated genes.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder affects 1 in 31 people yet exhibits remarkable genetic heterogeneity with over 1000 genes identified in autistic populations producing convergent neurobiological phenotypes through not yet understood mechanisms. Here, we employed systems-level network analysis to test if diverse autism risk genes converge onto common cellular vulnerabilities across brain cell types. Using 1238 autism-associated genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) database, we stratified genes by cell-type-specific expression patterns and constructed protein-protein interaction networks to map functional clusters and identify critical connector proteins. Through permutation-based statistical analysis, we identified convergent downstream proteins targets, representing molecular vulnerabilities where multiple autism-associated protein pathways converge for miscoordination of cellular function. Network analysis revealed cell-type-specific vulnerability signatures: SYN1 in inhibitory neurons, GRIN/DLG/CAMK2 proteins in excitatory neurons, GRIA2A/DLG4/GRIN2 in oligodendrocyte precursor cells, ACTL6B in oligodendrocytes, and ARHGAP/DOCK proteins in astrocytes. Remarkably, these computationally predicted targets have been independently validated in human genetics and autism research, demonstrating that network-based convergent vulnerability analysis successfully identifies critical nodes where diverse genetic insults disrupt coordinated cellular responses. This framework provides a molecular basis for understanding autism pathophysiology and identifies promising targets for intervention in the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1-3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this 'female protective effect' (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

primary.title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
primary.abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

primary.title: Cell Type-Specific Assessment of Cholesterol Distribution in Models of Neurodevelopmental Disorders.
primary.abstract: Most nervous system disorders manifest through alterations in neuronal signaling based on abnormalities in neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, and cell survival. However, such neuronal phenotypes are frequently accompanied or even caused by metabolic dysfunctions in neuronal or non-neuronal cells. The tight packing and highly heterogeneous properties of neural, glial, and vascular cell types pose significant challenges to dissecting metabolic aspects of brain disorders. Perturbed cholesterol homeostasis has recently emerged as a key parameter associated with subsets of neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration. However, approaches for tracking and visualizing endogenous cholesterol distribution in the brain have limited capability of resolving cell type-specific differences. We here develop tools for genetically encoded sensors that report on accessible cholesterol distribution in the mouse brain with cellular resolution. We apply these probes to examine subcellular cholesterol accumulation in two genetic mouse models of brain disorders, male Ptchd1 knock-out and male and female Npc1 knock-out mice. While both genes encode proteins with sterol-sensing domains that have been implicated in cholesterol transport, we uncover highly selective and cell type-specific phenotypes in cholesterol homeostasis. The tools established in this work should facilitate probing subcellular cholesterol distribution in complex tissues like the mammalian brain and enable capturing cell type-specific alterations in cholesterol flow between cells in models of brain disorders.

primary.title: A massively parallel reporter assay of MECP2 cis-regulatory elements reveals genetic candidates for male-biased autism.
primary.abstract: Autism affects male individuals four times more often than female individuals, yet the basis of this sex bias remains unclear. One hypothesis is that this sex bias is due to genetic variants in X chromosome genes where haploinsufficiency causes neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). In heterozygous XX female probands, a complete loss-of-function variant in one of these genes often causes syndromic NDD, but the same variant is too deleterious for survival in hemizygous XY males. A mild hypomorphic variant, however, may be tolerated in a female carrier but may produce milder neurological phenotypes in a male proband. We tested this by investigating cis-regulatory elements (CREs) of MECP2, a dosage-sensitive gene on the X chromosome where total loss-of-function variants cause Rett syndrome in female children and severe, usually fatal neonatal encephalopathies in male infants. Using a massively parallel reporter assay in human neurons, we mapped transcription factor binding sites within MECP2 CREs and tested autism-associated variants for functional impact. We identified two noncoding variants that change CRE activity and are associated with male-biased autism phenotypes in the proband pedigrees. One of these, a promoter variant, disrupts NFY binding and reduces MECP2 expression by ∼30%, a magnitude that produces social deficits, hyperactivity, and anxiety-like phenotypes in mice. These findings suggest noncoding MECP2 variants can cause idiopathic, male-biased autism and provide a framework for uncovering regulatory variants in other X chromosome neurodevelopmental genes that may contribute to autism's missing heritability.

primary.title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic Ih current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype-phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8bnano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.

primary.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
primary.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

primary.title: Integrating clinical diagnostics with interventional genetics for neurodevelopmental disorders.
primary.abstract: Interventional genetics (IG) refers to the development of therapies aimed at treating the underlying genetic cause of disease. Diagnostic sequencing has advanced to the point where genetic results can be returned within weeks, meaning that therapeutically actionable variants associated with specific diseases could be developed immediately after diagnosis. Here, we describe 81 probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and family matched controls with full genotype/phenotype information and biobanked stem cells, most of which are consented for sharing. We outline a rapid and scalable pipeline for induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation directly from clinical collection, without the need for peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) storage, paired with induction to neurons. We provide a proof of principle for rapid creation of oligonucleotide therapeutics for Kleefstra syndrome. This work introduces a cohort of individuals with NDDs and an implemental pipeline to integrate IG with clinical diagnostics for NDDs. This information documents our experience and provides useful details for clinical centers interested in integrating IG for NDDs with diagnostic sequencing.

primary.title: Genomic landscape of rare variants in a Chinese autism cohort and discovery of novel risk genes.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a genetically complex neurodevelopmental condition with a high heritability. However, genomic studies of ASD have been underrepresented in East Asian populations, and the molecular yield in ASD cohorts remains modest. Here, we present a whole-genome sequencing analysis of 3109 samples across 1033 Chinese ASD families. By examining a wide spectrum of genetic variation, we identified rare ASD-associated variants in 19.2% of affected individuals, providing a population-specific view of the genetic architecture of ASD. We identify significant enrichment of de novo variants in probands, nominate or strengthen candidate risk genes (e.g., NCL, SPPL3, ADGRB1, SLC9A3, KIF1B) through mutational burden, evolutionary constraint, recurrent missense site, and functional assays, and implicate convergent pathways including protein palmitoylation. By integrating over 40,000 ASD cases across unpublished and published global cohorts, we identify 245 ASD risk genes, including 45 with limited prior evidence and 32 with no prior association. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the developing human cortex reveals that ASD risk genes exhibit widespread yet heterogeneous expression across all major cell types, with peak expression in excitatory neurons, particularly intratelencephalic neurons, and enriched expression in microglia (e.g., C1QC, CARD11, SNX13, MEF2C, FOXP2, TCF12, MED13L), suggesting convergent involvement of both synaptic and neuroimmune mechanisms. Together, our findings expand the ASD genetic landscape and suggest convergent pathogenic axes involving transcriptional regulation, synaptic signaling and plasticity, and neuroimmune interactions. This work supports the development of inclusive diagnostic strategies and provides a foundation for mechanistic and intervention exploration in ASD.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: Monoallelic variants in BRSK1 are associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Brain-specific serine/threonine kinase (BRSK1; synapses of amphids defective [SAD]-B) encodes an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-related serine/threonine kinase required for neuronal polarization and synaptic function. An individual with a variant in BRSK1 was identified in the Texome Project, which provides genomic diagnosis to financially disadvantaged individuals in Texas, using AI-MARRVEL. We subsequently found nine individuals harboring rare heterozygous BRSK1 variants through GeneMatcher. Affected individuals present with developmental delay and variable phenotypes including anxiety, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism, and seizures. All variants (missense and nonsense) are predicted to be deleterious by pathogenicity prediction tools. We utilized Drosophila to model three missense variants to assess the impact of the variants in vivo. We show that Drosophila sff (sugar-free frosting; ortholog of BRSK1) is expressed in neurons of the larval central nervous system (CNS) and adult brain. Loss of sff leads to viable flies with severe locomotor impairment, bang and heat sensitivity, and a short lifespan. In addition, the third-instar neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) in sff null mutants display a significant overgrowth, associated with elevated levels of Futsch (MAP1B), a microtubule-associated protein. Expression of the human reference BRSK1 cDNA in the sff null mutant rescues the behavioral, NMJ morphology, and Futsch phenotypes, showing that the human gene is functional in flies. In contrast, the three individual-derived alleles (BRSK1p.Ile202Val, BRSK1p.Arg237Cys, and BRSK1p.Thr406Ile) provide only a partial rescue and fail to normalize NMJ morphology and Futsch levels, suggesting that they are partial loss-of-function alleles. In summary, our data support a model that heterozygous loss of BRSK1 leads to a neurodevelopmental syndrome with variable phenotypes.

secondary.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Hypothalamic Hamartoma: Early Developmental Trajectory, Symptom Profile, and Relevance for Autism Research.
secondary.abstract: Focal brain lesions occurring during critical developmental periods can shed light on the neural substrates underlying autistic symptoms. Hypothalamic hamartomas (HH) are rare congenital malformations that are typically characterized by pharmacoresistant epilepsy, endocrine disturbances, and behavioral or psychiatric disorders. Although autistic symptoms have occasionally been reported in children with HH, they remain poorly described and are rarely documented with standardized diagnostic tools. We present a case report of a 3-year-old boy with HH who was followed from 2 years of age. The report combines detailed early neurodevelopmental history, neuroimaging data, and standardized autism assessments. The child exhibited global developmental delay, early intense sensory features, and marked social communication deficits. The first developmental difficulties preceded the onset of seizures. At 29 months of age, magnetic resonance imaging identified a small intrahypothalamic hamartoma. At 36 months, the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised confirmed the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). A comparison with 3 subjects with ASD matched for sex, chronological age, and developmental age showed that the child presented less severe deficits in sharing enjoyment and less intense unusual preoccupations than age-matched autistic peers. This case highlights the importance of systematic ASD screening in children with HH, allowing timely referral to evidence-based early interventions. Moreover, HH may offer a valuable framework for investigating early neurodevelopmental mechanisms associated with ASD, while highlighting the potential contribution of the hypothalamus to early autism mechanisms.

secondary.title: Intron Retention Caused by a Novel Homozygous LNPK Splice-Site Variant Leading to Severe Neurodevelopmental Disorder and Epilepsy.
secondary.abstract: Loss-of-function variants in LNPK have been shown to cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome associated with developmental delay, epilepsy, regression, and a distinct neuroimaging pattern including corpus callosum hypoplasia and abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity at the tip of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricles ("ear-of-the-lynx" sign). To date, 21 affected individuals from 16 families have been reported. Here, we identify a novel homozygous LNPK splice-site variant (NM_030650.3:c.27 + 1G>T) in a patient with developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, epilepsy, and a brain MRI demonstrating corpus callosum hypoplasia, "ear-of-the-lynx" sign, and substantia nigra signal alterations. To determine the variant's pathogenicity, we first used in silico splice prediction models AlphaGenome, SAI-10 k-calc, SpliceAI, and Pangolin. Then, by implementing targeted RNA sequencing of patient-derived fibroblasts following nonsense-mediated decay inhibition, we showed that the variant causes activation of a cryptic donor site, which results in a 5 bp intron retention and introduction of a premature stop codon into the transcript. We also delineate the phenotypic features of the proband with a comprehensive review of the literature. These findings expand the molecular spectrum of LNPK deficiency and demonstrate the complementary value of computational splicing prediction and functional RNA analysis for establishing the consequences of splice-site variants in rare-disease diagnostics.

secondary.title: Association of Neuronal Cell Adhesion Molecule (NrCAM) Gene with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Indian Cohorts.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is the most complex neurodevelopmental disorder with impairments in communication, social interaction and stereotyped behaviours. ASD has been found to increase immeasurably in India, with estimates ranging from 1 in 68 to 1 in 100 children. Genetically, more than 1,000 genes have been linked with ASD. Among them, the neuronal cell adhesion molecule (NrCAM) gene is one of the candidate genes and is important for its critical role in the development and function of the nervous system, particularly in wiring the brain through axon guidance and organising myelinated nerve structures. Disruptions in this gene are associated with various neurodevelopmental, psychiatric and cancer-related disorders. PURPOSE: The present study aimed to understand the association of the NrCAM gene with ASD. METHODS: Ten exons of the NrCAM gene (one from 5'UTR, five from the immunoglobulin domain, three from the fibronectin domains and one from 3'UTR region) were selected and screened for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) by Sanger sequencing. Several in silico analyses were used for the association study. RESULTS: The results revealed four SNPs from coding and untranslated regions (rs2072546, rs401433, rs1269634 and rs449077) of the NrCAM gene which were analysed for association by linkage disequilibrium analysis. CONCLUSION: The present study clearly suggests that these SNPs of the NrCAM gene are associated with ASD.

secondary.title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome.
secondary.abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. While SHANK3 is critical for synapses, its role in early human neurodevelopment remains elusive. Here, we generated induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived 2D neuronal cultures and 3D cerebral organoids from two twin Phelan-McDermid syndrome patients with a 1.7 Mb 22q13 deletion encompassing SHANK3 gene. PMDS organoids showed reduced volume due to impaired neural progenitor cells (NPCs) proliferation. PMDS NPCs exhibited biased differentiation with decreased excitatory neurons but increased GFAP+ astroglia and GABAergic neurons. PMDS neurons displayed simplified morphology, reduced synapse density and diminished excitability. Importantly, lentiviral-mediated SHANK3 overexpression largely rescued these defects. Our findings identify SHANK3 as a key regulator of early neurodevelopment and provide mechanistic insights into PMDS pathogenesis.

secondary.title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
secondary.abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.

secondary.title: Effects of Lovastatin on Autism-Like Behavioral, Metabolic, and Neuroinflammatory Alterations in Male BTBR T+ Tf/J Mice.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, thereby reducing cellular cholesterol and isoprenoid biosynthesis. In addition to lowering serum cholesterol, statins exert pleiotropic neuroprotective effects, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory actions mediated through the mevalonate pathway. Statins are increasingly being explored for drug repurposing in neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of lovastatin in the BTBR T+ tf/J mouse model of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a well-established idiopathic model exhibiting core behavioral deficits and dysregulated cholesterol homeostasis characterized by elevated serum cholesterol and reduced brain cholesterol, consistent with reports of altered cholesterol metabolism in ASD. METHODS: BTBR mice received lovastatin (10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, i.p. for 21 days) and were assessed for repetitive behaviour, cognitive performance and social interaction. Cholesterol-related markers, HMG-CoA reductase levels and neuroinflammatory markers were also examined. RESULTS: BTBR mice exhibited increased marble-burying behaviour, reduced spontaneous alternation and social interaction, elevated HMG-CoA reductase levels, decreased brain free cholesterol, increased serum cholesterol, and heightened brain levels of TNF-α and IL-6 compared with C57BL/6J controls. Lovastatin was associated with improvements across the evaluated autism related behavioral outcomes. The 40 mg/kg dose of Lovastatin showed the largest observed behavioral effects overall. Following 21 days of treatment, lovastatin reduced brain HMG-CoA reductase levels at all tested doses and reduced elevated serum cholesterol levels. Exploratory neuroinflammatory analyses showed that lovastatin at 40 mg/kg significantly lowered brain TNF-α and IL-6 levels in BTBR mice. CONCLUSION: Lovastatin was associated with improvements in autism related behavioral outcomes in male BTBR mice, while modulating systemic cholesterol dysregulation and neuroinflammatory responses. These findings provide preclinical evidence supporting further investigation of lovastatin in ASD-related phenotypes.

secondary.title: Disruption of GAD1 protein architecture by a novel missense variant in a consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intellectual disability represents a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders marked by significant impairments in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior. Among the various causes, genetic factors play a major role, with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID) constituting a genetically diverse subgroup. ARID is prevalent in consanguineous families and arises from homozygous mutations that disrupt critical genes involved in brain development and function. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify disease-causing genetic variants responsible for ARID in a consanguineous Pakistani family and to evaluate the structural and functional impact of a novel variant identified in GAD1 through protein modeling. METHODS: A consanguineous family affected with intellectual disability was enrolled. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on an affected individual, followed by bioinformatics analysis including alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome, variant calling, and annotation. Variants were filtered based on rarity, predicted functional impact, and autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Candidate variants were validated and assessed by Sanger sequencing and segregation analysis. Protein modeling was performed to evaluate the structural impact of the identified variant. RESULTS: A novel homozygous missense variant NM_000817:c.1700G>A;p.Arg567Gln in GAD1 was identified. Segregation analysis confirmed co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype. Protein modeling suggested that the variant may disrupt GAD1 enzymatic function involved in gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis. CONCLUSION: This study emphasizes the significance of genetic investigation in familial cases and the crucial role that GAD1 mutations play in neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability. The results advance the knowledge of molecular causes of ARID and broaden the mutational range.

secondary.title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

secondary.title: Critical advances and translational bottlenecks of gut microbiota-gut-brain axis targeted therapy for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: Neurological diseases have become a major global public health burden. Existing central nervous system-targeted therapies can only alleviate clinical symptoms but fail to halt the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, presenting mechanistic limitations and therapeutic bottlenecks. The gut microbiota participates in the regulation of central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis and neuropathological processes via the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA). Notably, dysbiosis may induce damage to the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and immune imbalance, thereby mediating the onset and progression of various neurological diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease (AD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and multiple sclerosis (MS). This article provides a systematic review of the core mechanisms by which the gut microbiome regulates neurological diseases, including inflammation regulation, oxidative stress responses, and neuroendocrine remodeling mediated by microbial metabolites. It also comprehensively summarizes the research progress, application advantages, and existing limitations of novel gut-targeted interventions, such as probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), dietary interventions, and live biological therapies. At the same time, the article critically examines key bottlenecks prevalent in the field: the causal relationship between the microbiota and disease remains unclear; there is a significant translational gap between animal and human studies; there is a lack of unified standards for multi-omics analysis systems; and interference from confounding factors such as age, diet, and medications is significant. Existing research indicates that gut microbiota interventions complement traditional symptomatic treatments and hold promising prospects for early disease intervention and adjunctive therapy for refractory patients. Future efforts should integrate multi-omics and artificial intelligence technologies to decipher the causal networks governing gut-central nervous system regulation, establish standardized research frameworks, advance the clinical translation of precision gut microbiota therapies, and provide new approaches for the comprehensive prevention, control, and personalized treatment of neurological disorders.

secondary.title: Disrupted neuronal expression of autism risk genes and white matter micro-organization after infant Zika infection.
secondary.abstract: Congenital and early-life Zika virus (ZIKV) infection can result in neurologic deficits. Precise mechanisms of injury, especially in the more subtle presentation of postnatal infection, are not fully elucidated. Here, we defined the effects of ZIKV on the developing brain using single-cell transcriptomics, histopathology, design-based stereology, diffusion MRI, and neurobehavioral assessments in infant rhesus macaques. ZIKV upregulated interferon-stimulated genes in activated microglia and cell death pathways in neurons and downregulated metabolism and differentiation genes in mature oligodendrocytes. Abnormal micro-organization of the corpus callosum and limbic white matter tracts was seen on diffusion-weighted imaging. A curated gene set associated with autism spectrum disorder risk was negatively enriched in inhibitory and excitatory neurons from ZIKV-infected infants, with increased emotional reactivity already evident 2 weeks after infection. From single cells to organism-level behaviors, these results define the pathways and processes disrupted by early-life ZIKV infection.

secondary.title: Differential frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics and behavioral flexibility in autism like VPA-exposed mice.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social impairments, repetitive behaviors, and behavioral inflexibility, defined as an inability to adapt behavior to changing contingencies, and is linked to frontostriatal dysfunction. How behavioral training modulates these circuits is unclear, but ΔFosB, a marker of sustained neural activity, may be useful to establish their relationship. The aim was to evaluate frontostriatal ΔFosB expression following prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) and to determine how experience in the midsession reversal (MSR) task modulates posterior ΔFosB expression. CD-1 mice were prenatally exposed to VPA (500 mg/kg) or vehicle. Brains from postnatal day (PND) 30 mice were analyzed to quantify baseline ΔFosB + cells in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), dorsal striatum (DS), and ventral striatum (VS). In the second experiment, mice performed the MSR task for 13 days. Then, ΔFosB was re-evaluated at PND43 to assess experience-dependent changes. At PND30, VPA-exposed mice showed a significant increase in ΔFosB + cells in mPFC, OFC, DS, and VS, suggesting sustained activity-dependent engagement of the frontostriatal circuit. In the MSR task, mice adapted to contingency shifts using mixed strategies, including win-stay/lose-shift behavior and temporal estimation, whereas VPA mice showed less consistent strategy selection after reversal. After MSR, ΔFosB expression in the OFC and striatum of VPA mice normalized to control levels and remained persistently elevated in the mPFC at PND43. Thus, prenatal VPA induces long-term increases in neuronal transcriptional changes, suggesting activity-dependent plasticity in the frontostriatal circuit. Despite these neural alterations, behavioral flexibility was preserved, suggesting circuit-level adaptations underlying ASD-related strategies. Future studies could broaden these results by examining sex differences and characterizing the cellular and molecular changes dependent on frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics.

best.title: Bioinformatic investigation of convergent proteins and cellular functions downstream of autism-associated genes.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder affects 1 in 31 people yet exhibits remarkable genetic heterogeneity with over 1000 genes identified in autistic populations producing convergent neurobiological phenotypes through not yet understood mechanisms. Here, we employed systems-level network analysis to test if diverse autism risk genes converge onto common cellular vulnerabilities across brain cell types. Using 1238 autism-associated genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) database, we stratified genes by cell-type-specific expression patterns and constructed protein-protein interaction networks to map functional clusters and identify critical connector proteins. Through permutation-based statistical analysis, we identified convergent downstream proteins targets, representing molecular vulnerabilities where multiple autism-associated protein pathways converge for miscoordination of cellular function. Network analysis revealed cell-type-specific vulnerability signatures: SYN1 in inhibitory neurons, GRIN/DLG/CAMK2 proteins in excitatory neurons, GRIA2A/DLG4/GRIN2 in oligodendrocyte precursor cells, ACTL6B in oligodendrocytes, and ARHGAP/DOCK proteins in astrocytes. Remarkably, these computationally predicted targets have been independently validated in human genetics and autism research, demonstrating that network-based convergent vulnerability analysis successfully identifies critical nodes where diverse genetic insults disrupt coordinated cellular responses. This framework provides a molecular basis for understanding autism pathophysiology and identifies promising targets for intervention in the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1-3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this 'female protective effect' (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

best.title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
best.abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

best.title: Cell Type-Specific Assessment of Cholesterol Distribution in Models of Neurodevelopmental Disorders.
best.abstract: Most nervous system disorders manifest through alterations in neuronal signaling based on abnormalities in neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, and cell survival. However, such neuronal phenotypes are frequently accompanied or even caused by metabolic dysfunctions in neuronal or non-neuronal cells. The tight packing and highly heterogeneous properties of neural, glial, and vascular cell types pose significant challenges to dissecting metabolic aspects of brain disorders. Perturbed cholesterol homeostasis has recently emerged as a key parameter associated with subsets of neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration. However, approaches for tracking and visualizing endogenous cholesterol distribution in the brain have limited capability of resolving cell type-specific differences. We here develop tools for genetically encoded sensors that report on accessible cholesterol distribution in the mouse brain with cellular resolution. We apply these probes to examine subcellular cholesterol accumulation in two genetic mouse models of brain disorders, male Ptchd1 knock-out and male and female Npc1 knock-out mice. While both genes encode proteins with sterol-sensing domains that have been implicated in cholesterol transport, we uncover highly selective and cell type-specific phenotypes in cholesterol homeostasis. The tools established in this work should facilitate probing subcellular cholesterol distribution in complex tissues like the mammalian brain and enable capturing cell type-specific alterations in cholesterol flow between cells in models of brain disorders.

best.title: A massively parallel reporter assay of MECP2 cis-regulatory elements reveals genetic candidates for male-biased autism.
best.abstract: Autism affects male individuals four times more often than female individuals, yet the basis of this sex bias remains unclear. One hypothesis is that this sex bias is due to genetic variants in X chromosome genes where haploinsufficiency causes neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). In heterozygous XX female probands, a complete loss-of-function variant in one of these genes often causes syndromic NDD, but the same variant is too deleterious for survival in hemizygous XY males. A mild hypomorphic variant, however, may be tolerated in a female carrier but may produce milder neurological phenotypes in a male proband. We tested this by investigating cis-regulatory elements (CREs) of MECP2, a dosage-sensitive gene on the X chromosome where total loss-of-function variants cause Rett syndrome in female children and severe, usually fatal neonatal encephalopathies in male infants. Using a massively parallel reporter assay in human neurons, we mapped transcription factor binding sites within MECP2 CREs and tested autism-associated variants for functional impact. We identified two noncoding variants that change CRE activity and are associated with male-biased autism phenotypes in the proband pedigrees. One of these, a promoter variant, disrupts NFY binding and reduces MECP2 expression by ∼30%, a magnitude that produces social deficits, hyperactivity, and anxiety-like phenotypes in mice. These findings suggest noncoding MECP2 variants can cause idiopathic, male-biased autism and provide a framework for uncovering regulatory variants in other X chromosome neurodevelopmental genes that may contribute to autism's missing heritability.
