best.title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy.
best.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic Ih current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype-phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8bnano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.

best.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Hypothalamic Hamartoma: Early Developmental Trajectory, Symptom Profile, and Relevance for Autism Research.
best.abstract: Focal brain lesions occurring during critical developmental periods can shed light on the neural substrates underlying autistic symptoms. Hypothalamic hamartomas (HH) are rare congenital malformations that are typically characterized by pharmacoresistant epilepsy, endocrine disturbances, and behavioral or psychiatric disorders. Although autistic symptoms have occasionally been reported in children with HH, they remain poorly described and are rarely documented with standardized diagnostic tools. We present a case report of a 3-year-old boy with HH who was followed from 2 years of age. The report combines detailed early neurodevelopmental history, neuroimaging data, and standardized autism assessments. The child exhibited global developmental delay, early intense sensory features, and marked social communication deficits. The first developmental difficulties preceded the onset of seizures. At 29 months of age, magnetic resonance imaging identified a small intrahypothalamic hamartoma. At 36 months, the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised confirmed the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). A comparison with 3 subjects with ASD matched for sex, chronological age, and developmental age showed that the child presented less severe deficits in sharing enjoyment and less intense unusual preoccupations than age-matched autistic peers. This case highlights the importance of systematic ASD screening in children with HH, allowing timely referral to evidence-based early interventions. Moreover, HH may offer a valuable framework for investigating early neurodevelopmental mechanisms associated with ASD, while highlighting the potential contribution of the hypothalamus to early autism mechanisms.

best.title: Intron Retention Caused by a Novel Homozygous LNPK Splice-Site Variant Leading to Severe Neurodevelopmental Disorder and Epilepsy.
best.abstract: Loss-of-function variants in LNPK have been shown to cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome associated with developmental delay, epilepsy, regression, and a distinct neuroimaging pattern including corpus callosum hypoplasia and abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity at the tip of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricles ("ear-of-the-lynx" sign). To date, 21 affected individuals from 16 families have been reported. Here, we identify a novel homozygous LNPK splice-site variant (NM_030650.3:c.27 + 1G>T) in a patient with developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, epilepsy, and a brain MRI demonstrating corpus callosum hypoplasia, "ear-of-the-lynx" sign, and substantia nigra signal alterations. To determine the variant's pathogenicity, we first used in silico splice prediction models AlphaGenome, SAI-10 k-calc, SpliceAI, and Pangolin. Then, by implementing targeted RNA sequencing of patient-derived fibroblasts following nonsense-mediated decay inhibition, we showed that the variant causes activation of a cryptic donor site, which results in a 5 bp intron retention and introduction of a premature stop codon into the transcript. We also delineate the phenotypic features of the proband with a comprehensive review of the literature. These findings expand the molecular spectrum of LNPK deficiency and demonstrate the complementary value of computational splicing prediction and functional RNA analysis for establishing the consequences of splice-site variants in rare-disease diagnostics.

best.title: Association of Neuronal Cell Adhesion Molecule (NrCAM) Gene with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Indian Cohorts.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is the most complex neurodevelopmental disorder with impairments in communication, social interaction and stereotyped behaviours. ASD has been found to increase immeasurably in India, with estimates ranging from 1 in 68 to 1 in 100 children. Genetically, more than 1,000 genes have been linked with ASD. Among them, the neuronal cell adhesion molecule (NrCAM) gene is one of the candidate genes and is important for its critical role in the development and function of the nervous system, particularly in wiring the brain through axon guidance and organising myelinated nerve structures. Disruptions in this gene are associated with various neurodevelopmental, psychiatric and cancer-related disorders. PURPOSE: The present study aimed to understand the association of the NrCAM gene with ASD. METHODS: Ten exons of the NrCAM gene (one from 5'UTR, five from the immunoglobulin domain, three from the fibronectin domains and one from 3'UTR region) were selected and screened for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) by Sanger sequencing. RESULTS: The results revealed four SNPs from coding and untranslated regions (rs2072546, rs401433, rs1269634 and rs449077) of the NrCAM gene which were analysed for association by linkage disequilibrium analysis. CONCLUSION: The present study clearly suggests that these SNPs of the NrCAM gene are associated with ASD.

best.title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome.
best.abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. best.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
best.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

best.title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
best.abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.

best.title: Integrating clinical diagnostics with interventional genetics for neurodevelopmental disorders.
best.abstract: Interventional genetics (IG) refers to the development of therapies aimed at treating the underlying genetic cause of disease. Diagnostic sequencing has advanced to the point where genetic results can be returned within weeks, meaning that therapeutically actionable variants associated with specific diseases could be developed immediately after diagnosis. Here, we describe 81 probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and family matched controls with full genotype/phenotype information and biobanked stem cells, most of which are consented for sharing. We outline a rapid and scalable pipeline for induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation directly from clinical collection, without the need for peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) storage, paired with induction to neurons. We provide a proof of principle for rapid creation of oligonucleotide therapeutics for Kleefstra syndrome. This work introduces a cohort of individuals with NDDs and an implemental pipeline to integrate IG with clinical diagnostics for NDDs. This information documents our experience and provides useful details for clinical centers interested in integrating IG for NDDs with diagnostic sequencing.

best.title: Genomic landscape of rare variants in a Chinese autism cohort and discovery of novel risk genes.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a genetically complex neurodevelopmental condition with a high heritability. However, genomic studies of ASD have been underrepresented in East Asian populations, and the molecular yield in ASD cohorts remains modest. Here, we present a whole-genome sequencing analysis of 3109 samples across 1033 Chinese ASD families. By examining a wide spectrum of genetic variation, we identified rare ASD-associated variants in 19.2% of affected individuals, providing a population-specific view of the genetic architecture of ASD. We identify significant enrichment of de novo variants in probands, nominate or strengthen candidate risk genes (e.g., NCL, SPPL3, ADGRB1, SLC9A3, KIF1B) through mutational burden, evolutionary constraint, recurrent missense site, and functional assays, and implicate convergent pathways including protein palmitoylation. By integrating over 40,000 ASD cases across unpublished and published global cohorts, we identify 245 ASD risk genes, including 45 with limited prior evidence and 32 with no prior association. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the developing human cortex reveals that ASD risk genes exhibit widespread yet heterogeneous expression across all major cell types, with peak expression in excitatory neurons, particularly intratelencephalic neurons, and enriched expression in microglia (e.g., C1QC, CARD11, SNX13, MEF2C, FOXP2, TCF12, MED13L), suggesting convergent involvement of both synaptic and neuroimmune mechanisms. Together, our findings expand the ASD genetic landscape and suggest convergent pathogenic axes involving transcriptional regulation, synaptic signaling and plasticity, and neuroimmune interactions. This work supports the development of inclusive diagnostic strategies and provides a foundation for mechanistic and intervention exploration in ASD.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

best.title: Effects of Lovastatin on Autism-Like Behavioral, Metabolic, and Neuroinflammatory Alterations in Male BTBR T+ Tf/J Mice.
best.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, thereby reducing cellular cholesterol and isoprenoid biosynthesis. In addition to lowering serum cholesterol, statins exert pleiotropic neuroprotective effects, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory actions mediated through the mevalonate pathway. Statins are increasingly being explored for drug repurposing in neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of lovastatin in the BTBR T+ tf/J mouse model of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a well-established idiopathic model exhibiting core behavioral deficits and dysregulated cholesterol homeostasis characterized by elevated serum cholesterol and reduced brain cholesterol, consistent with reports of altered cholesterol metabolism in ASD. METHODS: BTBR mice received lovastatin (10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, i.p. for 21 days) and were assessed for repetitive behaviour, cognitive performance and social interaction. Cholesterol-related markers, HMG-CoA reductase levels and neuroinflammatory markers were also examined. RESULTS: BTBR mice exhibited increased marble-burying behaviour, reduced spontaneous alternation and social interaction, elevated HMG-CoA reductase levels, decreased brain free cholesterol, increased serum cholesterol, and heightened brain levels of TNF-α and IL-6 compared with C57BL/6J controls. Lovastatin was associated with improvements across the evaluated autism related behavioral outcomes. The 40 mg/kg dose of Lovastatin showed the largest observed behavioral effects overall. Following 21 days of treatment, lovastatin reduced brain HMG-CoA reductase levels at all tested doses and reduced elevated serum cholesterol levels. Exploratory neuroinflammatory analyses showed that lovastatin at 40 mg/kg significantly lowered brain TNF-α and IL-6 levels in BTBR mice. CONCLUSION: Lovastatin was associated with improvements in autism related behavioral outcomes in male BTBR mice, while modulating systemic cholesterol dysregulation and neuroinflammatory responses. These findings provide preclinical evidence supporting further investigation of lovastatin in ASD-related phenotypes.

best.title: Monoallelic variants in BRSK1 are associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without epilepsy.
best.abstract: Brain-specific serine/threonine kinase (BRSK1; synapses of amphids defective [SAD]-B) encodes an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-related serine/threonine kinase required for neuronal polarization and synaptic function. An individual with a variant in BRSK1 was identified in the Texome Project, which provides genomic diagnosis to financially disadvantaged individuals in Texas, using AI-MARRVEL. We subsequently found nine individuals harboring rare heterozygous BRSK1 variants through GeneMatcher. Affected individuals present with developmental delay and variable phenotypes including anxiety, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism, and seizures. All variants (missense and nonsense) are predicted to be deleterious by pathogenicity prediction tools. We utilized Drosophila to model three missense variants to assess the impact of the variants in vivo. We show that Drosophila sff (sugar-free frosting; ortholog of BRSK1) is expressed in neurons of the larval central nervous system (CNS) and adult brain. Loss of sff leads to viable flies with severe locomotor impairment, bang and heat sensitivity, and a short lifespan. In addition, the third-instar neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) in sff null mutants display a significant overgrowth, associated with elevated levels of Futsch (MAP1B), a microtubule-associated protein. Expression of the human reference BRSK1 cDNA in the sff null mutant rescues the behavioral, NMJ morphology, and Futsch phenotypes, showing that the human gene is functional in flies. In contrast, the three individual-derived alleles (BRSK1p.Ile202Val, BRSK1p.Arg237Cys, and BRSK1p.Thr406Ile) provide only a partial rescue and fail to normalize NMJ morphology and Futsch levels, suggesting that they are partial loss-of-function alleles. In summary, our data support a model that heterozygous loss of BRSK1 leads to a neurodevelopmental syndrome with variable phenotypes.

best.title: Disruption of GAD1 protein architecture by a novel missense variant in a consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intellectual disability represents a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders marked by significant impairments in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior. Among the various causes, genetic factors play a major role, with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID) constituting a genetically diverse subgroup. ARID is prevalent in consanguineous families and arises from homozygous mutations that disrupt critical genes involved in brain development and function. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify disease-causing genetic variants responsible for ARID in a consanguineous Pakistani family and to evaluate the structural and functional impact of a novel variant identified in GAD1 through protein modeling. METHODS: A consanguineous family affected with intellectual disability was enrolled. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on an affected individual, followed by bioinformatics analysis including alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome, variant calling, and annotation. Variants were filtered based on rarity, predicted functional impact, and autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Candidate variants were validated and assessed by Sanger sequencing and segregation analysis. Protein modeling was performed to evaluate the structural impact of the identified variant. RESULTS: A novel homozygous missense variant NM_000817:c.1700G>A;p.Arg567Gln in GAD1 was identified. Segregation analysis confirmed co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype. Protein modeling suggested that the variant may disrupt GAD1 enzymatic function involved in gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis. CONCLUSION: This study emphasizes the significance of genetic investigation in familial cases and the crucial role that GAD1 mutations play in neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability. The results advance the knowledge of molecular causes of ARID and broaden the mutational range.

best.title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

best.title: Critical advances and translational bottlenecks of gut microbiota-gut-brain axis targeted therapy for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders.
best.abstract: Neurological diseases have become a major global public health burden. Existing central nervous system-targeted therapies can only alleviate clinical symptoms but fail to halt the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, presenting mechanistic limitations and therapeutic bottlenecks. The gut microbiota participates in the regulation of central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis and neuropathological processes via the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA). Notably, dysbiosis may induce damage to the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and immune imbalance, thereby mediating the onset and progression of various neurological diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease (AD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and multiple sclerosis (MS). This article provides a systematic review of the core mechanisms by which the gut microbiome regulates neurological diseases, including inflammation regulation, oxidative stress responses, and neuroendocrine remodeling mediated by microbial metabolites. It also comprehensively summarizes the research progress, application advantages, and existing limitations of novel gut-targeted interventions, such as probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), dietary interventions, and live biological therapies. At the same time, the article critically examines key bottlenecks prevalent in the field: the causal relationship between the microbiota and disease remains unclear; there is a significant translational gap between animal and human studies; there is a lack of unified standards for multi-omics analysis systems; and interference from confounding factors such as age, diet, and medications is significant. Existing research indicates that gut microbiota interventions complement traditional symptomatic treatments and hold promising prospects for early disease intervention and adjunctive therapy for refractory patients. Future efforts should integrate multi-omics and artificial intelligence technologies to decipher the causal networks governing gut-central nervous system regulation, establish standardized research frameworks, advance the clinical translation of precision gut microbiota therapies, and provide new approaches for the comprehensive prevention, control, and personalized treatment of neurological disorders.

best.title: Disrupted neuronal expression of autism risk genes and white matter micro-organization after infant Zika infection.
best.abstract: Congenital and early-life Zika virus (ZIKV) infection can result in neurologic deficits. Precise mechanisms of injury, especially in the more subtle presentation of postnatal infection, are not fully elucidated. Here, we defined the effects of ZIKV on the developing brain using single-cell transcriptomics, histopathology, design-based stereology, diffusion MRI, and neurobehavioral assessments in infant rhesus macaques. ZIKV upregulated interferon-stimulated genes in activated microglia and cell death pathways in neurons and downregulated metabolism and differentiation genes in mature oligodendrocytes. Abnormal micro-organization of the corpus callosum and limbic white matter tracts was seen on diffusion-weighted imaging. A curated gene set associated with autism spectrum disorder risk was negatively enriched in inhibitory and excitatory neurons from ZIKV-infected infants, with increased emotional reactivity already evident 2 weeks after infection. From single cells to organism-level behaviors, these results define the pathways and processes disrupted by early-life ZIKV infection.

best.title: Differential frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics and behavioral flexibility in autism like VPA-exposed mice.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social impairments, repetitive behaviors, and behavioral inflexibility, defined as an inability to adapt behavior to changing contingencies, and is linked to frontostriatal dysfunction. How behavioral training modulates these circuits is unclear, but ΔFosB, a marker of sustained neural activity, may be useful to establish their relationship. The aim was to evaluate frontostriatal ΔFosB expression following prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) and to determine how experience in the midsession reversal (MSR) task modulates posterior ΔFosB expression. CD-1 mice were prenatally exposed to VPA (500 mg/kg) or vehicle. Brains from postnatal day (PND) 30 mice were analyzed to quantify baseline ΔFosB + cells in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), dorsal striatum (DS), and ventral striatum (VS). In the second experiment, mice performed the MSR task for 13 days. Then, ΔFosB was re-evaluated at PND43 to assess experience-dependent changes. At PND30, VPA-exposed mice showed a significant increase in ΔFosB + cells in mPFC, OFC, DS, and VS, suggesting sustained activity-dependent engagement of the frontostriatal circuit. In the MSR task, mice adapted to contingency shifts using mixed strategies, including win-stay/lose-shift behavior and temporal estimation, whereas VPA mice showed less consistent strategy selection after reversal. After MSR, ΔFosB expression in the OFC and striatum of VPA mice normalized to control levels and remained persistently elevated in the mPFC at PND43. Thus, prenatal VPA induces long-term increases in neuronal transcriptional changes, suggesting activity-dependent plasticity in the frontostriatal circuit. Despite these neural alterations, behavioral flexibility was preserved, suggesting circuit-level adaptations underlying ASD-related strategies. Future studies could broaden these results by examining sex differences and characterizing the cellular and molecular changes dependent on frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics.

primary.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
primary.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

primary.title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
primary.abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

primary.title: A Cilia-Centered Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+) Signaling Network Regulates Hypothalamic Lysosomal Homeostasis and Metabolic Aging.
primary.abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolite that regulates diverse cellular metabolic processes. Primary cilia, hair-like organelles on the cell surface, function as critical signaling hubs. Here, we demonstrate that cellular NAD+ levels are key regulators of both primary cilia growth and lysosomal function in hypothalamic neurons. NAD+ depletion induces ciliary shortening and diminishes lysosomal activity in a cilia-dependent manner. Mechanistically, the lysosomal repair complex protein CHMP4B translocates from periciliary satellites to lysosomes during lysosomal stress, a process impaired by ciliary dysgenesis. Disrupted lysosomal recruitment of CHMP4B leads to abnormal lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and lysosomal dysfunction. Aged mice with hypothalamic NAD+ deficiency exhibit shortened cilia and lysosomal stress phenotypes, both of which are restored by calorie restriction (CR). Moreover, CR improves aging-associated metabolic dysfunction, at least in part, through hypothalamic cilia-dependent mechanisms. These findings identify a primary cilium-mediated-NAD+ signaling axis that maintains lysosomal homeostasis in hypothalamic neurons, the disruption of which drives metabolic aging.

primary.title: The VPS33B-VPS16B protein complex facilitates Golgi ribbon formation and Golgi-endosome trafficking.
primary.abstract: Loss of expression of VIPAS39/VPS16B or the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) family protein VPS33B causes early lethal ARC syndrome in humans. These proteins have been shown to form a complex containing 2 opposed VPS33B molecules known as VPS33B-VPS16B. ARC patient-derived fibroblasts have dispersed Golgi elements and absence of ribbons, an abnormality also observed in VPS16B-knockout HEK293 cells. These observations indicate that VPS33B-VPS16B is involved in Golgi formation/stability. Immunofluorescence microscopy studies showed colocalization of VPS33B-VPS16B with several Golgi-associated proteins, and co-immunoprecipitation studies indicated interactions involving the Golgi tethering factor GRASP55/GORASP2. Interactions were also detected involving VPS33B-VPS16B and VPS51 and VPS53, components of the Golgi-associated retrograde protein (GARP) and endosome-associated recycling protein (EARP) complexes. Abnormalities were observed in retrograde trafficking of mannose-6-phosphate receptors, and of cathepsin B between Golgi and endosomes in VPS33B-VPS16B deficient cells, along with abnormally large late endosomes/lysosomes. These observations suggest that VPS33B-VPS16B has previously unreported roles in key aspects of Golgi apparatus formation/stability, Golgi-endosome trafficking, and perhaps lysosome dynamics.

primary.title: Lysosomal multi-omics reveals altered sphingolipid catabolism associated with lysosomal dysfunction in the aging brain.
primary.abstract: Lipids dynamically reside in multiple intracellular locations, and their organellar distribution is important for function. During brain aging, lysosomal lipid changes have been noted, but lipid identity, interactions, and functional relevance have not been characterized. We used mass spectrometry to assess longitudinal changes in the lipidome and proteome of lysosomal fractions from the murine cortex, from 3 to 24 months, followed by multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) to identify factors underlying lysosomal aging. Our data uncover an age-dependent increase in lysosomal abundance of lipid and protein myelin components and suggest altered sphingolipid catabolism favoring degradation of sphingomyelins over glycosphingolipids. We experimentally corroborate MOFA predictions to demonstrate that age-dependent accumulation of myelin-derived glycosphingolipids is associated with lysosomal enlargement and dysfunction and is most pronounced in microglia. Our findings suggest that age-related lysosomal lipidome changes resemble those observed in lysosomal storage diseases and underscore the importance of organelle-specific analyses for elucidating lipid function.

primary.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
primary.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

primary.title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
primary.abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

primary.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
primary.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR hyperactivity is implicated in early pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is associated with impaired autophagy. We recently uncovered a mechanism linking RYR activity to lysosome availability for autophagy. RYRs localize to ER-lysosome contact sites via direct binding to ATP6V0A1, a V-ATPase subunit that also suppresses RYR-mediated Ca2+ release. In human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, spontaneous RYR activity promotes lysosomal secretion, depleting the intracellular lysosomal pool and inhibiting autophagic flux. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. In this Punctum, we discuss how this RYR2:ATP6V0A1 "contact-site hub" may be perturbed in disease and highlight open questions on how lysosomes decode RYR-derived Ca2+ signals.

primary.title: Isozyme-Specific Inhibition of GSK-3 Reveals Distinct Cellular Responses in Huntington's Disease Fibroblasts.
primary.abstract: Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) has been implicated in alleviating Huntington's disease (HD)-associated phenotypes. However, the mechanisms linking GSK-3 to HD pathogenesis, and particularly the distinct roles of GSK-3 isozymes in regulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cellular responses of patient-derived HD fibroblasts to selective inhibition of GSK-3α or GSK-3β using isozyme-specific inhibitors, focusing on metabolic and bioenergetic pathways. Although inhibition of either isozyme suppressed mTORC1 signaling, selective GSK-3β inhibition elicited broader cellular responses, including altered oxidative stress signaling, increased expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fission, enhanced lysosomal activity, and mitophagy, together with lysosomal redistribution and increased α-tubulin acetylation, suggesting improved microtubule-dependent intracellular trafficking. Quantitative proteomic analysis of four independent patient-derived HD fibroblasts corroborated these findings: GSK-3β inhibition elicited a broad set of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion signaling, and metabolic adaptation, whereas GSK-3α inhibition produced a more restricted and heterogeneous response. Collectively, these findings identify distinct cellular responses to selective GSK-3 isozyme inhibition and reveal GSK-3β as a predominant regulator of intracellular trafficking and mitochondrial and cytoskeletal dynamics in HD fibroblasts. Thus, inhibition of GSK-3β may represent a potential therapeutic approach for modulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction.

primary.title: Autolysosomal enhancer GHF201 attenuates pathophysiology in a mucopolysaccharidosis type I mouse model.
primary.abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS-I) is a hereditary lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency in the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase (IDUA) leading to pathogenic over-accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major constituent of connective tissue and mediators of cell signaling. We tested the therapeutic efficacy of the autolysosomal activator GHF201 in the Idua -/- mouse model of MPS-I. We show that GHF201 reduced GAGs and increased cathepsin activity in Idua -/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and brain cells. In vivo GHF201 improved aberrant locomotion and behavior, reduced interstitial cathepsins in joints and liver, increased systemic catabolism, corrected bone dysplasia, increased autophagic flux, and ameliorated CNS neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation. GHF201 also reduced brain N-glycans, which are degraded in lysosomes. In conclusion, the lysosomal and autophagic activator GHF201 was demonstrated to improve various pathophysiological parameters in MPS-I-modeling Idua -/- female mice. Our results suggest that GHF201 can complement the inadequate Aldurazyme enzyme replacement therapy as an add-on therapy.

primary.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

primary.title: Early reduction of myelin-associated glycoprotein at myelin membranes in Huntington's disease.
primary.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is marked by progressive neuronal loss and atrophy of grey matter structures, particularly the caudate and putamen. Brain imaging studies reveal that the white matter starts to decay in the brain of individuals bearing the HD mutation many years before symptomatic onset. However, the mechanism by which the HD mutation causes white matter loss remains to be further defined. In this study, we examined white matter pathology and explored the underlying mechanism in the HDQ140 knock-in mouse model of HD. Western blot analysis of proteins localized at different layers of the myelin sheath showed that myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), which is localized at the innermost myelin layer, was decreased earlier than proteins localized at outer layers of the myelin. The loss of MAG occurred at fully myelinated axons and was progressive with age. In postmortem symptomatic human HD brains, the level of MAG as well as other myelin proteins was also decreased. In HD mouse brains, MAG labeling was reduced at fiber bundles but accumulated in perinuclear structures of cells that expressed breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1, a marker for new oligodendrocytes. While their abundance was normal, new oligodendrocytes in HD brains were impeded in acquiring the expression of MAG. Compared with those in wild-type mouse brains, oligodendrocytes in HD mouse brains had a reduced frequency of MAG-bearing small vesicles and an increased abundance and enlargement of MAG-containing perinuclear structures. Further studies suggest that the MAG-accumulating perinuclear structures were derived from the late endosomal lysosomal compartment. Our study suggests that white matter decay in HD brains involves an early progressive loss of MAG in myelin membranes.

primary.title: CROP2, a Retriever-PROPPIN complex mediating protein export from endosomes to the plasma membrane in human cells.
primary.abstract: Endosomes generate tubulo-vesicular carriers to redistribute proteins between plasma membrane, Golgi, and lysosomes. These transport routes employ distinct combinations of sorting nexins with complexes such as Retromer or Retriever. We now show that, while Retromer associates with the PROPPIN WIPI1 to form the previously described CROP complex, Retriever associates with WIPI2, forming CROP2. WIPI2 integrates into Retriever-dependent coat complexes since it interacts both with the Commander subunit CCDC93 and its cognate sorting nexin SNX17. CROP and CROP2 are exclusive in their physical associations and pathway selective. Whereas CROP2 is required for endosomal exit of Integrin β1, it does not affect CROP-dependent cargos such as EGFR or GLUT1. Vice versa, CROP is not required for Integrin β1 trafficking. WIPI1 and WIPI2 rely on similar molecular features. Their activity depends on the same FSSS motif to integrate into Retromer and Retriever complexes, respectively, and on an amphipathic membrane-inserting α-helix, which conveys membrane fission activity to PROPPINs. This suggests that Retromer and Retriever coats integrate distinct PROPPIN isoforms to promote fission of the respective endosomal carriers formed by them.

secondary.title: Lipid Droplet-Associated Hsp70 Palmitoylation Drives Lysosomal Dysfunction in Ischemic Stroke.
secondary.abstract: Lipid droplet (LDs) accumulate in glial cells across neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathologies. LDs modulate cellular stress via organelle crosstalk, particularly with lysosomes, whose dysfunction and cathepsin leakage drive glial activation after cerebral ischemia. However, the molecular link between accumulated LDs and lysosomes in pathological glial activation remains incompletely understood. Using a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/Re) cell models, we found that both LD signal intensity and lysosomal cathepsin B leakage progressively increased from day 1 to day 14 after I/R. Etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 A (CPT1A), the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid β-oxidation, aggravated I/R-induced LD accumulation and lysosomal damage in glial cells. Exogenous LDs derived from OGD/Re-treated glial cells aggravated lysosomal damage and promoted the proliferation of astrocytes and microglia. LD accumulation was associated with Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution of Hsp70 from lysosomes to the extracellular space, leading to lysosomal damage and reactive glial activation. Mechanistically, using multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches, including Plin3 knockdown, an Hsp70 palmitoylation‑site mutant, recombinant human Hsp70 (rhHsp70), as well as a pan-palmitoylation inhibitor and TLR2/4 antagonist, we consistently validated that Plin3, an LD surface protein, interacts with lysosomal Hsp70, causing Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, and lysosomal damage. Extracellular Hsp70 activates TLR2/4 on glial cells, promoting cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Collectively, these findings indicate that pathological LDs interacting with lysosomes drive Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, causing lysosomal impairment and astrogliosis in ischemic stroke. We uncover Hsp70 palmitoylation as a potential drug target for ischemic stroke therapy.

secondary.title: Impaired autophagy and lysosome function in human fibroblast aging.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human aging is characterized by a progressive, time-dependent deterioration in physiological and cognitive functioning. Aging is driven by an array of interconnected cellular hallmarks, including genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, telomere attrition, epigenetic alteration and dysfunctional autophagy. Autophagy is a cytoprotective (cellular degradation and recycling) pathway that maintains homeostasis during starvation or stress, and whose activity is associated with extended lifespan. This multi-step process comprises autophagosome formation and maturation, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and cargo degradation. Thus, analysis of autophagy flux is necessary to precisely design therapeutic interventions aimed at restoring autophagy in aging. METHODS: The autophagy flux was comprehensively analyzed in human skin fibroblasts from donors of different ages (20-96 years old), a cell system that retains age-associated cellular and molecular signatures. The subcellular localization and activity of the master transcription factor of autophagy and lysosome biogenesis, TFEB, was analyzed by confocal microscopy assays and transcriptional expression of TFEB target genes (RT-qPCR) respectively. The autophagy flux was evaluated by monitoring the autophagy markers LC3 and p62 by Western blotting and confocal microscopy analyses, using inhibitor drugs to block autophagy or lysosomal activity. Autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion were analyzed by colocalizing LC3 with Sintaxin-17 and LC3 with the lysosomal protein LAMP1 respectively, using inhibitor drugs and confocal microscopy assays. The analysis of lysosomal morphology and function was evaluated by lysobrite dye staining and live-cell confocal microscopy analysis. RESULTS: The initial stages of autophagy, including activation of TFEB, and autophagosome formation, remained apparently functional in fibroblast aging. In contrast, the rate of both autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as well as the lysosomal function appears to be altered in aged fibroblasts. Specifically, enlarged dysfunctional lysosomes were identified as a hallmark of the fibroblasts of the 96-year-old donor. This lysosomal dysfunction may lead to a reduced ability to degrade canonical autophagy markers, LC3-II and p62, and the accumulation of lipofuscin. CONCLUSION: Overall, the results provide evidence that autophagy flux is impaired at the late stages in aged fibroblasts, specifically in autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion steps. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that this failure correlates with the presence of enlarged dysfunctional lysosomes. This study underscores the significance of enhancing lysosomal activity to counteract autophagy decline in aging.

secondary.title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
secondary.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

secondary.title: Paclitaxel-induced disruption of lysosome motility and function in DRG neurons.
secondary.abstract: Lysosomal trafficking and homeostasis are biological functions that are pivotal for DRG neurons, given their metabolic demands and extremely long axons. Previous studies indicate that lysosomal signaling is altered in a mouse model of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) and that blocking mitogen activated protein kinase-associated kinase (MNK1/2) signaling can alleviate pain behaviors in CIPN. Here, we investigated lysosome dynamics and lysosome-associated signaling in a mouse model of CIPN induced by paclitaxel (PTX), a chemotherapeutic agent used for various types of cancer. Using spinning disk super-resolution microscope (SPINSR), we demonstrate that PTX treatment in vivo causes reduced lysosome motility observed in vitro. PTX likewise drives the accumulation of Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1), also known as P62, in cultured mouse DRG neurons, indicating lysosomal dysfunction in DRG neurons. The transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, was also upregulated in the nucleus of cultured mouse DRG neurons treated with PTX. In line with this, increased lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) expression was observed in PTX-treated mice. Given that our previous work demonstrated PTX treatment increases MNK1/2-eIF4E signaling in DRG neurons, we examined whether MNK1/2 inhibition could rescue lysosomal dysfunction. Treatment with Tomivosertib (eFT508), a potent MNK1/2 inhibitor, restored P62 levels in DRG neurons of PTX-treated mice and reduced TFEB in DRG treated in vitro. To establish translation relevance, we further show that PTX elevates phosphorylated eiF4E (p-eIF4E) in human DRG neurons, and concurrent eFT508 administration attenuates this effect. Collectively, these findings indicated that PTX disrupts lysosome trafficking and biogenesis, and that MNK inhibition with eFT508 restores lysosomal signaling and can serve as a neuroprotective strategy for CIPN.

secondary.title: Nano Proton Scavengers Modulate Endosomal pH to Inhibit Microglial Activation and Enhance Stroke Recovery.
secondary.abstract: Endosomes play a crucial role in immune regulation, yet their effect on microglial behavior in ischemic stroke is not well-documented. While drug-loaded nanoparticles can modulate microglial inflammation, their intrinsic biological effects on microglial activation are underexplored. We demonstrate that inhibiting endosomal acidification reduces pro-inflammatory microglial polarization, limits pathological engulfment of neurons, and reduces neuronal apoptosis. To achieve the same effects in vivo, building on a validated dual-site buffering mechanism of sulfonated chitosan, we develop sulfonated Nano Proton Scavengers (sNPS) as a materials-based strategy to modulate endo/lysosomal pH. After cerebral ischemia, sNPS showed greater fluorescence-associated enrichment in the ipsilateral than in the contralateral hemisphere and was associated with brain-resident and infiltrating immune-cell populations. In the injured brain, sNPS alleviated endo/lysosomal acid stress, suppressed TLR3/4-linked inflammatory signaling, and normalized inflammation-driven endo/lysosomal remodeling and proton-loading machinery, thereby restraining maladaptive microglial activation. This immunomodulation was accompanied by improved neural structural preservation and post-stroke survival and functional outcomes. These findings identify endosomal pH homeostasis as a tractable intracellular cue for material-driven immunoregulation and suggest that sNPS offers a complementary therapeutic direction for ischemic stroke.

secondary.title: Aβ-induced CaMKII hyperactivation is associated with impaired lysosomal maturation and mitophagy.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-β (Aβ)-associated synaptic failure, intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation, and progressive impairment of lysosome-dependent clearance pathways. Aβ induces sustained Ca2+ overload, resulting in pathological hyperactivation of CaMKII, which normally participates in the regulation of autophagy. However, whether CaMKII hyperactivation contributes to Aβ-induced late-stage autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction and mitophagy failure remains unclear. This study aimed to examine the effects of the CaMKII inhibitor KN93 in Aβ25-35-exposed rat organotypic hippocampal slice cultures (OHSCs, ex vivo model) and the mouse brain in vivo. The results showed that Aβ25-35 induced intracellular Ca2+ elevation, CaMKII hyperactivation, and marked accumulation of LC3-II and p62. Ultrastructural and biochemical analyses revealed impaired lysosomal maturation, defective autophagosome-lysosome coupling, and accumulation of autophagic vacuoles, consistent with a blockade of late-stage autophagic flux. Increased levels of immature cathepsin D and reduced colocalization of LC3 with lysosomal markers further supported compromised lysosomal competence. Damaged mitochondria were recruited to lysosomal compartments but failed to undergo effective degradation, indicating abortive mitophagy under Aβ25-35 exposure. KN93 attenuated Aβ25-35-induced defects in lysosomal protease maturation, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and mitochondrial clearance in both the ex vivo OHSCs model and the in vivo mouse brain. KN93 also ameliorated cognitive impairment in Aβ25-35-exposed mice. Taken together, these findings indicate that CaMKII hyperactivation contributes to Aβ25-35-induced autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction and neuronal damage, and that pharmacological inhibition of CaMKII with KN93 restores intracellular degradative capacity and ameliorates cognitive impairment under Aβ stress.

best.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
best.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. best.title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
best.abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

best.title: A Cilia-Centered Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+) Signaling Network Regulates Hypothalamic Lysosomal Homeostasis and Metabolic Aging.
best.abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolite that regulates diverse cellular metabolic processes. Primary cilia, hair-like organelles on the cell surface, function as critical signaling hubs. Here, we demonstrate that cellular NAD+ levels are key regulators of both primary cilia growth and lysosomal function in hypothalamic neurons. NAD+ depletion induces ciliary shortening and diminishes lysosomal activity in a cilia-dependent manner. Mechanistically, the lysosomal repair complex protein CHMP4B translocates from periciliary satellites to lysosomes during lysosomal stress, a process impaired by ciliary dysgenesis. Disrupted lysosomal recruitment of CHMP4B leads to abnormal lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and lysosomal dysfunction. Aged mice with hypothalamic NAD+ deficiency exhibit shortened cilia and lysosomal stress phenotypes, both of which are restored by calorie restriction (CR). Moreover, CR improves aging-associated metabolic dysfunction, at least in part, through hypothalamic cilia-dependent mechanisms. These findings identify a primary cilium-mediated-NAD+ signaling axis that maintains lysosomal homeostasis in hypothalamic neurons, the disruption of which drives metabolic aging.

best.title: The VPS33B-VPS16B protein complex facilitates Golgi ribbon formation and Golgi-endosome trafficking.
best.abstract: Loss of expression of VIPAS39/VPS16B or the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) family protein VPS33B causes early lethal ARC syndrome in humans. These proteins have been shown to form a complex containing 2 opposed VPS33B molecules known as VPS33B-VPS16B. ARC patient-derived fibroblasts have dispersed Golgi elements and absence of ribbons, an abnormality also observed in VPS16B-knockout HEK293 cells. These observations indicate that VPS33B-VPS16B is involved in Golgi formation/stability. Immunofluorescence microscopy studies showed colocalization of VPS33B-VPS16B with several Golgi-associated proteins, and co-immunoprecipitation studies indicated interactions involving the Golgi tethering factor GRASP55/GORASP2. These observations suggest that VPS33B-VPS16B has previously unreported roles in key aspects of Golgi apparatus formation/stability, Golgi-endosome trafficking, and perhaps lysosome dynamics.

best.title: Lysosomal multi-omics reveals altered sphingolipid catabolism associated with lysosomal dysfunction in the aging brain.
best.abstract: Lipids dynamically reside in multiple intracellular locations, and their organellar distribution is important for function. During brain aging, lysosomal lipid changes have been noted, but lipid identity, interactions, and functional relevance have not been characterized. We used mass spectrometry to assess longitudinal changes in the lipidome and proteome of lysosomal fractions from the murine cortex, from 3 to 24 months, followed by multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) to identify factors underlying lysosomal aging. Our data uncover an age-dependent increase in lysosomal abundance of lipid and protein myelin components and suggest altered sphingolipid catabolism favoring degradation of sphingomyelins over glycosphingolipids. We experimentally corroborate MOFA predictions to demonstrate that age-dependent accumulation of myelin-derived glycosphingolipids is associated with lysosomal enlargement and dysfunction and is most pronounced in microglia. Our findings suggest that age-related lysosomal lipidome changes resemble those observed in lysosomal storage diseases and underscore the importance of organelle-specific analyses for elucidating lipid function.

best.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
best.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

best.title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
best.abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

best.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
best.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR hyperactivity is implicated in early pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is associated with impaired autophagy. We recently uncovered a mechanism linking RYR activity to lysosome availability for autophagy. RYRs localize to ER-lysosome contact sites via direct binding to ATP6V0A1, a V-ATPase subunit that also suppresses RYR-mediated Ca2+ release. In human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, spontaneous RYR activity promotes lysosomal secretion, depleting the intracellular lysosomal pool and inhibiting autophagic flux. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. In this Punctum, we discuss how this RYR2:ATP6V0A1 "contact-site hub" may be perturbed in disease and highlight open questions on how lysosomes decode RYR-derived Ca2+ signals.

best.title: Isozyme-Specific Inhibition of GSK-3 Reveals Distinct Cellular Responses in Huntington's Disease Fibroblasts.
best.abstract: Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) has been implicated in alleviating Huntington's disease (HD)-associated phenotypes. However, the mechanisms linking GSK-3 to HD pathogenesis, and particularly the distinct roles of GSK-3 isozymes in regulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cellular responses of patient-derived HD fibroblasts to selective inhibition of GSK-3α or GSK-3β using isozyme-specific inhibitors, focusing on metabolic and bioenergetic pathways. Although inhibition of either isozyme suppressed mTORC1 signaling, selective GSK-3β inhibition elicited broader cellular responses, including altered oxidative stress signaling, increased expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fission, enhanced lysosomal activity, and mitophagy, together with lysosomal redistribution and increased α-tubulin acetylation, suggesting improved microtubule-dependent intracellular trafficking. Quantitative proteomic analysis of four independent patient-derived HD fibroblasts corroborated these findings: GSK-3β inhibition elicited a broad set of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion signaling, and metabolic adaptation, whereas GSK-3α inhibition produced a more restricted and heterogeneous response. Collectively, these findings identify distinct cellular responses to selective GSK-3 isozyme inhibition and reveal GSK-3β as a predominant regulator of intracellular trafficking and mitochondrial and cytoskeletal dynamics in HD fibroblasts. Thus, inhibition of GSK-3β may represent a potential therapeutic approach for modulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction.

best.title: Lipid Droplet-Associated Hsp70 Palmitoylation Drives Lysosomal Dysfunction in Ischemic Stroke.
best.abstract: Lipid droplet (LDs) accumulate in glial cells across neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathologies. LDs modulate cellular stress via organelle crosstalk, particularly with lysosomes, whose dysfunction and cathepsin leakage drive glial activation after cerebral ischemia. However, the molecular link between accumulated LDs and lysosomes in pathological glial activation remains incompletely understood. Using a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/Re) cell models, we found that both LD signal intensity and lysosomal cathepsin B leakage progressively increased from day 1 to day 14 after I/R. Etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 A (CPT1A), the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid β-oxidation, aggravated I/R-induced LD accumulation and lysosomal damage in glial cells. Exogenous LDs derived from OGD/Re-treated glial cells aggravated lysosomal damage and promoted the proliferation of astrocytes and microglia. LD accumulation was associated with Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution of Hsp70 from lysosomes to the extracellular space, leading to lysosomal damage and reactive glial activation. Mechanistically, using multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches, including Plin3 knockdown, an Hsp70 palmitoylation‑site mutant, recombinant human Hsp70 (rhHsp70), as well as a pan-palmitoylation inhibitor and TLR2/4 antagonist, we consistently validated that Plin3, an LD surface protein, interacts with lysosomal Hsp70, causing Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, and lysosomal damage. Extracellular Hsp70 activates TLR2/4 on glial cells, promoting cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Collectively, these findings indicate that pathological LDs interacting with lysosomes drive Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, causing lysosomal impairment and astrogliosis in ischemic stroke. We uncover Hsp70 palmitoylation as a potential drug target for ischemic stroke therapy.

best.title: Impaired autophagy and lysosome function in human fibroblast aging.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human aging is characterized by a progressive, time-dependent deterioration in physiological and cognitive functioning. Aging is driven by an array of interconnected cellular hallmarks, including genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, telomere attrition, epigenetic alteration and dysfunctional autophagy. Autophagy is a cytoprotective (cellular degradation and recycling) pathway that maintains homeostasis during starvation or stress, and whose activity is associated with extended lifespan. This multi-step process comprises autophagosome formation and maturation, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and cargo degradation. Thus, analysis of autophagy flux is necessary to precisely design therapeutic interventions aimed at restoring autophagy in aging. METHODS: The autophagy flux was comprehensively analyzed in human skin fibroblasts from donors of different ages (20-96 years old), a cell system that retains age-associated cellular and molecular signatures. The subcellular localization and activity of the master transcription factor of autophagy and lysosome biogenesis, TFEB, was analyzed by confocal microscopy assays and transcriptional expression of TFEB target genes (RT-qPCR) respectively. The autophagy flux was evaluated by monitoring the autophagy markers LC3 and p62 by Western blotting and confocal microscopy analyses, using inhibitor drugs to block autophagy or lysosomal activity. Autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion were analyzed by colocalizing LC3 with Sintaxin-17 and LC3 with the lysosomal protein LAMP1 respectively, using inhibitor drugs and confocal microscopy assays. The analysis of lysosomal morphology and function was evaluated by lysobrite dye staining and live-cell confocal microscopy analysis. RESULTS: The initial stages of autophagy, including activation of TFEB, and autophagosome formation, remained apparently functional in fibroblast aging. In contrast, the rate of both autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as well as the lysosomal function appears to be altered in aged fibroblasts. Specifically, enlarged dysfunctional lysosomes were identified as a hallmark of the fibroblasts of the 96-year-old donor. This lysosomal dysfunction may lead to a reduced ability to degrade canonical autophagy markers, LC3-II and p62, and the accumulation of lipofuscin. CONCLUSION: Overall, the results provide evidence that autophagy flux is impaired at the late stages in aged fibroblasts, specifically in autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion steps. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that this failure correlates with the presence of enlarged dysfunctional lysosomes. This study underscores the significance of enhancing lysosomal activity to counteract autophagy decline in aging.

best.title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
best.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.
