best.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
best.abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

best.title: EGR1 mediates neuronal damage via suppressing HIF1A-induced mitophagy following traumatic brain injury.
best.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of neurological morbidity and mortality, characterized by complex pathophysiological cascades. Here, we investigate the role of the transcription factor EGR1 (early growth response 1) in modulating mitochondrial homeostasis via the HIF1A (hypoxia inducible factor 1, alpha subunit)-BNIP3 (BCL2/adenovirus E1B interacting protein 3) axis following TBI. Using integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses, we identified EGR1 as a critical regulator of TBI pathology, with its expression acutely upregulated in neurons post-injury. Genetic ablation of Egr1 in mice significantly reduced neuronal apoptosis, preserved dendritic integrity, and ameliorated cognitive and sensorimotor deficits. Mechanistically, chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase assays revealed that EGR1 directly binds to the Hif1a promoter, repressing its transcription. Loss of EGR1 enhanced HIF1A-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy, reducing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress both in vitro and in vivo. Conversely, silencing HIF1A or BNIP3 abrogated the neuroprotective effects of EGR1 deficiency. best.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
best.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.

primary.title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
primary.abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

primary.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
primary.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. primary.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
primary.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. To identify the netrin-1 vesicle population, co-localization analyses demonstrated that netrin-1 puncta overlap with the dense-core vesicle marker Chromogranin A. Netrin-1-mRFP and Chromogranin A-eGFP also undergo co-transport within the axon. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

primary.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

primary.title: Integrating clinical diagnostics with interventional genetics for neurodevelopmental disorders.
primary.abstract: Interventional genetics (IG) refers to the development of therapies aimed at treating the underlying genetic cause of disease. Diagnostic sequencing has advanced to the point where genetic results can be returned within weeks, meaning that therapeutically actionable variants associated with specific diseases could be developed immediately after diagnosis. Here, we describe 81 probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and family matched controls with full genotype/phenotype information and biobanked stem cells, most of which are consented for sharing. We outline a rapid and scalable pipeline for induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation directly from clinical collection, without the need for peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) storage, paired with induction to neurons. We provide a proof of principle for rapid creation of oligonucleotide therapeutics for Kleefstra syndrome. This work introduces a cohort of individuals with NDDs and an implemental pipeline to integrate IG with clinical diagnostics for NDDs. This information documents our experience and provides useful details for clinical centers interested in integrating IG for NDDs with diagnostic sequencing.

primary.title: Time-dependent effects of rapid-acting antidepressants in iPSC-derived neurons from treatment-resistant depression and healthy volunteers.
primary.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics show promise for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their therapeutic effects remain unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer a platform to model human cortical neurons and investigate drug effects in a human-relevant system. Here, iPSCs from individuals with TRD and healthy volunteers (HVs) were differentiated into mature cortical-like neurons and treated for six and 24 h with agents being investigated as rapid-acting antidepressants, including (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine (HNK), psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI). Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing assessed global and cell-type-specific transcriptomic responses. Synaptic proteins were evaluated via Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To validate translational relevance, transcriptomic results were compared to CSF proteomics from ketamine-treated HVs. Despite differing initial pharmacological targets, overall gene expression across all compounds was highly correlated at matched timepoints compared to vehicle control, suggesting shared downstream effects. Both glutamatergic and serotonergic drugs converged on pathways involving inflammation, mTORC1 signaling, and cellular growth. At the single-cell level, (2 R,6 R)-HNK showed distinct cell-type specific alterations: upregulation in excitatory neurons and concomitant downregulation of inhibitory neuron populations. Differentially expressed genes from (2 R,6 R)-HNK-treated neurons also overlapped with CSF proteomic signatures from ketamine-treated individuals, supporting the model's translational relevance. This study is the first to assess multiple putative rapid-acting antidepressants in parallel using an iPSC-derived neuron model. Both convergent and drug-specific changes in gene expression and pathway enrichment were observed across diverse compounds, supporting the use of human iPSC-derived neurons in antidepressant drug discovery. primary.title: Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics.
primary.abstract: Despite distinct receptor targets, both ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics produce a rapid clinical response and share biological signatures that suggest convergence on common downstream molecular mediators. To identify shared biomarkers of rapid antidepressant response, this study integrated CSF proteomics from healthy volunteers (HVs) who received intravenous ketamine with transcriptomic analyses from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from participants with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and HVs; iPSCs were treated with ketamine, its metabolite (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), or psilocybin. Multimodal clinical characterization (transcriptomics (n = 16 TRD; 11 HV), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (n = 30 TRD; 25 HV), and plasma cytokines (n = 39 TRD; 25 HV) were also performed on TRD and HV participants who received a single dose of intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo. Conserved immune pathways were identified across CSF and iPSC neurons with interleukin-15 (IL)-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) emerging as key regulatory hubs. Transcriptomically, in whole blood, ketamine responders exhibited decreased IL-15 and elevated B-cell signaling pathways at baseline that were reversed post-treatment. At the protein level, plasma IL-7 levels (primary B-cell driver) correlated with baseline MEG gamma power, reaching brain-wide significance across all participants (main effect pFDR < 0.05). The association was most pronounced in the TRD participants across subcortical regions (diagnosis x IL-7 pFDR < 10-14). Post-ketamine, the TRD IL-7-gamma relationship inverted, paralleling widespread gamma power reductions throughout default-mode network regions (session x IL-7 pclc < 0.05). In mixed-effects models, cytokine ratios linked to IL-7/IL-15 signaling predicted antidepressant response (IL-4/interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pFDR < 0.041) and non-response (MCP-1/IL-7 pFDR < 0.009), suggesting that rebalancing within the IL-7/IL-15 axis may contribute to therapeutic efficacy. secondary.title: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical neurons from monozygotic twins with the Gαo1 K278del mutation reveal disease mechanisms relevant to GNAO1-related encephalopathy.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Rare de novo variants in GNAO1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a heterogenous display of early onset epilepsy, movement abnormalities, and global developmental delay. More than 100 pathogenic variants in GNAO1 have been identified and categorized into four groups according to their protein features. Most pathogenic variants affect both GNAO1 isoforms, whereas approximately 20% of patients have a GNAO1A-specific variant. Response to therapy is notoriously variable, even among patients harboring the same variant. Here, we set out to model GNAO1A-related encephalopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from monozygotic twins carrying the Gαo1 K278del variant and uncovered-while taking advantage of the identical genomic setting-phenotypic features that further our understanding of the defects underlying the disorder. METHODS: We generated hiPSCs expressing the c.832_834delAAG; p.K278del variant in GNAO1A obtained from monozygotic twins who both developed seizures 2 days after birth. For either twin, Gαo1 K278del and CRISPR-Cas9-repaired isogenic control hiPSC lines were differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and subsequently into cortical neurons. Variant-specific transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological characteristics were analyzed. RESULTS: Gαo1 K278del mutated hiPSC-derived NPCs showed disorganized neural rosette structures and revealed an altered transcriptome. In cortical neurons, the Gαo1 K278del variant caused a reduction in the size and complexity of dendrites that was accompanied by an increase in pre- and postsynaptic puncta. Multielectrode array (MEA) recordings revealed an abnormal cortical neuron bursting activity pattern with fewer bursts and more spikes per burst. The antiepileptic drug levetiracetam reduced the spike frequency and the number of spikes per burst in cortical neurons from both patients. SIGNIFICANCE: The developed GNAO1A hiPSC-derived in vitro model uncovered key structural and functional features of GNAO1-related encephalopathy. The comparable in vitro phenotypes in neurons from both twins underscore the utility of hiPSC-derived models to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying GNAO1-related encephalopathy as well as effects of therapeutic intervention.

secondary.title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome.
secondary.abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. While SHANK3 is critical for synapses, its role in early human neurodevelopment remains elusive. Here, we generated induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived 2D neuronal cultures and 3D cerebral organoids from two twin Phelan-McDermid syndrome patients with a 1.7 Mb 22q13 deletion encompassing SHANK3 gene. PMDS organoids showed reduced volume due to impaired neural progenitor cells (NPCs) proliferation. PMDS NPCs exhibited biased differentiation with decreased excitatory neurons but increased GFAP+ astroglia and GABAergic neurons. PMDS neurons displayed simplified morphology, reduced synapse density and diminished excitability. Importantly, lentiviral-mediated SHANK3 overexpression largely rescued these defects. Our findings identify SHANK3 as a key regulator of early neurodevelopment and provide mechanistic insights into PMDS pathogenesis.

secondary.title: Base editing rescues a hereditary motor neuron disease in mouse and patient-derived iPSC organoid models.
secondary.abstract: In hereditary motor neuron diseases (MNDs), including forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) caused by single-nucleotide variants, effective therapeutic strategies need to address both gain- and loss-of-function mechanisms. Genome editing-based gene therapy represents a promising approach for simultaneously targeting these mechanisms. To establish proof-of-concept for base editing in a hereditary MND, we targeted the P285L variant in the TRK-fused gene (TFG), which causes hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with proximal dominant involvement (HMSN-P), a disorder that shares clinical and histopathological features with ALS. We identified the optimal adenine base editor by comparing candidate editors in HMSN-P patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We then generated a transgenic mouse model expressing human TFG P285L and evaluated the selected editor by subpial delivery of adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors to the spinal cord. AAV-mediated base editing prolonged survival, preserved motor neurons, and attenuated axon loss in ventral nerve roots. Treatment with the selected base editing vector reduced TFG aggregation and suppressed neuronal death in HMSN-P iPSC-derived neuromuscular organoids. Collectively, these findings support the therapeutic potential of base editing for hereditary MNDs.

secondary.title: High-resolution genomic architecture of a 1.71-Mb inverted SNCA triplication in a patient-derived PARK4 model.
secondary.abstract: PARK4, caused by SNCA locus multiplications, is a severe, early-onset form of autosomal dominant parkinsonism. However, the precise structural topography of these massive genomic rearrangements remains inadequately resolved. In this study, we resolved the nucleotide-level architecture of a novel 1.71-Mb PARK4 triplication lineage (PARK4-4) and elucidated its early-stage biochemical consequences in a patient-derived cortical model. By integrating Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing, we mapped a complex 1.71-Mb inverted triplication spanning the HERC6 to CCSER1 loci. This rearrangement is organized in a Forward-Inverted-Forward (F-I-F) architecture, punctuated by precisely defined Head-to-Head (H2H) and Tail-to-Tail (T2T) junctions. Using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) differentiated into forebrain cortical neurons, targeted RT-qPCR and automated capillary western blotting demonstrated SNCA gene-dosage-associated α-synuclein overexpression, with a robust ∼2.3-fold increase. Furthermore, exploratory transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) revealed candidate synchronized upregulation of co-triplicated neighboring genes (PIGY, FAM13A, and TIGD2), supporting a regional gene-dosage effect. To our knowledge, this is the first structural characterization of a 1.71-Mb F-I-F inverted SNCA triplication at nucleotide resolution, revealing a complex architecture distinct from previously reported tandem triplications. While future isogenic and functional studies are required to establish mature disease-relevant pathology, this precisely mapped model provides an invaluable platform for studying dosage-dependent early biochemical phenotypes and evaluating targeted therapeutics.

best.title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
best.abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

best.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
best.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

best.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
best.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. To identify the netrin-1 vesicle population, co-localization analyses demonstrated that netrin-1 puncta overlap with the dense-core vesicle marker Chromogranin A. Netrin-1-mRFP and Chromogranin A-eGFP also undergo co-transport within the axon. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

best.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

best.title: Integrating clinical diagnostics with interventional genetics for neurodevelopmental disorders.
best.abstract: Interventional genetics (IG) refers to the development of therapies aimed at treating the underlying genetic cause of disease. Diagnostic sequencing has advanced to the point where genetic results can be returned within weeks, meaning that therapeutically actionable variants associated with specific diseases could be developed immediately after diagnosis. Here, we describe 81 probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and family matched controls with full genotype/phenotype information and biobanked stem cells, most of which are consented for sharing. We outline a rapid and scalable pipeline for induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation directly from clinical collection, without the need for peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) storage, paired with induction to neurons. We provide a proof of principle for rapid creation of oligonucleotide therapeutics for Kleefstra syndrome. This work introduces a cohort of individuals with NDDs and an implemental pipeline to integrate IG with clinical diagnostics for NDDs. This information documents our experience and provides useful details for clinical centers interested in integrating IG for NDDs with diagnostic sequencing.

best.title: Time-dependent effects of rapid-acting antidepressants in iPSC-derived neurons from treatment-resistant depression and healthy volunteers.
best.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics show promise for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their therapeutic effects remain unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer a platform to model human cortical neurons and investigate drug effects in a human-relevant system. Here, iPSCs from individuals with TRD and healthy volunteers (HVs) were differentiated into mature cortical-like neurons and treated for six and 24 h with agents being investigated as rapid-acting antidepressants, including (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine (HNK), psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI). Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing assessed global and cell-type-specific transcriptomic responses. Synaptic proteins were evaluated via Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To validate translational relevance, transcriptomic results were compared to CSF proteomics from ketamine-treated HVs. Despite differing initial pharmacological targets, overall gene expression across all compounds was highly correlated at matched timepoints compared to vehicle control, suggesting shared downstream effects. Both glutamatergic and serotonergic drugs converged on pathways involving inflammation, mTORC1 signaling, and cellular growth. At the single-cell level, (2 R,6 R)-HNK showed distinct cell-type specific alterations: upregulation in excitatory neurons and concomitant downregulation of inhibitory neuron populations. Differentially expressed genes from (2 R,6 R)-HNK-treated neurons also overlapped with CSF proteomic signatures from ketamine-treated individuals, supporting the model's translational relevance. This study is the first to assess multiple putative rapid-acting antidepressants in parallel using an iPSC-derived neuron model. Both convergent and drug-specific changes in gene expression and pathway enrichment were observed across diverse compounds, supporting the use of human iPSC-derived neurons in antidepressant drug discovery. best.title: High-resolution genomic architecture of a 1.71-Mb inverted SNCA triplication in a patient-derived PARK4 model.
best.abstract: PARK4, caused by SNCA locus multiplications, is a severe, early-onset form of autosomal dominant parkinsonism. However, the precise structural topography of these massive genomic rearrangements remains inadequately resolved. In this study, we resolved the nucleotide-level architecture of a novel 1.71-Mb PARK4 triplication lineage (PARK4-4) and elucidated its early-stage biochemical consequences in a patient-derived cortical model. By integrating Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing, we mapped a complex 1.71-Mb inverted triplication spanning the HERC6 to CCSER1 loci. This rearrangement is organized in a Forward-Inverted-Forward (F-I-F) architecture, punctuated by precisely defined Head-to-Head (H2H) and Tail-to-Tail (T2T) junctions. Using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) differentiated into forebrain cortical neurons, targeted RT-qPCR and automated capillary western blotting demonstrated SNCA gene-dosage-associated α-synuclein overexpression, with a robust ∼2.3-fold increase. Furthermore, exploratory transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) revealed candidate synchronized upregulation of co-triplicated neighboring genes (PIGY, FAM13A, and TIGD2), supporting a regional gene-dosage effect. To our knowledge, this is the first structural characterization of a 1.71-Mb F-I-F inverted SNCA triplication at nucleotide resolution, revealing a complex architecture distinct from previously reported tandem triplications. While future isogenic and functional studies are required to establish mature disease-relevant pathology, this precisely mapped model provides an invaluable platform for studying dosage-dependent early biochemical phenotypes and evaluating targeted therapeutics.

best.title: Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics.
best.abstract: Despite distinct receptor targets, both ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics produce a rapid clinical response and share biological signatures that suggest convergence on common downstream molecular mediators. To identify shared biomarkers of rapid antidepressant response, this study integrated CSF proteomics from healthy volunteers (HVs) who received intravenous ketamine with transcriptomic analyses from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from participants with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and HVs; iPSCs were treated with ketamine, its metabolite (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), or psilocybin. Multimodal clinical characterization (transcriptomics (n = 16 TRD; 11 HV), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (n = 30 TRD; 25 HV), and plasma cytokines (n = 39 TRD; 25 HV) were also performed on TRD and HV participants who received a single dose of intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo. Conserved immune pathways were identified across CSF and iPSC neurons with interleukin-15 (IL)-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) emerging as key regulatory hubs. Transcriptomically, in whole blood, ketamine responders exhibited decreased IL-15 and elevated B-cell signaling pathways at baseline that were reversed post-treatment. At the protein level, plasma IL-7 levels (primary B-cell driver) correlated with baseline MEG gamma power, reaching brain-wide significance across all participants (main effect pFDR < 0.05). The association was most pronounced in the TRD participants across subcortical regions (diagnosis x IL-7 pFDR < 10-14). Post-ketamine, the TRD IL-7-gamma relationship inverted, paralleling widespread gamma power reductions throughout default-mode network regions (session x IL-7 pclc < 0.05). In mixed-effects models, cytokine ratios linked to IL-7/IL-15 signaling predicted antidepressant response (IL-4/interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pFDR < 0.041) and non-response (MCP-1/IL-7 pFDR < 0.009), suggesting that rebalancing within the IL-7/IL-15 axis may contribute to therapeutic efficacy. primary.title: Integrated Multi-omics Reveals Molecular Signatures of Rett Syndrome, Informing Future Biomarker Discovery.
primary.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. Despite numerous clinical trials being conducted, there are limited disease-modifying options available for individuals with RTT. This paucity of effective treatments can in part be attributed to the lack of clinically useful biomarkers that can objectively assess treatment response. Moreover, diagnosis of RTT continues to be clinical, when clinical manifestations are apparent, precluding early therapeutic approaches. Thus, clinical biomarkers of disease stage could improve diagnosis and enable real-time monitoring of response to treatment, providing the earliest possible indications of therapeutic efficacy. Given MeCP2's role as a key regulator of gene transcription, we used an untargeted omics approach to evaluate transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolic profiles in blood from individuals with RTT (n = 9) and age- and sex-matched controls (n = 8). In addition to characterising differential expression at each omic layer, to understand the shared biology and coordinated molecular signals across all omic datasets, we used the unsupervised machine learning framework Multi-Omics Factor Analysis version 2 (MOFA2). The individual omic data consisted of a robust upregulation of genes involved in ribosomal structure and translation together with a downregulation in vesicle trafficking genes. An upregulation in ribosomal machinery and mitochondrial function together with a concomitant downregulation of critical epigenetic regulators, immune-signalling molecules, and cytoskeletal structural anchors was observed in the proteomics, which was supported by the phosphoproteomics. Notably, plasma metabolomics pointed towards alterations in energy substrates and lipid/cholesterol handling, suggesting systemic downstream consequences of primary intracellular disturbances. The integrated MOFA2 data supported the individual omic data revealing a central disease axis principally shaped by the proteome and transcriptome and supported by the metabolome and phosphoproteome, identifying potential biomarkers, including latent biological processes that distinguish RTT from controls (Latent Factor 1) and correlates of clinical severity (Latent Factor 2). Overall, our data reveal a distinctive 'disease state' molecular signature that distinguishes individuals with RTT from controls, where the findings in RTT blood cells are consistent with previously reported altered translational and mitochondrial function and disrupted chromatin regulation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and metabolic signalling. Our integrated multi-omics analyses revealed that PBMC's LTN1, ATRX, CHD8, SPTB, DMTN, PRF1, CD40LG, and PTPRCAP and plasma glutamate are the most promising disease-state (complementary diagnostic) candidate biomarkers while sphingomyelin, RTN3, and MMP1 appear to be the most suitable biomarkers of disease severity. Here, we demonstrate that blood from individuals with RTT reflects the molecular systemic consequences of MeCP2 dysfunction.

primary.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1-3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this 'female protective effect' (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

primary.title: Spatial transcriptomics maps region and isoform specific brain alterations in mdx and mdx4cv models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
primary.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is accompanied by cognitive and neurodevelopmental difficulties. To investigate how the loss of different dystrophin isoforms affects gene expression across brain regions, we performed spatial transcriptomics on brains from mdx and mdx4cv mouse models (lacking Dp427 or Dp427 + Dp140 respectively) and healthy controls aged 2 weeks. Both dystrophic models showed transcriptional changes converging on myelin and oligodendrocyte biology and oxidative phosphorylation, but with distinct regional patterns. In mdx mice, myelin genes were upregulated in the amygdala and hippocampus and downregulated in fiber tract regions, while mitochondrial genes were upregulated in most regions but downregulated in the thalamus and isocortex. In mdx4cv mice, myelin genes were broadly upregulated and mitochondrial genes downregulated across almost all regions. Direct comparison between mdx and mdx4cv mice demonstrated that the additional loss of Dp140 expanded localized myelin upregulation across the brain and shifts the mitochondrial response toward widespread downregulation. These differences in regional changes between the mouse models is in line with their dystrophin isoform(s) loss. Our findings provide a molecular basis for the brain-related impairments of DMD and a foundation for future therapeutic studies.

primary.title: Single-cell atlas uncovers layer 4 heterogeneity and functional gradients in rhesus macaque visual cortex.
primary.abstract: Non-human primates like rhesus macaques are pivotal models for decoding human visual cortex physiology and disorders. However, there is a lack of high-resolution transcriptomic atlases comparing distinct areas of the visual cortex in macaque. Here, we developed BrainSPACE, an innovative pipeline for rapid and precise brain tissue banking, to sample visual cortex areas: V1, V2, V4, MT, and TEO. We applied single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) to unravel neuronal diversity in BrainSPACE-banked V1 and V4 areas ( ~ 100,000 nuclei). We uncovered conserved GABAergic neuron profiles but stark area-specific diversity in principal neurons, featuring seven unique layer 4 subtypes in V1 and one in V4. Complementary smFISH validated transcriptional gradients across these areas, aligning with ventral and dorsal stream hierarchies. Gene ontology analyses highlighted plasticity-related pathways in unique layer 4 subtypes, with genes like NTNG1 and NLGN1 linked to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and schizophrenia. Our insights bridge molecular architecture to visual processing, offering an interactive atlas for community use. By revealing how layer 4 heterogeneity drives hierarchical specialization, our work advances primate brain mapping and informs therapeutic strategies for vision-related pathologies.

primary.title: Parkinson's disease-linked D620N mutation selectively alters the brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35.
primary.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

primary.title: Single-cell machine learning uncovers genetically anchored, cell-type specific programs of Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: Univariate differential expression analysis dominates single-cell transcriptomic studies of Alzheimer's disease, yet marginal testing alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure or distinguish clinical from neuropathological signatures. Here we introduce TriSCOPE, a framework integrating multivariate predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression, and pseudotime inference, applied to six Alzheimer's disease snRNA-seq datasets comprising ~4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors. Across six major brain cell types and 41 subclusters, we identify cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that are largely non-overlapping with differentially expressed genes, revealing disease-relevant signals invisible to univariate approaches. Conditional GWAS-eQTL colocalization anchors a subset of these predictively expressed genes to inherited Alzheimer's disease risk loci, including 27 genetically supported gene-cell type pairs (among them ARL17B, JAZF1) with no significant differential expression. Integration across all three analytical branches nominates high-confidence convergent programs including astrocytic stress markers (such as GFAP, MT2A), neuronal signaling genes (like RASGEF1B, LINGO1, NRG1), and microglial and oligodendrocyte regulators (including SYTL3, SPP1, APOD). Comparison of clinical and neuropathological models reveals cell-type-specific divergence between cognitive and pathological Alzheimer's disease signatures. Key predictively expressed genes including ARL17B, LINGO1, and APOE replicate across independent cohorts, with cross-cohort generalizability confirmed across all three analytical branches of TriSCOPE.

primary.title: Lysosomal multi-omics reveals altered sphingolipid catabolism associated with lysosomal dysfunction in the aging brain.
primary.abstract: Lipids dynamically reside in multiple intracellular locations, and their organellar distribution is important for function. During brain aging, lysosomal lipid changes have been noted, but lipid identity, interactions, and functional relevance have not been characterized. We used mass spectrometry to assess longitudinal changes in the lipidome and proteome of lysosomal fractions from the murine cortex, from 3 to 24 months, followed by multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) to identify factors underlying lysosomal aging. Our data uncover an age-dependent increase in lysosomal abundance of lipid and protein myelin components and suggest altered sphingolipid catabolism favoring degradation of sphingomyelins over glycosphingolipids. We experimentally corroborate MOFA predictions to demonstrate that age-dependent accumulation of myelin-derived glycosphingolipids is associated with lysosomal enlargement and dysfunction and is most pronounced in microglia. Our findings suggest that age-related lysosomal lipidome changes resemble those observed in lysosomal storage diseases and underscore the importance of organelle-specific analyses for elucidating lipid function.

primary.title: Single-cell multiome landscape reveals elovanoid-mediated suppression of inflammatory glial states and induction of homeostatic signaling after ischemic stroke.
primary.abstract: Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of death and disability. Administration of the lipid mediators elovanoids (ELVs) is protective in human neuronal-glia cultures and in experimental ischemic stroke. We now report using a single-cell multiome approach that intranasally-delivered (IN) ELV34 or its precursor reduced the loss of neuronal markers and upregulated homeostatic microglia signatures after stroke. Thus, ELV reduces disease-associated microglia (expressing Spp1, Gpnmb, Lgals3, Clec7a) and the expression of neuroinflammatory signaling genes. In astrocytes, ELV decreased reactive astrocytes (expressing Gfap, Vim, Nes, Lcn2) and upregulated genes involved in synaptic organization. Also, ELV reduced abundance of oligodendrocytes and OPCs expressing immune markers. ELV induced a phenotype shift from pro-inflammatory microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs in response to ischemic stroke damage. ELV upregulated gene pathways promoting synaptic integrity, reducing immune cell activation and neuronal loss.

primary.title: Identification of new targets for the protection against radiation-induced brain injury through integrated dual-omics analysis.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a serious complication of cranial radiotherapy, yet its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to identify novel therapeutic targets for RIBI through integrated dual-omics analysis. METHODS: A mouse model of RIBI was established using 15 Gy of whole-brain X-ray irradiation. Behavioral tests and histopathological examinations were performed to validate cognitive dysfunction and neuronal damage. Hippocampal tissues were analyzed via transcriptomics and metabolomics to uncover key molecular changes. RESULTS: Transcriptomic analysis identified 29 significantly differentially expressed genes, including upregulated neuroinflammatory genes (Pcsk9, Ifi213) and downregulated neuroprotective factors (Tlx3, Irx1, Irx5), implicating exacerbated neuroinflammatory responses and impaired neurodevelopmental processes. Metabolomic profiling revealed 63 significantly altered metabolites, including elevated DNA oxidative damage markers and depleted branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction and increased oxidative stress. Integrated analysis highlighted correlations among neuroinflammation, DNA damage, and metabolic dysregulation, pointing to a potential interplay between these pathways. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that RIBI pathogenesis involves synergistic interactions between neuroinflammation, DNA damage, and metabolic dysregulation. Targeting Pcsk9, enhancing DNA repair capacity, or supplementing BCAAs could represent potential neuroprotective strategies, although these correlative findings require functional validation. These findings provide a foundation for future studies on mitigating cognitive decline in patients receiving cranial radiotherapy.

secondary.title: High-Resolution Spatial Proteomics Uncovers Molecular Diversity across Mouse Hippocampal Subregions.
secondary.abstract: The hippocampus (HP) is a structurally and functionally heterogeneous brain region critical for learning, memory, and spatial navigation. Although transcriptomic studies have revealed subregion-specific gene expression patterns, the corresponding high-resolution spatial proteomic landscape remains largely unexplored. Here, we applied a single-voxel proteomics workflow at 50 μm resolution to profile the protein composition of HP subregions, including the dentate gyrus (DG) and Cornu Ammonis fields 1-3 (CA1-CA3). Across the four subregions, we identified over 2,200 protein groups and found both conserved and region-specific proteins. Differential expression and network analyses revealed molecular signatures associated with specific subregions, including synaptic plasticity in CA1, mitochondrial metabolism in CA2, cytoskeletal organization and protein homeostasis in CA3, and excitatory signaling in DG. Integration with transcriptomic data confirmed consistent region-enriched markers at both the gene and protein levels, including Homer1 and Itpka in CA1, Homer3 in CA3, and Calb1/2 in DG. Thus, our data set demonstrates subregion-specific molecular specialization at the proteome level and provides a high-resolution resource to link structural, functional, and metabolic diversity in the hippocampus. Further application of our high-resolution spatial proteomics will lay the foundation for studying HP development, circuit function, and disease-associated proteomic alterations.

secondary.title: An Optimized Stem Cell Secretome Proteomics Platform: Application to Progranulin-Deficient iPSCs.
secondary.abstract: Stem cells secrete diverse extracellular proteins that regulate pluripotency, differentiation, and cell-cell communication, making them powerful model systems for studying development, disease mechanisms, and regenerative medicine. However, robust stem cell secretome analysis remains technically challenging. Unlike many other cell types, pluripotent stem cells cannot tolerate serum starvation or growth factor deprivation, while low-abundance secreted proteins are often masked by media-derived proteins and intracellular contamination. Here, we systematically optimized the secretome proteomics workflow in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by evaluating culture medium composition, conditioned-media collection time, cell plating density, media harvest and preparation methods, LC-MS acquisition methods, and data analysis strategies. Full-strength Essential 8 medium, 48 h media collection, 80% cell confluency, two-step centrifugation, and data-independent acquisition (DIA)LC-MS/MS provided the optimal secretome proteomics data quality. We then applied the optimized platform to an isogenic iPSC disease model to investigate how progranulin deficiency reshapes the extracellular and intracellular proteomes. Progranulin-deficient iPSCs showed a coordinated reduction of extracellular lysosomal hydrolases despite relatively modest intracellular proteome changes, suggesting altered lysosome trafficking and possible impairment of lysosomal exocytosis. Together, this work establishes a robust and standardized workflow for stem cell secretome proteomics and demonstrates its utility for investigating extracellular proteome remodeling in human disease models.

secondary.title: Evaluation of the SPEED Sample Preparation Protocol for Metabolomics.
secondary.abstract: Multiomic (paired proteomic and metabolomic) analyses allow researchers to better decipher the underlying biology being studied. While sample preparation techniques for multiomic analyses exist, they are often automation-unfriendly or secondary to preferred techniques for proteomic analyses. The recently published, popular Sample Preparation by Easy Extraction and Digestion (SPEED) protocol offers a single sample preparation technique for near-universal sample preparation across sample types and is used routinely in many proteomics laboratories; however, this protocol has not previously been investigated as to its suitability for metabolomic analyses. We tested the compatibility of two variations of the SPEED protocol: trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) lysis followed by drying and methanol extraction and TFA lysis and neutralization followed with SP4 cleanup. We compared these protocols with standard metabolomics sample preparation protocols of direct extraction with methanol or ACN and bead-beating in ammonium acetate lysis. The results show that TFA lysis with drying and methanol extraction yielded quantification results that were comparable to or better than those of the other protocols tested. We additionally demonstrated the utility of this technique by performing multiomic analysis of iPSCs before and after differentiation into neurons and identified coordinated dysregulation of metabolites and proteins in key neuronal differentiation pathways. We also observed that ACN extraction performed similarly to the gold standard methanol extraction. Consequently, we conclude that laboratories that already routinely use the SPEED protocol for dedicated proteomics can obtain functional metabolomics samples for little to no additional effort or cost with regard to sample preparation.

secondary.title: Integrated multi-omics identifies PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte state remodeling in paraquat-associated Parkinson's disease.
secondary.abstract: Paraquat (PQ) is an environmentally relevant herbicide associated with neurotoxicity and Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, yet the key molecular determinants linking PQ exposure to PD and the cellular states in which these alterations occur remain incompletely understood. We integrated network toxicology, human PD transcriptomics, machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, virtual perturbation, model-inferred protein analysis, molecular docking, and tissue validation to characterize PQ-associated molecular and cellular remodeling. Integrating PQ-associated targets with PD-related genes identified 293 candidates, among which prostaglandin D2 synthase (PTGDS) was consistently prioritized by random forest, XGBoost, and LASSO, with its PD-associated expression pattern reproduced across the discovery and independent validation cohorts. Single-cell analysis localized Ptgds expression predominantly to oligodendrocytes and identified two PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte (MOL) states with PQ-associated compositional patterns. CytoTRACE placed these PTGDS-enriched populations among relatively mature oligodendrocyte states. Functional analyses revealed distinct state-specific programs, with Ptgds+Mag+ MOL associated with myelin-associated programs, axon ensheathment-related programs, cholesterol metabolism, and lipid transport, whereas Ptgds+Il33+ MOL was linked to neuron-interaction-related programs, synaptic organization, cell adhesion, and neuron-glia communication. Ligand-receptor inference and spatial analyses supported state-specific changes in neuron-glia communication and spatial relationships. Spatial metabolomics showed significantly increased phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin signals in regions with higher inferred representation of Ptgds+Mag+ MOL states. Virtual Ptgds perturbation and scTranslator-based protein prediction further suggested state-specific myelin-lipid and neuron-interaction programs, while molecular docking provided preliminary structural predictions regarding a potential PQ-PTGDS interaction. Immunofluorescence further confirmed PTGDS localization in mature oligodendrocytes within the substantia nigra. Collectively, these findings identify PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte states as cellular contexts associated with PQ-related brain remodeling and extend our understanding of PQ neurotoxicity beyond classical neuron-centered mechanisms. This integrative framework provides mechanistic insight into how an environmental neurotoxicant may reshape myelin-lipid homeostasis and neuron-glia interactions in the context of PD-related brain pathology.

secondary.title: Conditional Mutant MAPT Overexpression in Neural Organoids Elicits Robust Tau Accumulation and Pathological Transcriptomic Responses.
secondary.abstract: Modeling neurodegenerative conditions in neural organoids presents a potential complement to existing preclinical translation pipelines. Prior neural organoid models have generally relied on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines containing disease-relevant alleles. However, this strategy limits temporal control over the initiation and progression of pathological events. In this study, we provide a proof-of-concept framework showing that neurodegenerative phenotypes can be triggered by inducible expression cassettes. We developed an iPSC line harboring doxycycline-inducible mutant MAPT, which encodes the microtubule-associated protein tau that is implicated in tauopathies. Induction of mutant MAPT via doxycycline treatment in differentiating neural organoids yielded accumulation of phosphorylated tau, which localized inside individual neuron somas within the cortical plate-like regions. Importantly, measured transcriptomic responses to tau overexpression bore key similarities to human clinical transcriptomic data. Taken together, we present an approach for controlling the initiation and progression of proteinopathy-like pathology in neural organoid systems.

secondary.title: Brain Region-Specific Peptide and Proteomic Signatures Inform Alzheimer's Disease Biomarker Panels.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder with region- and severity-specific molecular signatures that complicate biomarker discovery. We combined peptide-centric quantitative proteomics data with machine learning, dimensionality reduction, nonlinear modeling, and network enrichment to identify candidate biomarkers across four brain regions and four AD severity stages. Dimensional reduction revealed disease-severity gradients (HCF-low ADNC → HCF-high ADNC → sporadic AD dementia (ADD) → autosomal-dominant AD) that were strongest in cortical regions (SMTG, IPL), moderate in the hippocampus, and weakest in the caudate. Machine-learning-based feature selection improved severity prediction, particularly at the peptide level, yielding panels of 10-22 region- and severity-specific biomarkers. Biomarker interaction modeling identified hubs centered on haptoglobin, VGF, APP, APOE, and midkine family members, partnering within neurosecretory, lipid transport, acute-phase response, and proteostasis pathways. STRING analysis validated these interactions, showing enrichment for secreted, hemoglobin-binding proteins with plasma and bone marrow tissue signals. Although biomarkers were predominantly region-specific, they converged on blood-linked pathways, supporting the translational potential of multi-marker, circulation-accessible panels. These findings show that peptide-level proteomics integrated with machine learning and network analysis clarifies AD heterogeneity and points to therapeutic avenues in neurovascular integrity, lipid transport, acute-phase response, and proteostasis, accelerating AD biomarker development.

secondary.title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

secondary.title: Proteomics analysis of small extracellular vesicles derived from human retinal Müller glial cells under high glucose condition.
secondary.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss and is characterized by early dysfunction of the retinal neurovascular unit (NVU), preceding neurodegenerative and vascular pathology. Müller glial cells are central regulators of retinal homeostasis, but the contribution of Müller glia-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) to intercellular communication during hyperglycemic stress remains incompletely understood. Here, we examined the effects of high-glucose (HG) challenge on sEV release and protein cargo in the immortalized human Müller glial cell line MIO-M1. Cells were exposed to 35 mM D-glucose or an osmotic control. sEVs were isolated from cell culture media and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, transmission electron microscopy, and immunoblotting. Quantitative proteomic profiling was performed using data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry. HG exposure did not significantly change sEV size distribution or particle yield but changed the proteomic profiles of both Müller glia cells and their secreted sEVs. Differentially abundant proteins were enriched in pathways and functional classes related to RNA binding and processing, protein translation, cytoskeletal organization, carbon metabolism, lysosomal function, and immune/inflammatory signaling. These findings provide a new proteomic resource and identify candidate pathways through which HG stress may modify Müller glia cellular and sEV protein profiles. Because the study used an immortalized cell line, a short-term in vitro exposure, and did not directly test the effects of HG-modified sEVs on recipient retinal cells, the functional and in-vivo relevance of these proteomic changes requires further investigation.

secondary.title: Integrated proteomics and network pharmacology reveal autophagy-lysosomal regulation underlying sulforaphane-mediated neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid-β (Aβ)-mediated neurotoxicity, impaired autophagy-lysosomal function, and neuronal apoptosis. Although sulforaphane (SFN) has demonstrated neuroprotective properties, its molecular actions against Aβ-related neuronal injury remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of SFN against Aβ-induced neuronal injury and explored the underlying molecular networks associated with its anti-AD activity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Integrated network pharmacology and proteomics approaches were complemented by experimental validation in retinoic acid-differentiated SH-SY5Y cells exposed to Aβ25-35. Cells were pretreated with SFN, which was withdrawn prior to Aβ exposure. Cell viability, apoptosis-related proteins (BAX/BCL-2), and autophagy-associated markers (LC3B and p62) were evaluated. Data-independent acquisition proteomics was performed to characterize global protein alterations. Target prioritization was conducted through integrated bioinformatics analysis and molecular docking, followed by western blot validation. RESULTS: Network pharmacology identified 331 overlapping targets between SFN and AD, mainly enriched in pathways related to apoptosis, autophagy, and oxidative stress. SFN pretreatment significantly attenuated Aβ-induced cytotoxicity and partially normalized apoptosis- and autophagy-related protein alterations, including reduction of the BAX/BCL-2 ratio, recovery of the LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio, and decrease in p62 accumulation. Integrated proteomic and network pharmacology analyses identified 28 candidate targets, among which CTSB, CTSD, CASP6, and IGF1R were validated by molecular docking and western blotting. CONCLUSION: SFN pretreatment protected against Aβ-induced neuronal injury in this in vitro model and was associated with modulation of autophagy-lysosomal and apoptosis-related pathways. The integration of network pharmacology, proteomics, and experimental validation provides a systems-level framework for understanding the multitarget neuroprotective actions of SFN.

secondary.title: Machine learning-assisted plasma PEA proteomics enables differential diagnosis of melancholic depression and bipolar disorder.
secondary.abstract: Differentiating bipolar disorder (BD) from major depressive disorder (MDD) remains a critical unmet need in psychiatry due to overlapping clinical presentations and the absence of reliable biological markers. In this study, we assessed the capacity of multivariate machine learning models to accurately differentiate BD from MDD with melancholic features using plasma proteomic profiles obtained via Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) technology. A total of 67 participants were included (23 BD, 20 MDD, and 24 HC), and plasma protein expression was assessed using the Olink Target 96 Neurology panel. Differential proteomic analysis revealed distinct disorder-specific expression patterns, identifying 21 differentially expressed proteins in BD versus MDD, 18 in BD versus healthy controls, and 7 in MDD versus healthy controls. Using a stepwise feature reduction strategy, machine learning models were trained on three feature sets comprising all proteins, the top 20 most informative proteins, and the top 5 most beneficial proteins, and evaluated across BD-MDD, BD-HC, and MDD-HC classification tasks using five algorithms. For BD-MDD discrimination, the Random Forest model achieved the highest performance when trained on the top 5 protein set (LXN, HAGH, MATN3, PLXNB1, and CTSC), yielding an AUC of 0.905, with similarly strong performance observed using the top 20 protein set. Feature importance analysis highlighted proteins involved in neurodevelopmental processes, immune regulation, and extracellular matrix organization. Overall, these findings demonstrate that integrating plasma proteomics with machine learning enables robust differentiation between BD and MDD with melancholic features, supporting the development of scalable and biologically informed diagnostic tools for precision psychiatry.

best.title: Integrated Multi-omics Reveals Molecular Signatures of Rett Syndrome, Informing Future Biomarker Discovery.
best.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. Despite numerous clinical trials being conducted, there are limited disease-modifying options available for individuals with RTT. This paucity of effective treatments can in part be attributed to the lack of clinically useful biomarkers that can objectively assess treatment response. Moreover, diagnosis of RTT continues to be clinical, when clinical manifestations are apparent, precluding early therapeutic approaches. Thus, clinical biomarkers of disease stage could improve diagnosis and enable real-time monitoring of response to treatment, providing the earliest possible indications of therapeutic efficacy. Given MeCP2's role as a key regulator of gene transcription, we used an untargeted omics approach to evaluate transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolic profiles in blood from individuals with RTT (n = 9) and age- and sex-matched controls (n = 8). In addition to characterising differential expression at each omic layer, to understand the shared biology and coordinated molecular signals across all omic datasets, we used the unsupervised machine learning framework Multi-Omics Factor Analysis version 2 (MOFA2). The individual omic data consisted of a robust upregulation of genes involved in ribosomal structure and translation together with a downregulation in vesicle trafficking genes. An upregulation in ribosomal machinery and mitochondrial function together with a concomitant downregulation of critical epigenetic regulators, immune-signalling molecules, and cytoskeletal structural anchors was observed in the proteomics, which was supported by the phosphoproteomics. Notably, plasma metabolomics pointed towards alterations in energy substrates and lipid/cholesterol handling, suggesting systemic downstream consequences of primary intracellular disturbances. The integrated MOFA2 data supported the individual omic data revealing a central disease axis principally shaped by the proteome and transcriptome and supported by the metabolome and phosphoproteome, identifying potential biomarkers, including latent biological processes that distinguish RTT from controls (Latent Factor 1) and correlates of clinical severity (Latent Factor 2). Overall, our data reveal a distinctive 'disease state' molecular signature that distinguishes individuals with RTT from controls, where the findings in RTT blood cells are consistent with previously reported altered translational and mitochondrial function and disrupted chromatin regulation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and metabolic signalling. Our integrated multi-omics analyses revealed that PBMC's LTN1, ATRX, CHD8, SPTB, DMTN, PRF1, CD40LG, and PTPRCAP and plasma glutamate are the most promising disease-state (complementary diagnostic) candidate biomarkers while sphingomyelin, RTN3, and MMP1 appear to be the most suitable biomarkers of disease severity. Here, we demonstrate that blood from individuals with RTT reflects the molecular systemic consequences of MeCP2 dysfunction.

best.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1-3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this 'female protective effect' (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

best.title: Spatial transcriptomics maps region and isoform specific brain alterations in mdx and mdx4cv models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
best.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is accompanied by cognitive and neurodevelopmental difficulties. To investigate how the loss of different dystrophin isoforms affects gene expression across brain regions, we performed spatial transcriptomics on brains from mdx and mdx4cv mouse models (lacking Dp427 or Dp427 + Dp140 respectively) and healthy controls aged 2 weeks. Both dystrophic models showed transcriptional changes converging on myelin and oligodendrocyte biology and oxidative phosphorylation, but with distinct regional patterns. In mdx mice, myelin genes were upregulated in the amygdala and hippocampus and downregulated in fiber tract regions, while mitochondrial genes were upregulated in most regions but downregulated in the thalamus and isocortex. In mdx4cv mice, myelin genes were broadly upregulated and mitochondrial genes downregulated across almost all regions. Direct comparison between mdx and mdx4cv mice demonstrated that the additional loss of Dp140 expanded localized myelin upregulation across the brain and shifts the mitochondrial response toward widespread downregulation. These differences in regional changes between the mouse models is in line with their dystrophin isoform(s) loss. Our findings provide a molecular basis for the brain-related impairments of DMD and a foundation for future therapeutic studies.
