best.title: Unsupervised deep learning enables blur-free resolution enhancement in two-photon microscopy.
best.abstract: Two-photon microscopy enables the non-invasive imaging of deep living tissue. Quantitative three-dimensional analysis is hampered by axial blur and anisotropic resolution in two-photon microscopy. We introduce the two-photon microscopy image enhancement network (TENET), a fully unsupervised framework that simultaneously performs deblurring, up to 12× resolution enhancement, and semantic segmentation on two-photon microscopy volumes in a single pass. TENET embeds a physics-informed blur-generation module with a trainable neural implicit point spread function (PSF), requiring only approximate PSF initialization rather than rigorous experimental measurement, paired "unblurred" images, or isotropy assumptions. On synthetic images, fluorescent beads, and in vivo microglia datasets, TENET surpasses the total-variation-regularized Richardson-Lucy (RLTV) algorithm, CARE, and Neuroclear in image fidelity and segmentation accuracy. Using time-lapse images of microglia surrounding metastatic brain tumors, TENET enables automated 3D morphometry that reveals dynamic microglia-tumor interactions. By converting blur-limited two-photon microscopy data into high-fidelity volumetric reconstructions with ready-to-use masks, TENET streamlines downstream analysis and expands the reach of deep-tissue live imaging.

best.title: BasNet: Attention U-Net-Based Automated Axon Segmentation in Bielschowsky Silver-Stained Histology.
best.abstract: Reliable automatic quantification of axon density in histologic sections is important for both research and clinical neuropathology applications - however, it remains a challenge for silver-impregnation stains, such as Bielschowsky. Classical color-deconvolution approaches perform poorly on silver stains, and manual annotation of densely packed axons is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability. We developed an automated axon segmentation pipeline in Bielschowsky silver-stained histological brain sections based on an attention U-Net architecture with attention-gated skip connections, trained using Focal Tversky Loss to handle class imbalance and thin structure recovery. Ground truth was manually annotated on 33 image tiles (covering over 25 million pixels) derived from 26 whole-slide images from varying brain regions of four multiple sclerosis patients. Slides were prepared by different laboratory technicians at different time points to capture realistic staining variability. Model performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of unseen tiles. On the test set (eight held-out tiles) the model achieved a mean pixel-wise F1/Dice of 0.717 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.584. A dedicated inter-rater experiment on two representative tiles yielded rater-to-rater F1 scores of 0.637 and 0.671, while model-to-rater agreement (F1: 0.681-0.736) met or exceeded that human ceiling. Generated whole-slide density and orientation visualizations accurately reflected regional axon distributions and provided quantitative readouts suitable for downstream analysis. Our attention U-Net provides an open-source solution for axon segmentation from Bielschowsky-stained sections, reducing manual effort and enabling reproducible, slide-level quantitative metrics. This tool can facilitate studies of axonal pathology across research and clinical settings.

primary.title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
primary.abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

primary.title: AKT is necessary for neuronal hypertrophy and epilepsy caused by Pten knockout.
primary.abstract: Phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is a key negative regulator of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Mutations in PTEN are highly implicated in autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, congenital hydrocephaly and macrocephaly. While the conditional genetic knockout of Pten in murine neurons results in hypertrophy, increased migration, excitatory synaptogenesis, hyperexcitability and epileptiform activity, the specific downstream signalling mediators of these pathologies remain to be fully elucidated. Using retroviral-mediated genetic manipulation of individual neurons within the Cre-lox recombination system, we have analysed pathway outputs in response to the manipulation of various genes using immunohistochemistry, confocal microscopy and extensive morphological analyses, alongside whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology and 120-h video-EEG monitoring for seizure assessment. Here, we demonstrate that signalling through AKT is necessary for the development of neuronal overgrowth, increased excitatory synapse formation, excessive migration and hyperexcitability fuelled by the loss of PTEN function. Notably, the concurrent deletion of Akt1 and Akt3 isoforms was sufficient to effectively rescue hypertrophic neuronal morphology and physiology. These findings establish AKT as the essential mediator through which PTEN deficiency manifests, providing a transformative therapeutic target to correct the morphological and functional defects central to PTEN-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
primary.abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

primary.title: Avocado Oil Nanoemulsion Ameliorates STZ-Induced Diabetic Brain Dysfunction through PI3K/AKT/mTOR-Related Gene Modulation and Attenuation of Apoptosis.
primary.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is associated with progressive neurological complications characterized by hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress, neuronal apoptosis, and disruption of intracellular survival signaling pathways. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of avocado cold-pressed oil (ACPO) and its nano-formulation against diabetes-induced cerebral alterations in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic rats. Seventy adult male Wistar rats were randomly allocated to ten groups (n = 7/group): normal control (NC), blank nano-formulation vehicle control (BC), metformin control (RC), ACPO control (OC), ACPO nano-formulation control (FC), diabetic positive control (PC), diabetic blank nano-formulation vehicle control (BT), diabetic + metformin (RT; 500 mg/kg), diabetic + ACPO (OT; 500 mg/kg), and diabetic + ACPO nano-formulation (FT; 500 mg/kg). The untreated diabetic group served as the reference for diabetes-associated alterations, whereas the diabetic vehicle-control group was included to account for potential effects of the nano-formulation vehicle. Diabetes was induced by a single intraperitoneal injection of STZ (40 mg/kg). Plasma glucose levels, cerebral gene expression of phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K), protein kinase B (AKT1), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), pannexin-1 (PANX1), and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) were evaluated. Histopathological examination and caspase-3 immunohistochemistry were performed to assess neuronal injury and apoptosis. Treatment with ACPO and its nano-formulation significantly reduced plasma glucose levels and modulated key molecular pathways involved in neuronal survival. Both treatments upregulated PI3K, AKT1, and mTOR expression while downregulating GSK3β, PANX1, and AChE compared with untreated diabetic rats. Histopathological examination demonstrated marked preservation of cerebral cortical architecture, accompanied by reduced caspase-3 immunoexpression, indicating attenuation of neuronal apoptosis. The nano-formulation exerted greater effects on the investigated molecular biomarkers than conventional ACPO and produced histopathological and immunohistochemical improvements comparable to those observed with metformin.

primary.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
primary.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

secondary.title: PDE2A is involved in negative emotional behaviors via the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway in the SPS&S model.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by negative affective symptoms, including anxiety, depression, anhedonia, and fear. The molecular mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain poorly understood. Phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A), a regulator of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling, has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of the PDE2A-cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway in negative emotional behaviors induced by traumatic stress. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways. A rat PTSD model was established using single prolonged stress combined with foot shocks (SPS&S). Behavioral tests were performed, and PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling alterations in the amygdala were examined. The effects of PDE2A inhibitor Hcyb1 and the PKA inhibitor H89 were evaluated. RESULTS: Bioinformatics analysis identified PDE2A as a hub gene associated with PTSD, with significant enrichment of the cAMP signaling pathway. SPS&S rats exhibited anxiety-, depression-like behaviors, and anhedonia, accompanied by increased PDE2A expression and reduced cAMP and phosphorylated PKA (p-PKA) levels in the amygdala. Hcyb1 treatment alleviated behavioral deficits, decreased PDE2A expression, and restored cAMP and p-PKA signaling. H89 blocked p-PKA activation and partially reversed the behavioral benefits of Hcyb1. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that amygdala PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling is associated with negative emotional behaviors in the SPS&S model. PDE2A inhibition may ameliorate behavioral deficits through PKA-related signaling. However, the peripheral blood transcriptomic data, lack of direct PDE2A activity and cAMP/cGMP measurements, and limited biochemical validation constrain mechanistic interpretation. Further studies using brain-derived datasets and comprehensive biochemical approaches are warranted.

secondary.title: Angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) drives human Tenon's capsule fibroblast activation and myofibroblast transformation via the RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway.
secondary.abstract: Although the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) participates in systemic tissue remodeling, its exact contribution to human subconjunctival fibrosis remains poorly understood. This study investigated the expression of AT1R in human clinical scar specimens, the downstream involvement of the RhoA/ROCK pathway, and the independent anti-fibrotic effects of receptor blockade. Primary human Tenon's capsule fibroblasts (HTCFs) were isolated from patient tissue biopsies and verified as a pure mesenchymal lineage using immunofluorescence and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). secondary.title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
secondary.abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

secondary.title: Restoration of mitophagy by crebanine suppresses sevoflurane-induced microglial activation and cognitive deficits by blocking mitochondrial DNA-triggered cGAS-STING pathway.
secondary.abstract: Sevoflurane, a volatile anesthetic in widespread clinical use, is increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of postoperative cognitive dysfunction. Although neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation is a recognized contributor, the upstream mechanisms linking anesthesia to this inflammatory response remain poorly defined. Crebanine, a natural isoquinoline alkaloid with well-known anti-inflammatory properties, remains unexplored for its impact on mitochondrial quality control during anesthetic neurotoxicity. We investigated whether crebanine protects against sevoflurane-induced cognitive deficits by restoring microglial mitophagy and suppressing the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-cGAS-STING pathway. Sevoflurane-exposed BV2 microglial cells and aged rats were employed as in vitro and in vivo models of anesthesia-induced neurotoxicity, respectively. The neuroprotective effects of crebanine were assessed by evaluating cell viability, microglial activation, inflammatory responses, mitophagy, mitochondrial function, hippocampal neuronal morphology, apoptosis, and cognitive deficits. The underlying mechanism was investigated by measuring cytosolic mitochondrial DNA levels and the activation status of the cGAS-STING pathway. In BV2 microglial cells, we found that sevoflurane exposure disrupted mitophagic flux, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive mitochondrial ROS generation, and subsequent leakage of mtDNA into the cytosol. This cytosolic mtDNA triggered the cGAS-STING pathway, driving pro-inflammatory cytokine production and promoting M1-like polarization. Crebanine treatment potently restored mitophagic flux, curtailed mtDNA release, and deactivated the inflammatory cascade, shifting microglia toward an anti-inflammatory M2-like phenotype. Pharmacological inhibition of mitophagy with 3-MA or direct activation of STING using DMXAA completely abolished the protective effects of crebanine, confirming its neuroprotection depends on this specific pathway. In animal experiments, administration of crebanine to aged male Sprague-Dawley rats markedly attenuated sevoflurane-induced hippocampal neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis, ultimately preserving spatial learning and memory function, as assessed by the Morris water maze test. Crebanine exerts its neuroprotective effects by restoring microglial mitophagy, thereby suppressing mtDNA-mediated cGAS-STING signaling and preserving cognitive function. This positions the mitophagy-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis as a viable therapeutic target for managing anesthesia-induced neurocognitive decline.

secondary.title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
secondary.abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.

best.title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
best.abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

best.title: AKT is necessary for neuronal hypertrophy and epilepsy caused by Pten knockout.
best.abstract: Phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is a key negative regulator of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Mutations in PTEN are highly implicated in autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, congenital hydrocephaly and macrocephaly. While the conditional genetic knockout of Pten in murine neurons results in hypertrophy, increased migration, excitatory synaptogenesis, hyperexcitability and epileptiform activity, the specific downstream signalling mediators of these pathologies remain to be fully elucidated. Using retroviral-mediated genetic manipulation of individual neurons within the Cre-lox recombination system, we have analysed pathway outputs in response to the manipulation of various genes using immunohistochemistry, confocal microscopy and extensive morphological analyses, alongside whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology and 120-h video-EEG monitoring for seizure assessment. Here, we demonstrate that signalling through AKT is necessary for the development of neuronal overgrowth, increased excitatory synapse formation, excessive migration and hyperexcitability fuelled by the loss of PTEN function. Notably, the concurrent deletion of Akt1 and Akt3 isoforms was sufficient to effectively rescue hypertrophic neuronal morphology and physiology. These findings establish AKT as the essential mediator through which PTEN deficiency manifests, providing a transformative therapeutic target to correct the morphological and functional defects central to PTEN-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
best.abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

best.title: Avocado Oil Nanoemulsion Ameliorates STZ-Induced Diabetic Brain Dysfunction through PI3K/AKT/mTOR-Related Gene Modulation and Attenuation of Apoptosis.
best.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is associated with progressive neurological complications characterized by hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress, neuronal apoptosis, and disruption of intracellular survival signaling pathways. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of avocado cold-pressed oil (ACPO) and its nano-formulation against diabetes-induced cerebral alterations in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic rats. Seventy adult male Wistar rats were randomly allocated to ten groups (n = 7/group): normal control (NC), blank nano-formulation vehicle control (BC), metformin control (RC), ACPO control (OC), ACPO nano-formulation control (FC), diabetic positive control (PC), diabetic blank nano-formulation vehicle control (BT), diabetic + metformin (RT; 500 mg/kg), diabetic + ACPO (OT; 500 mg/kg), and diabetic + ACPO nano-formulation (FT; 500 mg/kg). The untreated diabetic group served as the reference for diabetes-associated alterations, whereas the diabetic vehicle-control group was included to account for potential effects of the nano-formulation vehicle. Diabetes was induced by a single intraperitoneal injection of STZ (40 mg/kg). Plasma glucose levels, cerebral gene expression of phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K), protein kinase B (AKT1), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), pannexin-1 (PANX1), and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) were evaluated. Histopathological examination and caspase-3 immunohistochemistry were performed to assess neuronal injury and apoptosis. Treatment with ACPO and its nano-formulation significantly reduced plasma glucose levels and modulated key molecular pathways involved in neuronal survival. Both treatments upregulated PI3K, AKT1, and mTOR expression while downregulating GSK3β, PANX1, and AChE compared with untreated diabetic rats. Histopathological examination demonstrated marked preservation of cerebral cortical architecture, accompanied by reduced caspase-3 immunoexpression, indicating attenuation of neuronal apoptosis. The nano-formulation exerted greater effects on the investigated molecular biomarkers than conventional ACPO and produced histopathological and immunohistochemical improvements comparable to those observed with metformin.

best.title: PDE2A is involved in negative emotional behaviors via the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway in the SPS&S model.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by negative affective symptoms, including anxiety, depression, anhedonia, and fear. The molecular mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain poorly understood. Phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A), a regulator of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling, has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of the PDE2A-cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway in negative emotional behaviors induced by traumatic stress. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways. A rat PTSD model was established using single prolonged stress combined with foot shocks (SPS&S). Behavioral tests were performed, and PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling alterations in the amygdala were examined. The effects of PDE2A inhibitor Hcyb1 and the PKA inhibitor H89 were evaluated. RESULTS: Bioinformatics analysis identified PDE2A as a hub gene associated with PTSD, with significant enrichment of the cAMP signaling pathway. SPS&S rats exhibited anxiety-, depression-like behaviors, and anhedonia, accompanied by increased PDE2A expression and reduced cAMP and phosphorylated PKA (p-PKA) levels in the amygdala. Hcyb1 treatment alleviated behavioral deficits, decreased PDE2A expression, and restored cAMP and p-PKA signaling. H89 blocked p-PKA activation and partially reversed the behavioral benefits of Hcyb1. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that amygdala PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling is associated with negative emotional behaviors in the SPS&S model. PDE2A inhibition may ameliorate behavioral deficits through PKA-related signaling. However, the peripheral blood transcriptomic data, lack of direct PDE2A activity and cAMP/cGMP measurements, and limited biochemical validation constrain mechanistic interpretation. Further studies using brain-derived datasets and comprehensive biochemical approaches are warranted.

best.abstract: Sevoflurane, a volatile anesthetic in widespread clinical use, is increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of postoperative cognitive dysfunction. Although neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation is a recognized contributor, the upstream mechanisms linking anesthesia to this inflammatory response remain poorly defined. Crebanine, a natural isoquinoline alkaloid with well-known anti-inflammatory properties, remains unexplored for its impact on mitochondrial quality control during anesthetic neurotoxicity. We investigated whether crebanine protects against sevoflurane-induced cognitive deficits by restoring microglial mitophagy and suppressing the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-cGAS-STING pathway. Sevoflurane-exposed BV2 microglial cells and aged rats were employed as in vitro and in vivo models of anesthesia-induced neurotoxicity, respectively. The neuroprotective effects of crebanine were assessed by evaluating cell viability, microglial activation, inflammatory responses, mitophagy, mitochondrial function, hippocampal neuronal morphology, apoptosis, and cognitive deficits. The underlying mechanism was investigated by measuring cytosolic mitochondrial DNA levels and the activation status of the cGAS-STING pathway. In BV2 microglial cells, we found that sevoflurane exposure disrupted mitophagic flux, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive mitochondrial ROS generation, and subsequent leakage of mtDNA into the cytosol. This cytosolic mtDNA triggered the cGAS-STING pathway, driving pro-inflammatory cytokine production and promoting M1-like polarization. Crebanine treatment potently restored mitophagic flux, curtailed mtDNA release, and deactivated the inflammatory cascade, shifting microglia toward an anti-inflammatory M2-like phenotype. Pharmacological inhibition of mitophagy with 3-MA or direct activation of STING using DMXAA completely abolished the protective effects of crebanine, confirming its neuroprotection depends on this specific pathway. In animal experiments, administration of crebanine to aged male Sprague-Dawley rats markedly attenuated sevoflurane-induced hippocampal neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis, ultimately preserving spatial learning and memory function, as assessed by the Morris water maze test. Crebanine exerts its neuroprotective effects by restoring microglial mitophagy, thereby suppressing mtDNA-mediated cGAS-STING signaling and preserving cognitive function. This positions the mitophagy-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis as a viable therapeutic target for managing anesthesia-induced neurocognitive decline.

best.title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
best.abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.

best.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
best.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

primary.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
primary.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

primary.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
primary.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

primary.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
primary.abstract: Recent work by Mao and colleagues identifies a distinct class of small extracellular vesicles, termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs), generated from amphisomes upon autophagy induction. In this commentary, we discuss how this study provides important mechanistic insight into the coupling between autophagy and secretion. AEVs are molecularly and functionally distinct from canonical exosomes, being enriched in autophagy-related components such as LC3 and p62, and dependent on core ATG machinery for their biogenesis. Notably, their secretion is enhanced by autophagy induction and contributes to intercellular communication, particularly in the context of viral infection. These findings position amphisomes as critical sorting hubs that direct cargo toward either degradation or secretion, thereby integrating autophagic and endolysosomal pathways. We further highlight how these results intersect with prior evidence implicating SNARE-dependent mechanisms, including VAMP7 and stress-responsive regulators such as GRASP55, in unconventional secretion. Finally, we discuss key unresolved questions, particularly the mechanisms underlying the generation of small intraluminal vesicles within amphisomes and the role of ESCRT machinery in this process. Overall, the identification of AEVs adds a new layer of complexity to extracellular vesicle biology and opens new avenues for understanding how autophagy contributes to intercellular signaling in health and disease.

primary.title: Recessive variants in ESCRT-II component VPS25 alter vesicular transport and small extracellular vesicle processing in lethal neonatal encephalopathy.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. METHODS: We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. RESULTS: The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25, one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. CONCLUSIONS: We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25. The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Glycoprotein-induced phase separation drives unconventional secretion of galectin-3.
primary.abstract: The mechanism of unconventional protein secretion remains an unresolved issue. Here, we describe an unconventional protein secretion pathway for galectin-3 that is mediated by phase separation and condensation. Using four lysosomal damage models, we observed a rapid, pronounced release of galectin-3 in large, non-exosomal particles. This secretion is driven by glycoprotein-induced galectin-3 phase separation and is independent of pyroptosis and secretory autophagy. During phase separation, the S-face of galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain binds glycoproteins that triggers galectin-3 N-terminal tail release and condensation. These condensates then recruit ALG-2 via the exposed N-terminal tail. ALG-2 directs the condensates to the endoplasmic reticulum-late endosome interface. After translocation into late endosomes, galectin-3 condensates are secreted into the extracellular milieu by SNARE-dependent vesicular transport. This mechanism of exporting phase-separated protein condensates may serve as a clean-up response to membrane damage.

primary.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

primary.title: GPNMB is a biomarker for lysosomal dysfunction and is secreted via LRRK2-modulated lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have identified Glycoprotein Nmb (GPNMB) as a risk factor for Parkinson's disease. The risk allele increases GPNMB transcription and GPNMB protein levels in the CSF highlighting GPMNB as a potential biomarker for Parkinson's disease. However, a lack of knowledge of GPNMB's function and mechanism of secretion has hindered an interpretation of secreted GPNMB levels. In this study, we assessed the mechanism of GPNMB secretion by macrophages, the primary cell type expressing GPNMB in the brain. We show that GPNMB is secreted in response to lysosomal stress via lysosomal exocytosis and highlight the Parkinson's disease risk factor LRRK2 as a strong modulator of GPNMB secretion.

primary.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
primary.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR hyperactivity is implicated in early pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is associated with impaired autophagy. We recently uncovered a mechanism linking RYR activity to lysosome availability for autophagy. RYRs localize to ER-lysosome contact sites via direct binding to ATP6V0A1, a V-ATPase subunit that also suppresses RYR-mediated Ca2+ release. In human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, spontaneous RYR activity promotes lysosomal secretion, depleting the intracellular lysosomal pool and inhibiting autophagic flux. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. In this Punctum, we discuss how this RYR2:ATP6V0A1 "contact-site hub" may be perturbed in disease and highlight open questions on how lysosomes decode RYR-derived Ca2+ signals.

primary.title: Autophagic extracellular vesicles: a distinct secretory route linking autophagy to extracellular communication.
primary.abstract: Macroautophagy/autophagy is classically defined as a degradative pathway that delivers cytoplasmic material to lysosomes. However, accumulating evidence indicates that autophagy can also support unconventional secretion. A recent study identifies a previously unrecognized subtype of small extracellular vesicles termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs). These vesicles originate from amphisomes formed by the fusion of autophagosomes with multivesicular bodies and are characterized by a size below 100 nm together with the presence of autophagic cargos, ESCRT-III components and RAB13. Importantly, biogenesis of AEVs is distinct from that of classical exosomes, which requires specific components of the ESCRT III complex and the GTPase RAB27A. The further finding that enterovirus can exploit AEVs to infect receptor-negative cells, thereby expanding viral tropism, suggests that secretory autophagy serves as a pivotal mechanism driving pathogen dissemination. This work provides the conceptual framework of extracellular vesicle heterogeneity and positions secretory autophagy as an important contributor to intercellular communication.

primary.title: MYO18B promotes lysosomal exocytosis by facilitating focal adhesion maturation.
primary.abstract: Many cancer cells exhibit increased amounts of paucimannose glycans, which are truncated N-glycan structures rarely found in mammals. Paucimannosidic proteins are proposedly generated within lysosomes and exposed on the cell surface through a yet uncertain mechanism. In this study, we revealed that paucimannosidic proteins are produced by lysosomal glycosidases and secreted via lysosomal exocytosis. Interestingly, lysosomal exocytosis preferentially occurred in the vicinity of focal adhesions, protein complexes connecting the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Through genome-wide knockout screening, we identified that MYO18B, an actin crosslinker, is required for focal adhesion maturation, facilitating lysosomal exocytosis and the release of paucimannosidic lysosomal proteins to the extracellular milieu. Moreover, a mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 locally activated at focal adhesions imports Ca2+ necessary for lysosome-plasma membrane fusion. Collectively, our study unveiled an intimate relationship between lysosomal exocytosis and focal adhesion, shedding light on the unexpected interplay between lysosomal activities and cellular mechanosensing.

primary.title: Molecular mechanisms underlying p62-dependent secretion of the Alzheimer-associated ubiquitin variant UBB+1.
primary.abstract: UBB+1, a ubiquitin variant protein resulting from a frameshift in the ubiquitin-B gene, is a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD). At the cellular level, UBB+1 disrupts the ubiquitin-proteasome system while inducing autophagy. Notably, UBB+1 itself is secreted via autophagosome-like vesicles. Here, we demonstrate that UBB+1 can be removed from the cell by degradative and secretory autophagy. Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1)/p62 functions as a pivotal ubiquitin receptor for UBB+1, recognizing its ubiquitin domain and facilitating loading into autophagosomes. Oligomerization of SQSTM1/p62 was critical to isolate UBB+1 in bodies preventing its aggregation. Intriguingly, both gain- and loss-of-function SQSTM1/p62 suppressed UBB+1 secretion, causing intracellular retention: SQSTM1/p62 knockout led to UBB+1 accumulation in insoluble aggregates, while its overexpression promoted the formation of p62-UBB+1 bodies. We further identified distinct roles for SNARE-mediated membrane fusion in secretory autophagy of UBB+1. Specifically, the R-SNARE SEC22B and the Q-SNAREs Syntaxin-4 and SNAP23 participated in UBB+1 exocytosis. Disruption of SEC22B impaired the fusion of UBB+1-containing autophagosomes with the plasma membrane, reducing UBB+1 secretion without affecting its intracellular turnover. Inhibition of lysosomes partially stabilized UBB+1 indicating that degradation and secretion are complementary processes that determine the fate of UBB+1. This study elucidates the dual roles of autophagy in managing neurotoxic proteins, highlighting SQSTM1/p62 as a key mediator of UBB+1 trafficking and secretion. Although ubiquitin typically acts as a degradation signal, our findings reveal a rare instance of a ubiquitin-related protein driving secretory autophagy. These findings advance our understanding of cellular mechanisms underlying the clearance of misfolded proteins in neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: Impaired MAPT/tau-secretory lysosomes are linked to cognitive vulnerability in Alzheimer patients.
primary.abstract: MAPT/tau proteins propagate between brain regions in a prion-like manner, driving the onset and progression of dementia in Alzheimer disease (AD). However, the basis for variability in dementia progression among AD patients remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that cognitively resilient AD patients, characterized by reduced MAPT/tau pathology, maintain lysosomal integrity, whereas cognitively vulnerable patients, exhibiting greater MAPT/tau burden, display lysosomal dysfunction. Lysosomes in cognitively vulnerable AD brains contain partially digested, seed-competent MAPT/tau species composed mainly of the amyloidogenic core with degraded peripheral regions. These pathogenic MAPT/tau forms are secreted via lysosomal exocytosis, facilitating MAPT/tau propagation and contributing to cognitive decline. Cognitively vulnerable female AD patients show increased lysosome-mediated MAPT/tau secretion relative to their male counterparts. Our findings suggest that lysosomal dysfunction, marked by altered protein expression, pH dysregulation, and MAPT/tau accumulation, underlies the heterogeneity in dementia severity. primary.title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
primary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

primary.title: Inactive ryanodine receptors sustain lysosomal availability for autophagy by promoting ER-lysosomal contact site formation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ release mutually influence each other's functions. Recent work revealed that ER-located ryanodine receptor(s) (RyR(s)) Ca2+ release channels suppress autophagosome turnover by the lysosomes. In familial Alzheimer's disease, inhibiting RyR hyperactivity restored autophagic flux by normalizing lysosomal vacuolar H+-ATPase (vATPase) levels. However, the mechanisms by which RyRs control lysosomal function and how this involves the vATPase remain unknown. Here, we show that RyRs interact with the ATP6v0a1 subunit of the vATPase, contributing to ER-lysosomal contact site formation. This interaction suppresses RyR-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to reduced lysosomal exocytosis. Pharmacological inhibition of RyR activity mimics these effects on lysosomal exocytosis. Retaining lysosomes inside cells via RyR inhibition increases ER-lysosomal contact site formation, rendering lysosomes more available for autophagic flux. In summary, these findings establish RyR/ATP6v0a1 complexes as ER-lysosomal tethers that dynamically and Ca2+ dependently regulate the intracellular availability of lysosomes to participate in autophagic flux.

secondary.title: Exosomes derived from N2 neutrophils reprogram the immune microenvironment to promote spinal cord injury repair.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord injury induces irreversible neurological impairments via secondary pathological cascades dominated by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. As the first-responder immune cells following spinal cord trauma, neutrophils can acquire an N2-like reparative phenotype, yet direct neutrophil transplantation is hampered by poor cellular survival. Exosomes, nanoscale cell-secreted vesicles with low immunogenicity and favourable biostability, constitute promising cell-free candidates for regenerative therapy. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils remains poorly defined for spinal cord injury repair. METHODS: Murine bone-marrow-derived neutrophils were polarized toward the N2 phenotype using interleukin-6 (IL-6) and granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), with non-polarized neutrophils set as the control group. Exosomes were purified by ultracentrifugation and comprehensively characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and western blotting. In vitro functional assays were performed to evaluate macrophage phenotypic reprogramming, neuronal axonal regeneration, and neuronal apoptosis. A modified Allen's weight-drop mouse spinal cord injury model was adopted for in vivo intervention. Motor functional recovery was evaluated using the Basso Mouse Scale and gait analysis, while neural tissue repair was assessed via immunofluorescence staining. RESULTS: Exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils (N2-exos) exhibited canonical exosomal hallmarks. In vitro, these exosomes drove lipopolysaccharide-primed macrophages to switch to an anti-inflammatory reparative phenotype, alleviated oxidative-stress-mediated axonal injury, and suppressed neuronal apoptosis. In vivo administration of N2-exos markedly enhanced hind-limb motor performance and gait coordination, and facilitated axonal regeneration across the injury epicenter. CONCLUSIONS: N2-exos remodel the post-traumatic immune microenvironment and confer combined neuroprotective and axon regenerative effects. This cell-free modality represents a promising therapeutic candidate for regenerative interventions against spinal cord injury.

secondary.title: Evaluation of the effect of p38γ gene delivery using exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells on Alzheimer's rat model.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia, memory loss, and cognitive decline. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of delivering the p38γ gene via exosomes derived from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-Exos) in a rat model of streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD. METHODS AND RESULTS: After the AD model was established, the rats were administered via intraperitoneal injections of p38γ, Exo, or p38γ-loaded ADSC-Exo (Exo+p38γ). Cognitive and memory assessments were performed via novel object recognition (NOR), passive avoidance, elevated plus-maze (EPM), and the Barnes maze (BM). Histological techniques were used to evaluate cell density and beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaque accumulation, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR) was used to measure the transcription levels of neuronal nuclei (NeuN), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and sex-determining region Y-box 2 (SOX2). Additionally, the expression of GDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), SOX2, and malondialdehyde (MDA) was analyzed via an ELISA kit. The Exo and Exo+p38γ groups demonstrated significant improvements in STZ-induced memory deficits across various assessments. However, no significant differences in the protein expression levels of GDNF, BDNF, SOX2, and MDA or the gene expression levels of SOX2, NeuN, GDNF, and NGF were detected between STZ-treated rats that received Exos+p38γ and those that received Exos alone. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, this study demonstrates that ADSC-derived exosomes effectively improve cognitive deficits in an AD rat model; Although Exo+p38γ was associated with a significant increase in SOX2 gene expression compared with the AD group, the direct comparison between Exo+p38γ and ADSC-Exos did not demonstrate a statistically significant additional effect.

secondary.title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
secondary.abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

secondary.title: Up-regulation of the kinase LRRK2, in enteric glia contributes to mucosal barrier impairment in Parkinson's disease via secretory autophagy.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) show intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) alterations, enteric gliosis and inflammation that could contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms. Moreover, changes in leucine rich-repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) expression/activity have been associated with PD development and related intestinal inflammation. However, the molecular determinants linking LRRK2, enteric gliosis and IEB impairment remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated the role of LRRK2 in IEB changes associated with PD, focusing on its role in the interplay between enteric glial cells (EGCs) and intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Human A53T α-synuclein transgenic (Tg) mice (9 months old) were provided a model of early PD. Central neuroinflammation was studied by IBA-1 staining. Intestinal motility, colonic α-synuclein and LRRK2 expression were assessed. Enteric gliosis was evaluated by detection of GFAP+ cells co-expressing LRRK2; IEB was tested by mucins detection and quantification of Muc-2, tight junction proteins and secretory autophagy. In vitro co-cultures between EGCs and IECs were performed to investigate glial LRRK2-mediated gut barrier alterations. KEY RESULTS: A53T mice, without central neuroinflammation, showed intestinal disturbances, colonic α-synuclein accumulation and an increase in colonic GFAP+/LRRK2+ glial cells before brain pathology. Moreover, PD animals displayed IEB alterations and increased colonic autophagosomes, suggesting a shift towards secretory autophagy. In co-culture experiments, α-synuclein and lipopolysaccharide promoted enteric gliosis and LRRK2 up-regulation in glial cells, contributing to IEB impairment via secretory autophagy. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: These changes could influence bowel symptoms and central pathology associated with PD, via the gut-brain axis.

secondary.title: Extracellular exosome signature links hypertension and Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: Untreated hypertension is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, this association is not well understood. The aim of this study was to reveal protein signatures that bridge the pathophysiological changes in hypertension to AD. Using untargeted proteomics, we analyzed brain samples from aged (30- and 40-week-old) spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs, n = 12), and age-matched normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY, n = 8) controls, and human AD patients (Braak stages 4-6) (n = 30), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) (n = 5), non-demented controls (Braak stages 0-3) (n = 37). Differential expression and pathway analyses in SHRs highlighted the 'extracellular exosome' pathway. This pathway also showed significant associations to differentially expressed proteins in AD and CAA patients. Comparison between species identified 24 proteins in SHRs and AD, whose trajectory pattern over the progression of hypertension, aligned with those observed during AD Braak stage progression, compared to respective controls. The proteins were similarly associated with extracellular exosomes. Immunostaining and spatial proteomics support vesicle accumulation and dysregulated exosome protein signatures in the cerebrovasculature of both SHR and AD brains. Additionally, the extracellular exosome pathway-association was not identified in a traditional model of familial AD (5xFAD). Our findings demonstrate cross-species translatability between AD and the SHR and provide novel mechanistic insights into a shared dysregulation of cerebral artery-associated exosomes.

best.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
best.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

best.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
best.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

best.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
best.abstract: Recent work by Mao and colleagues identifies a distinct class of small extracellular vesicles, termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs), generated from amphisomes upon autophagy induction. In this commentary, we discuss how this study provides important mechanistic insight into the coupling between autophagy and secretion. AEVs are molecularly and functionally distinct from canonical exosomes, being enriched in autophagy-related components such as LC3 and p62, and dependent on core ATG machinery for their biogenesis. Notably, their secretion is enhanced by autophagy induction and contributes to intercellular communication, particularly in the context of viral infection. These findings position amphisomes as critical sorting hubs that direct cargo toward either degradation or secretion, thereby integrating autophagic and endolysosomal pathways. We further highlight how these results intersect with prior evidence implicating SNARE-dependent mechanisms, including VAMP7 and stress-responsive regulators such as GRASP55, in unconventional secretion. Finally, we discuss key unresolved questions, particularly the mechanisms underlying the generation of small intraluminal vesicles within amphisomes and the role of ESCRT machinery in this process. Overall, the identification of AEVs adds a new layer of complexity to extracellular vesicle biology and opens new avenues for understanding how autophagy contributes to intercellular signaling in health and disease.

best.title: Recessive variants in ESCRT-II component VPS25 alter vesicular transport and small extracellular vesicle processing in lethal neonatal encephalopathy.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. METHODS: We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. RESULTS: The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25, one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. CONCLUSIONS: We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25. The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Glycoprotein-induced phase separation drives unconventional secretion of galectin-3.
best.abstract: The mechanism of unconventional protein secretion remains an unresolved issue. Here, we describe an unconventional protein secretion pathway for galectin-3 that is mediated by phase separation and condensation. Using four lysosomal damage models, we observed a rapid, pronounced release of galectin-3 in large, non-exosomal particles. This secretion is driven by glycoprotein-induced galectin-3 phase separation and is independent of pyroptosis and secretory autophagy. During phase separation, the S-face of galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain binds glycoproteins that triggers galectin-3 N-terminal tail release and condensation. These condensates then recruit ALG-2 via the exposed N-terminal tail. ALG-2 directs the condensates to the endoplasmic reticulum-late endosome interface. After translocation into late endosomes, galectin-3 condensates are secreted into the extracellular milieu by SNARE-dependent vesicular transport. This mechanism of exporting phase-separated protein condensates may serve as a clean-up response to membrane damage.

best.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
best.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

best.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
best.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR hyperactivity is implicated in early pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is associated with impaired autophagy. We recently uncovered a mechanism linking RYR activity to lysosome availability for autophagy. RYRs localize to ER-lysosome contact sites via direct binding to ATP6V0A1, a V-ATPase subunit that also suppresses RYR-mediated Ca2+ release. In human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, spontaneous RYR activity promotes lysosomal secretion, depleting the intracellular lysosomal pool and inhibiting autophagic flux. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. In this Punctum, we discuss how this RYR2:ATP6V0A1 "contact-site hub" may be perturbed in disease and highlight open questions on how lysosomes decode RYR-derived Ca2+ signals.

best.title: Autophagic extracellular vesicles: a distinct secretory route linking autophagy to extracellular communication.
best.abstract: Macroautophagy/autophagy is classically defined as a degradative pathway that delivers cytoplasmic material to lysosomes. However, accumulating evidence indicates that autophagy can also support unconventional secretion. A recent study identifies a previously unrecognized subtype of small extracellular vesicles termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs). These vesicles originate from amphisomes formed by the fusion of autophagosomes with multivesicular bodies and are characterized by a size below 100 nm together with the presence of autophagic cargos, ESCRT-III components and RAB13. Importantly, biogenesis of AEVs is distinct from that of classical exosomes, which requires specific components of the ESCRT III complex and the GTPase RAB27A. The further finding that enterovirus can exploit AEVs to infect receptor-negative cells, thereby expanding viral tropism, suggests that secretory autophagy serves as a pivotal mechanism driving pathogen dissemination. This work provides the conceptual framework of extracellular vesicle heterogeneity and positions secretory autophagy as an important contributor to intercellular communication.
