best.title: Evaluation of the effect of p38γ gene delivery using exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells on Alzheimer's rat model.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia, memory loss, and cognitive decline. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of delivering the p38γ gene via exosomes derived from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-Exos) in a rat model of streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD. METHODS AND RESULTS: After the AD model was established, the rats were administered via intraperitoneal injections of p38γ, Exo, or p38γ-loaded ADSC-Exo (Exo+p38γ). Cognitive and memory assessments were performed via novel object recognition (NOR), passive avoidance, elevated plus-maze (EPM), and the Barnes maze (BM). Histological techniques were used to evaluate cell density and beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaque accumulation, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR) was used to measure the transcription levels of neuronal nuclei (NeuN), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and sex-determining region Y-box 2 (SOX2). Additionally, the expression of GDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), SOX2, and malondialdehyde (MDA) was analyzed via an ELISA kit. The Exo and Exo+p38γ groups demonstrated significant improvements in STZ-induced memory deficits across various assessments. However, no significant differences in the protein expression levels of GDNF, BDNF, SOX2, and MDA or the gene expression levels of SOX2, NeuN, GDNF, and NGF were detected between STZ-treated rats that received Exos+p38γ and those that received Exos alone. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, this study demonstrates that ADSC-derived exosomes effectively improve cognitive deficits in an AD rat model; Although Exo+p38γ was associated with a significant increase in SOX2 gene expression compared with the AD group, the direct comparison between Exo+p38γ and ADSC-Exos did not demonstrate a statistically significant additional effect.

best.title: MYO18B promotes lysosomal exocytosis by facilitating focal adhesion maturation.
best.abstract: Many cancer cells exhibit increased amounts of paucimannose glycans, which are truncated N-glycan structures rarely found in mammals. Paucimannosidic proteins are proposedly generated within lysosomes and exposed on the cell surface through a yet uncertain mechanism. In this study, we revealed that paucimannosidic proteins are produced by lysosomal glycosidases and secreted via lysosomal exocytosis. Interestingly, lysosomal exocytosis preferentially occurred in the vicinity of focal adhesions, protein complexes connecting the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Through genome-wide knockout screening, we identified that MYO18B, an actin crosslinker, is required for focal adhesion maturation, facilitating lysosomal exocytosis and the release of paucimannosidic lysosomal proteins to the extracellular milieu. Moreover, a mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 locally activated at focal adhesions imports Ca2+ necessary for lysosome-plasma membrane fusion. Collectively, our study unveiled an intimate relationship between lysosomal exocytosis and focal adhesion, shedding light on the unexpected interplay between lysosomal activities and cellular mechanosensing.

best.title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
best.abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

best.title: Up-regulation of the kinase LRRK2, in enteric glia contributes to mucosal barrier impairment in Parkinson's disease via secretory autophagy.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) show intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) alterations, enteric gliosis and inflammation that could contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms. Moreover, changes in leucine rich-repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) expression/activity have been associated with PD development and related intestinal inflammation. However, the molecular determinants linking LRRK2, enteric gliosis and IEB impairment remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated the role of LRRK2 in IEB changes associated with PD, focusing on its role in the interplay between enteric glial cells (EGCs) and intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Human A53T α-synuclein transgenic (Tg) mice (9 months old) were provided a model of early PD. Central neuroinflammation was studied by IBA-1 staining. Intestinal motility, colonic α-synuclein and LRRK2 expression were assessed. Enteric gliosis was evaluated by detection of GFAP+ cells co-expressing LRRK2; IEB was tested by mucins detection and quantification of Muc-2, tight junction proteins and secretory autophagy. In vitro co-cultures between EGCs and IECs were performed to investigate glial LRRK2-mediated gut barrier alterations. KEY RESULTS: A53T mice, without central neuroinflammation, showed intestinal disturbances, colonic α-synuclein accumulation and an increase in colonic GFAP+/LRRK2+ glial cells before brain pathology. Moreover, PD animals displayed IEB alterations and increased colonic autophagosomes, suggesting a shift towards secretory autophagy. In co-culture experiments, α-synuclein and lipopolysaccharide promoted enteric gliosis and LRRK2 up-regulation in glial cells, contributing to IEB impairment via secretory autophagy. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: These changes could influence bowel symptoms and central pathology associated with PD, via the gut-brain axis.

best.title: Molecular mechanisms underlying p62-dependent secretion of the Alzheimer-associated ubiquitin variant UBB+1.
best.abstract: UBB+1, a ubiquitin variant protein resulting from a frameshift in the ubiquitin-B gene, is a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD). At the cellular level, UBB+1 disrupts the ubiquitin-proteasome system while inducing autophagy. Notably, UBB+1 itself is secreted via autophagosome-like vesicles. Here, we demonstrate that UBB+1 can be removed from the cell by degradative and secretory autophagy. Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1)/p62 functions as a pivotal ubiquitin receptor for UBB+1, recognizing its ubiquitin domain and facilitating loading into autophagosomes. Oligomerization of SQSTM1/p62 was critical to isolate UBB+1 in bodies preventing its aggregation. Intriguingly, both gain- and loss-of-function SQSTM1/p62 suppressed UBB+1 secretion, causing intracellular retention: SQSTM1/p62 knockout led to UBB+1 accumulation in insoluble aggregates, while its overexpression promoted the formation of p62-UBB+1 bodies. We further identified distinct roles for SNARE-mediated membrane fusion in secretory autophagy of UBB+1. Specifically, the R-SNARE SEC22B and the Q-SNAREs Syntaxin-4 and SNAP23 participated in UBB+1 exocytosis. Disruption of SEC22B impaired the fusion of UBB+1-containing autophagosomes with the plasma membrane, reducing UBB+1 secretion without affecting its intracellular turnover. Inhibition of lysosomes partially stabilized UBB+1 indicating that degradation and secretion are complementary processes that determine the fate of UBB+1. This study elucidates the dual roles of autophagy in managing neurotoxic proteins, highlighting SQSTM1/p62 as a key mediator of UBB+1 trafficking and secretion. Although ubiquitin typically acts as a degradation signal, our findings reveal a rare instance of a ubiquitin-related protein driving secretory autophagy. These findings advance our understanding of cellular mechanisms underlying the clearance of misfolded proteins in neurodegenerative diseases.

best.title: Impaired MAPT/tau-secretory lysosomes are linked to cognitive vulnerability in Alzheimer patients.
best.abstract: MAPT/tau proteins propagate between brain regions in a prion-like manner, driving the onset and progression of dementia in Alzheimer disease (AD). However, the basis for variability in dementia progression among AD patients remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that cognitively resilient AD patients, characterized by reduced MAPT/tau pathology, maintain lysosomal integrity, whereas cognitively vulnerable patients, exhibiting greater MAPT/tau burden, display lysosomal dysfunction. Lysosomes in cognitively vulnerable AD brains contain partially digested, seed-competent MAPT/tau species composed mainly of the amyloidogenic core with degraded peripheral regions. These pathogenic MAPT/tau forms are secreted via lysosomal exocytosis, facilitating MAPT/tau propagation and contributing to cognitive decline. Cognitively vulnerable female AD patients show increased lysosome-mediated MAPT/tau secretion relative to their male counterparts. Our findings suggest that lysosomal dysfunction, marked by altered protein expression, pH dysregulation, and MAPT/tau accumulation, underlies the heterogeneity in dementia severity. Targeting lysosomal exocytosis and the amyloidogenic core of MAPT/tau fibrils offer a promising therapeutic avenue to mitigate MAPT/tau pathology and promote cognitive resilience in AD and related dementias.Abbreviation: AD: Alzheimer disease, LAMP1; lysosomal associated membrane protein 1, NFT: neurofibrillary tangles; MAPT: microtubule associated protein tau; PHF: paired helical filaments; TIRF: total internal reflection fluorescence; TARDBP/TDP-43:TAR DNA binding protein.

best.title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
best.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

best.title: Extracellular exosome signature links hypertension and Alzheimer's disease.
best.abstract: Untreated hypertension is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, this association is not well understood. The aim of this study was to reveal protein signatures that bridge the pathophysiological changes in hypertension to AD. Using untargeted proteomics, we analyzed brain samples from aged (30- and 40-week-old) spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs, n = 12), and age-matched normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY, n = 8) controls, and human AD patients (Braak stages 4-6) (n = 30), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) (n = 5), non-demented controls (Braak stages 0-3) (n = 37). Differential expression and pathway analyses in SHRs highlighted the 'extracellular exosome' pathway. This pathway also showed significant associations to differentially expressed proteins in AD and CAA patients. Comparison between species identified 24 proteins in SHRs and AD, whose trajectory pattern over the progression of hypertension, aligned with those observed during AD Braak stage progression, compared to respective controls. The proteins were similarly associated with extracellular exosomes. Immunostaining and spatial proteomics support vesicle accumulation and dysregulated exosome protein signatures in the cerebrovasculature of both SHR and AD brains. Additionally, the extracellular exosome pathway-association was not identified in a traditional model of familial AD (5xFAD). Our findings demonstrate cross-species translatability between AD and the SHR and provide novel mechanistic insights into a shared dysregulation of cerebral artery-associated exosomes.

best.title: Inactive ryanodine receptors sustain lysosomal availability for autophagy by promoting ER-lysosomal contact site formation.
best.abstract: Lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ release mutually influence each other's functions. Recent work revealed that ER-located ryanodine receptor(s) (RyR(s)) Ca2+ release channels suppress autophagosome turnover by the lysosomes. In familial Alzheimer's disease, inhibiting RyR hyperactivity restored autophagic flux by normalizing lysosomal vacuolar H+-ATPase (vATPase) levels. However, the mechanisms by which RyRs control lysosomal function and how this involves the vATPase remain unknown. Here, we show that RyRs interact with the ATP6v0a1 subunit of the vATPase, contributing to ER-lysosomal contact site formation. This interaction suppresses RyR-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to reduced lysosomal exocytosis. Pharmacological inhibition of RyR activity mimics these effects on lysosomal exocytosis. Retaining lysosomes inside cells via RyR inhibition increases ER-lysosomal contact site formation, rendering lysosomes more available for autophagic flux. In summary, these findings establish RyR/ATP6v0a1 complexes as ER-lysosomal tethers that dynamically and Ca2+ dependently regulate the intracellular availability of lysosomes to participate in autophagic flux.

primary.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: Two functionally distinct amyloid-β intermediates link aggregation pathways to pathology in Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: Neurotoxic intermediates formed during amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation are thought to drive Alzheimer's disease, yet their rarity and transient nature have obscured their identity and formation pathways in the human brain. Here, we combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify Aβ intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them. Applying this framework to recombinant Aβ42, an Alzheimer's knock-in mouse model and human Alzheimer's brain tissue, we find two functionally distinct intermediate populations present across all systems. They form through separate aggregation routes and differ in their neurotoxicity, abundance and susceptibility to inhibition. Both damage neurons and glia, but only one converts into plaques. Suppressing these intermediates pharmacologically in mice reduces plaque burden, attenuates astrogliosis and improves cognition. Our findings connect model systems with human pathology and identify intermediate formation pathways as actionable therapeutic targets across protein-misfolding disorders.

primary.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
primary.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

primary.title: Tau monomers and fibrils escape microglial clearance via distinct cellular mechanisms.
primary.abstract: Tauopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease, are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the accumulation and propagation of toxic extracellular forms of the microtubule-associated protein tau across brain regions. Microglia, the resident macrophages of the brain, are known for clearing and degrading toxic proteins. However, emerging evidence suggests that microglia also enhance tau spreading. To dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying microglial responses to extracellular tau, we use high-resolution imaging and biochemical approaches to assess the trafficking dynamics of different extracellular tau species in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Here we find that tau monomers are internalized by microglia via cell-surface LRP1 receptors but fail to reach terminally degradative lysosomes; instead, they are persistently recycled back to the extracellular space. In contrast, tau fibrils are not internalized and primarily adhere to the cell surface through an HSPG-dependent mechanism, triggering TLR4-mediated microglial activation and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Heparin or anti-tau treatments dampen tau fibril-mediated microglial activation. In addition, disease-associated variants of the Alzheimer's disease-related protein APOE reduce microglia-tau interactions, further reducing tau uptake. Together, these findings demonstrate that microglia fail to efficiently clear extracellular tau monomers and fibrils through mechanistically distinct cellular processes, emphasizing the need for tailored therapeutic strategies to enhance extracellular tau clearance in neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
primary.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

primary.title: Hepatocyte-derived exosomal miR-122 mediates liver-to-brain crosstalk and neuroinflammation in alcohol-exposed Alzheimer's disease mice.
primary.abstract: Neuroinflammation and microglial activation are common features in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and excessive alcohol consumption. Alcohol induces liver damage and inflammation, and altered serum aminotransferases have been reported in patients with AD. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) and their cargo are emerging as mediators of intercellular communication in AD and alcohol-induced liver injury. However, the effects of alcohol use on AD progression remain to be elucidated. In this study, we evaluated the effects of repeated binge drinking on the liver and brain in the APP/PS1 mouse model of AD. Alcohol-exposed APP/PS1 mice showed elevated serum alanine aminotransferase levels, indicating liver injury absent in controls, along with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in both liver and brain. Alcohol increased the biogenesis and release of sEVs in AD mice and in mouse hepatocytes. These sEVs were enriched in mature miR-122-5p that is predominant in hepatocytes. In vivo, miR-122-5p was detected in the brain of alcohol-exposed AD mice suggesting EV-mediated miR-122-5p transfer to the brain. Microglial uptake of hepatocyte-derived sEVs was confirmed in vitro. sEVs from alcohol-treated hepatocytes sensitized BV-2 microglia to LPS stimulation, significantly enhancing CCL2, CXCL2, CCL3, and TNF-α production. Transfection of microglia with a miR-122-5p mimic partially recapitulated the pro-inflammatory sensitization by sEVs from alcohol-exposed hepatocytes, which was reversed by miR-122-5p inhibitor delivery. ADAM10, a miR-122-5p target, was reduced in both wild-type and AD brains after alcohol exposure, with cell-specific effects. These results suggest that alcohol-induced hepatocyte-derived sEVs may modulate liver-to-brain signaling via miR-122-5p and contribute to neuroinflammation in AD.

primary.title: Single-cell machine learning uncovers genetically anchored, cell-type specific programs of Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: Univariate differential expression analysis dominates single-cell transcriptomic studies of Alzheimer's disease, yet marginal testing alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure or distinguish clinical from neuropathological signatures. Here we introduce TriSCOPE, a framework integrating multivariate predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression, and pseudotime inference, applied to six Alzheimer's disease snRNA-seq datasets comprising ~4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors. Across six major brain cell types and 41 subclusters, we identify cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that are largely non-overlapping with differentially expressed genes, revealing disease-relevant signals invisible to univariate approaches. Conditional GWAS-eQTL colocalization anchors a subset of these predictively expressed genes to inherited Alzheimer's disease risk loci, including 27 genetically supported gene-cell type pairs (among them ARL17B, JAZF1) with no significant differential expression. Integration across all three analytical branches nominates high-confidence convergent programs including astrocytic stress markers (such as GFAP, MT2A), neuronal signaling genes (like RASGEF1B, LINGO1, NRG1), and microglial and oligodendrocyte regulators (including SYTL3, SPP1, APOD). Comparison of clinical and neuropathological models reveals cell-type-specific divergence between cognitive and pathological Alzheimer's disease signatures. Key predictively expressed genes including ARL17B, LINGO1, and APOE replicate across independent cohorts, with cross-cohort generalizability confirmed across all three analytical branches of TriSCOPE.

primary.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
primary.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

primary.title: Blood-Based Lipid Peroxidation and Ferroptosis-Related Markers in Friedreich's Ataxia.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a neurodegenerative disease caused by reduced levels the mitochondrial frataxin protein. Systemic oxidative stress and iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, commonly associated with ferroptosis, have a critical role in disease pathogenesis. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to evaluate longitudinal changes of blood-based indexes of oxidative stress and ferroptosis-related molecules in adults and children with FRDA. METHODS: We measured plasma levels of 4-hydroxyl-2-nonenals (4-HNE) and hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (15-HETE), and blood concentration of glutathione (GSH), glutathione disulfide (GSSG), in 62 FRDA patients (48 adults and 14 children) and 63 age matched healthy controls. mRNA levels of major genes targeting the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) were also evaluated. Peripheral concentrations of lipid peroxidation markers and ferroptosis-related molecules were correlated with age, disease duration, and severity of ataxia signs. Clinical and biochemical evaluations were performed at baseline and at 1-year follow-up. RESULTS: FRDA patients had significantly increased levels of 4-HNE and GSSG and decreased levels of GSH, compared to controls. Children with FRDA had lower levels of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) mRNA than adult patients. At 1-year follow up, plasma 4-HNE levels remained stable, and blood GPX4 mRNA increased only in adult patient cohort. GPX4 correlated with age, disease duration, and clinical scores. CONCLUSIONS: We provide preliminary evidence of defective GPX4 expression in the early phase of the disease. Our data suggest that GPX4 may represent a biomarker for disease progression and a possible candidate target for therapeutic strategies. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

primary.title: Hyperactive KIF5A in Neurodegeneration.
primary.abstract: The highly polarised morphology of neurons and the sheer length of their axons make transport of cargoes throughout the cell a formidable task. Decades of evidence obtained from genetic studies on patients and animal models highlight deficits in axonal transport as a recurrent cause, or early contributing factor, in a plethora of neurodegenerative diseases. Axonal transport abnormalities usually manifest as a slowing of cargo trafficked by molecular motors along microtubules; however, hyperactivation of motors can also lead to disease. That is the case for the kinesin-1 protein KIF5A, in which hyperactive mutations are linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and neonatal intractable myoclonus (NEIMY). In this Perspective, we summarise the latest insights into the impact of KIF5A hyperactivity, such as loss of autoinhibition, aggregation, altered cargo binding and microtubule damage. We conclude by discussing possible strategies to counteract these disruptions, with an emphasis on the necessity of restoring axonal transport to physiological levels, a key requirement to maintain neuronal homeostasis.

primary.title: Alzheimer's disease-associated presenilin 2 N141I mutation impairs neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics through selective downregulation of the Golgi exchange factor Gbf1.
primary.abstract: Presenilin 2 (PS2) mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease, yet their effects beyond amyloid processing remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how PS2 deletion and the N141I mutation affect neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics in mouse primary neurons. Both PS2 deletion and N141I mutation reduced neuronal lipid content. However, exogenous lipid supplementation rescued this deficit only in N141I-expressing neurons, indicating a partial loss-of-function effect. N141I neurons also displayed reduced OPA1, a mitochondrial fusion regulator, restored by lipid supplementation. RNA-sequencing identified Gbf1, a Golgi-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor, as selectively downregulated in N141I but not knockout tissue, which was confirmed at the protein level in mouse brain and primary neurons. Gbf1 knockdown in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) recapitulated the N141I lipid profile. Together, these findings reveal a PS2-GBF1-lipid-mitochondria axis disrupted specifically by the N141I mutation, suggesting an amyloid-independent pathway contributing to neurodegeneration and identifying potential therapeutic targets for familial Alzheimer's disease.

primary.title: VPS35 mutation inhibits PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via increased LRRK2 kinase activity.
primary.abstract: The p.D620N mutation in VPS35 causes an autosomal dominant form of Parkinson's disease via mechanisms that are poorly understood. PINK1 and parkin, two proteins whose loss-of-function underlies autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, cooperate to mediate mitophagy, a quality control pathway for selective elimination of damaged mitochondria. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy is disrupted by LRRK2 mutations, which are the most prevalent cause of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease. Here, we investigated whether the p.D620N VPS35 mutation has an effect on PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy. We identified a novel family with autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease caused by a p.D620N VPS35 mutation. We cultured skin fibroblasts and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic neurons from the proband and from a second, unrelated Parkinson's disease patient with the p.D620N VPS35 mutation, and compared them with isogenic and non-isogenic control cells. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy was severely impaired in VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons, while non-selective, starvation-induced autophagy and lysosomal degradative capacity were preserved. siRNA-mediated VPS35 knockdown rescued the mitophagy defect in VPS35 mutant cells, whereas overexpression of wild-type VPS35 did not, suggesting a gain-of-function mechanism of the mutation. The VPS35 mutation did not interfere with activation of PINK1 or parkin after mitochondrial depolarization, but impaired mitochondrial recruitment of the autophagy receptor optineurin. LRRK2 kinase activity was increased in the VPS35 mutant cells, as shown by enhanced levels of the T73-phosphorylated form of the LRRK2 substrate RAB10. The enhanced level of phosphorylated RAB10 in VPS35 mutant cells was decreased by treatment with LRRK2 kinase inhibitors and by VPS35 knockdown. Importantly, the mitophagy defect of VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons was fully rescued by LRRK2 kinase inhibitors as well as by overexpression of PPM1H, a phosphatase that dephosphorylates multiple RAB substrates of LRRK2. Finally, in situ proximity ligation experiments revealed that endogenous VPS35 and LRRK2 are proximity partners in human dopaminergic neurons and that this proximity relationship is enhanced by the VPS35 mutation. In conclusion, the VPS35 mutation impairs PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via a gain-of-function mechanism that involves stimulation of LRRK2 kinase activity. Thus, a VPS35/LRRK2 axis linked to dominant Parkinson's disease intersects with a pathway mediated by proteins encoded by the recessive Parkinson's disease genes.

primary.title: Parkinson's disease-linked D620N mutation selectively alters the brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35.
primary.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

primary.title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
primary.abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

primary.title: BAG3 coordinates astrocytic proteostasis of Alzheimer's disease-linked proteins via proteasome, autophagy, and retromer interactions.
primary.abstract: Bcl-2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3) is a mediator of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy, and in the brain, is most highly expressed in astrocytes. However, its role in astrocytes remains poorly defined. Given the genetic and pathological links of BAG3 to proteostasis and neurodegenerative diseases, we investigated how BAG3 contributes to astrocyte function and Alzheimer's disease (AD). To define its function and relevance, we used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to confirm BAG3 enrichment in astrocytes and employed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of human induced pluripotent stem cells followed by proteomic and transcriptomic profiling, which revealed that BAG3 loss caused greater disruption in astrocytes than in neurons. BAG3-deficient astrocytes displayed reduced autophagy, lysosomal abundance and activity, and proteasome function. Coimmunoprecipitation identified BAG3 known binding partners (e.g., HSPB8, proteasome regulators), as well as an interactor in the retromer complex, VPS35. BAG3 deficiency resulted in altered retromer activity as measured by amyloid precursor protein (APP) localization in endosomes. In addition to validating these binding partners, integrative -omics analyses showed that BAG3 regulates AD-relevant proteins (GFAP, BIN1), as well as HSPB8. Functionally, BAG3 knockout astrocytes exhibited impaired amyloid-β proteostasis when cocultured with APP/PSEN1 mutant neurons, directly linking BAG3 to a disease-relevant astrocyte phenotype. Finally, analysis of postmortem human brain revealed that BAG3 expression marks a stress-responsive astrocyte subtype in aged individuals. Together, these findings demonstrate that BAG3 coordinates astrocyte proteostasis through interactions with regulators of autophagy, proteasome activity, and retromer function, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target and central node of astrocytic protein quality control in neurodegeneration.

primary.title: Calpain-mediated TBP cleavage disturbs neuronal AMOT-YAP1 signalling.
primary.abstract: The transcription factor TATA-box-binding protein (TBP) plays a crucial role in neurons, as highlighted by its involvement in spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17), where pathological polyglutamine expansions disrupt its function. While the molecular pathomechanisms remain unclear, our previous study showed that calcium-activated calpains cleave TBP in SCA17 cell and animal models. Here, we pinpoint a major calpain cleavage site after residue T106, C-terminal to TBP's polyglutamine tract. The resulting polyglutamine-containing N-terminal fragments mislocalise to the cytoplasm and exhibit increased aggregation. Both the N-terminal and the nuclear-localised C-terminal fragments contribute to calpain overactivation. SCA17 cell line-based multi-omics analyses revealed that TBP fragments alter pathways linked to neuronal function and neurodegeneration, identifying AMOT as a key player. Further analyses in SCA17 cell lines, patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons as well as in rat and zebrafish models confirmed AMOT's pivotal role in neurons, regulated by TBP and mediated via YAP1-dependent signalling. These findings offer further insights into TBP's neuronal function and suggest broader implications of AMOT for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
primary.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

primary.title: Early reduction of myelin-associated glycoprotein at myelin membranes in Huntington's disease.
primary.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is marked by progressive neuronal loss and atrophy of grey matter structures, particularly the caudate and putamen. Brain imaging studies reveal that the white matter starts to decay in the brain of individuals bearing the HD mutation many years before symptomatic onset. However, the mechanism by which the HD mutation causes white matter loss remains to be further defined. In this study, we examined white matter pathology and explored the underlying mechanism in the HDQ140 knock-in mouse model of HD. Western blot analysis of proteins localized at different layers of the myelin sheath showed that myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), which is localized at the innermost myelin layer, was decreased earlier than proteins localized at outer layers of the myelin. The loss of MAG occurred at fully myelinated axons and was progressive with age. In postmortem symptomatic human HD brains, the level of MAG as well as other myelin proteins was also decreased. In HD mouse brains, MAG labeling was reduced at fiber bundles but accumulated in perinuclear structures of cells that expressed breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1, a marker for new oligodendrocytes. While their abundance was normal, new oligodendrocytes in HD brains were impeded in acquiring the expression of MAG. Compared with those in wild-type mouse brains, oligodendrocytes in HD mouse brains had a reduced frequency of MAG-bearing small vesicles and an increased abundance and enlargement of MAG-containing perinuclear structures. Further studies suggest that the MAG-accumulating perinuclear structures were derived from the late endosomal lysosomal compartment. Our study suggests that white matter decay in HD brains involves an early progressive loss of MAG in myelin membranes.

primary.title: Neuropathological and functional impact of astrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles in an aged model of Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid-bound particles that transfer cargos between cells. While plasma neuronal-derived EVs (NEVs) from individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) have been reported to exhibit high pathogenic potential, this study examined the impact of astrocyte-derived EVs (AEVs) in an aged AD mouse model. Plasma AEVs were isolated from cognitively normal control (CNC), MCI, and AD individuals using GLAST-based immunocapture and AEV size, purity, and tetraspanin were validated by flow cytometry, nanoparticle tracking, and super-resolution microscopy. AEVs pooled by clinical cohort were injected into the hippocampus of 6-month-old female PSAPP mice. Behavioral, biochemical, and neuropathological outcomes were assessed 6 months later. Rotarod assessment revealed significant impairment in motor coordination (p < 0.0001) in mice receiving MCI- and AD-AEVs compared with those receiving CNC-AEVs. While Morris water maze (MWM) also demonstrated that CNC-AEVs injected mice exhibited a trend toward increased target quadrant entries and faster escape latencies, these measures did not reach did not reach statistical significance. No overt changes were observed in the staining of amyloid plaque burden (6E10), and astrogliosis (GFAP). Immunoblotting of 82E1 and 22C11 confirmed Aβ/AAP levels remained similar across all injected mice, whereas increased cortical tau accumulation was observed in MCI- and AD-AEV injected mice. Cerebellar synaptic density (SY-38) remained unchanged. These findings suggest that while human-derived AEVs can precipitate early tau-related changes and motor coordination deficits, they do not significantly alter overall amyloidosis or astrocyte-reactivity at this time point. Further investigation is required to determine the viability of AEVs as biomarkers or therapeutic targets given the subtle nature of the observed structural pathology.

primary.title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
primary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

secondary.title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
secondary.abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

secondary.title: Up-regulation of the kinase LRRK2, in enteric glia contributes to mucosal barrier impairment in Parkinson's disease via secretory autophagy.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) show intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) alterations, enteric gliosis and inflammation that could contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms. Moreover, changes in leucine rich-repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) expression/activity have been associated with PD development and related intestinal inflammation. However, the molecular determinants linking LRRK2, enteric gliosis and IEB impairment remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated the role of LRRK2 in IEB changes associated with PD, focusing on its role in the interplay between enteric glial cells (EGCs) and intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Human A53T α-synuclein transgenic (Tg) mice (9 months old) were provided a model of early PD. Central neuroinflammation was studied by IBA-1 staining. Intestinal motility, colonic α-synuclein and LRRK2 expression were assessed. Enteric gliosis was evaluated by detection of GFAP+ cells co-expressing LRRK2; IEB was tested by mucins detection and quantification of Muc-2, tight junction proteins and secretory autophagy. In vitro co-cultures between EGCs and IECs were performed to investigate glial LRRK2-mediated gut barrier alterations. KEY RESULTS: A53T mice, without central neuroinflammation, showed intestinal disturbances, colonic α-synuclein accumulation and an increase in colonic GFAP+/LRRK2+ glial cells before brain pathology. Moreover, PD animals displayed IEB alterations and increased colonic autophagosomes, suggesting a shift towards secretory autophagy. In co-culture experiments, α-synuclein and lipopolysaccharide promoted enteric gliosis and LRRK2 up-regulation in glial cells, contributing to IEB impairment via secretory autophagy. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: These changes could influence bowel symptoms and central pathology associated with PD, via the gut-brain axis.

secondary.title: The UCHL1-HIF-1α axis mediates microglial metabolic reprogramming and neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease.
secondary.abstract: Microglial-mediated neuroinflammation is a key driver of Parkinson's disease (PD) progression. Ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1) is a neuron-enriched deubiquitinating enzyme, yet its role in microglial immunometabolism and PD pathogenesis remains poorly understood. We investigated the role of UCHL1 using lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated BV2 microglial cells, and brain tissues from a 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced mouse model. UCHL1 expression, inflammatory responses, HIF-1α signaling, and glycolytic activity were assessed using Western blotting, RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence, and metabolic assays. The effects of UCHL1 modulation on neuronal survival were examined using conditioned medium transfer experiments. The neuroprotective effects of UCHL1 inhibition in an MPTP-induced mouse model were evaluated by behavioral assessments and immunofluorescence analysis. In BV2 microglia, LPS stimulation partially reduced endogenous UCHL1 expression, the remaining UCHL1 continued to microglial neuroinflammation. Pharmacological inhibition of UCHL1 attenuated inflammatory responses, whereas UCHL1 overexpression exacerbated microglial activation and bystander neuronal injury. UCHL1 promoted glycolytic reprogramming through upregulation of HK2, PKM2, and LDHA. Mechanistically, Inhibition of HIF-1α diminished the increases in pro-inflammatory mediators and glycolytic enzyme expression associated with UCHL1 overexpression. In vivo, immunofluorescence demonstrated UCHL1 expression in activated microglia within the substantia nigra, and UCHL1 inhibition attenuated microglial activation, preserved TH-positive dopaminergic (DA) neurons, and improved motor deficits in MPTP-treated mice. Collectively, our findings identify UCHL1 as a key regulator of microglial immunometabolism in PD. By promoting HIF-1α-dependent glycolytic reprogramming, UCHL1 amplifies neuroinflammation and contributes to DA neurodegeneration, highlighting the UCHL1/HIF-1α/glycolysis axis as a potential therapeutic target for PD.

secondary.title: A human gut-BBB-brain microphysiological model for studying Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: The gut-brain axis (GBA) has emerged as a crucial contributor to neurodegenerative diseases, with growing evidence implicating gut-derived metabolic and signaling alterations in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the lack of human-relevant in vitro models limits our ability to explore the mechanisms of this axis effectively. To address this limitation, we developed a human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived gut-blood-brain barrier (BBB)-brain microphysiological system that enables systematic investigation of gut-brain interactions in AD under controlled conditions. Using this platform, we showed that communication between gut and brain compartments was associated with increased expression of neuronal and glial markers, as well as phenotypes indicative of enhanced maturation-associated molecular features. Integrating gut and brain compartments also revealed disease-associated molecular and cellular alterations not observed in brain organoids alone. Importantly, exposure of healthy brain organoids to signals from AD patient-derived gut organoids induced changes in neuronal and glial phenotypes, indicating that gut-derived factors may contribute to brain dysfunction in AD. Collectively, our findings establish a human iPSC-derived gut-BBB-brain platform for studying brain organoid responses under combined intestinal and BBB co-culture conditions and provide an experimental framework for exploratory studies of AD-associated inter-organ influences.

secondary.title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
secondary.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

secondary.title: TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis-induced microglial senescence underlies benzo[a]pyrene-associated Parkinson's disease-like lesions.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence has linked environmental polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), with benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) as a representative ubiquitous member, to elevated PD risk and disease pathogenesis. The present study aimed to investigate whether B[a]P can trigger typical PD-like lesions in mice, and further dissects the functional role of microglial senescence as well as its underlying regulatory mechanism, using complementary systems in vivo mouse model and in vitro BV2 microglia cell. Behavioral assessments revealed that B[a]P exposure induced significant, dose-dependent impairments in motor coordination and cognitive function compared with the control group. Moreover, the degree of functional impairments measured in the high-dose B[a]P group was comparable to that observed in the MPTP positive-control group. Following B[a]P treatment, brain-resident microglia cells exhibited signs of cell senescence, as evidenced by typical ultrastructural alterations, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, and elevated expression of the core senescence markers p16, p21, and p53 proteins. Consistent with these in vivo observations, B[a]P was confirmed to also induce cell cycle arrest in cultured BV2 microglia cells. This pro-senescent effect was significnatly attenuated by Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) overexpression, whereas it was markedly exacerbated following TREM2 knockout. Subsequent experiments further validated that insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as a direct downstream effector regulated by TREM2, is functionally required for B[a]P-triggered microglial senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that B[a]P exposure can induce PD-like lesions and microglial senescence, and which is primarily mediated via the TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis.

secondary.title: Integrated multi-omics identifies PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte state remodeling in paraquat-associated Parkinson's disease.
secondary.abstract: Paraquat (PQ) is an environmentally relevant herbicide associated with neurotoxicity and Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, yet the key molecular determinants linking PQ exposure to PD and the cellular states in which these alterations occur remain incompletely understood. We integrated network toxicology, human PD transcriptomics, machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, virtual perturbation, model-inferred protein analysis, molecular docking, and tissue validation to characterize PQ-associated molecular and cellular remodeling. Integrating PQ-associated targets with PD-related genes identified 293 candidates, among which prostaglandin D2 synthase (PTGDS) was consistently prioritized by random forest, XGBoost, and LASSO, with its PD-associated expression pattern reproduced across the discovery and independent validation cohorts. Single-cell analysis localized Ptgds expression predominantly to oligodendrocytes and identified two PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte (MOL) states with PQ-associated compositional patterns. CytoTRACE placed these PTGDS-enriched populations among relatively mature oligodendrocyte states. Functional analyses revealed distinct state-specific programs, with Ptgds+Mag+ MOL associated with myelin-associated programs, axon ensheathment-related programs, cholesterol metabolism, and lipid transport, whereas Ptgds+Il33+ MOL was linked to neuron-interaction-related programs, synaptic organization, cell adhesion, and neuron-glia communication. Ligand-receptor inference and spatial analyses supported state-specific changes in neuron-glia communication and spatial relationships. Spatial metabolomics showed significantly increased phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin signals in regions with higher inferred representation of Ptgds+Mag+ MOL states. Virtual Ptgds perturbation and scTranslator-based protein prediction further suggested state-specific myelin-lipid and neuron-interaction programs, while molecular docking provided preliminary structural predictions regarding a potential PQ-PTGDS interaction. Immunofluorescence further confirmed PTGDS localization in mature oligodendrocytes within the substantia nigra. Collectively, these findings identify PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte states as cellular contexts associated with PQ-related brain remodeling and extend our understanding of PQ neurotoxicity beyond classical neuron-centered mechanisms. This integrative framework provides mechanistic insight into how an environmental neurotoxicant may reshape myelin-lipid homeostasis and neuron-glia interactions in the context of PD-related brain pathology.

secondary.title: Brain Region-Specific Peptide and Proteomic Signatures Inform Alzheimer's Disease Biomarker Panels.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder with region- and severity-specific molecular signatures that complicate biomarker discovery. We combined peptide-centric quantitative proteomics data with machine learning, dimensionality reduction, nonlinear modeling, and network enrichment to identify candidate biomarkers across four brain regions and four AD severity stages. Dimensional reduction revealed disease-severity gradients (HCF-low ADNC → HCF-high ADNC → sporadic AD dementia (ADD) → autosomal-dominant AD) that were strongest in cortical regions (SMTG, IPL), moderate in the hippocampus, and weakest in the caudate. Machine-learning-based feature selection improved severity prediction, particularly at the peptide level, yielding panels of 10-22 region- and severity-specific biomarkers. Biomarker interaction modeling identified hubs centered on haptoglobin, VGF, APP, APOE, and midkine family members, partnering within neurosecretory, lipid transport, acute-phase response, and proteostasis pathways. STRING analysis validated these interactions, showing enrichment for secreted, hemoglobin-binding proteins with plasma and bone marrow tissue signals. Although biomarkers were predominantly region-specific, they converged on blood-linked pathways, supporting the translational potential of multi-marker, circulation-accessible panels. These findings show that peptide-level proteomics integrated with machine learning and network analysis clarifies AD heterogeneity and points to therapeutic avenues in neurovascular integrity, lipid transport, acute-phase response, and proteostasis, accelerating AD biomarker development.

secondary.title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
secondary.abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. secondary.title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
secondary.abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

secondary.title: miR-19b-3p Attenuates Ferroptosis-Related Changes in Experimental Models of Parkinson's Disease.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), a major global health challenge and a neurodegenerative disorder posing an escalating global burden, is associated with microRNA dysregulation. In PD patients, miR-19b-3p was downregulated; however, its underlying mechanisms are unknown. miR-19b-3p expression was evaluated by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The levels of the acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) were assessed via Western blot. Cell damage was assessed by measuring the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) into the culture supernatant. The levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), Fe2⁺, and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity were measured by assay kits to evaluate miR-19b-3p's effect on ferroptosis. In 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP⁺)-treated cells and 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-treated mice, miR-19b-3p was downregulated. Luciferase assays supported ACSL4 as a direct target of miR-19b-3p. Overexpression of miR-19b-3p attenuated ferroptosis-related changes, MPP⁺-induced cell damage, and MPTP-induced motor deficits, whereas ACSL4 overexpression partially reversed these effects. These findings support a role for the miR-19b-3p/ACSL4 axis in regulating ferroptosis-related responses in MPP⁺- and MPTP-based experimental models.

secondary.title: Integrated proteomics and network pharmacology reveal autophagy-lysosomal regulation underlying sulforaphane-mediated neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid-β (Aβ)-mediated neurotoxicity, impaired autophagy-lysosomal function, and neuronal apoptosis. Although sulforaphane (SFN) has demonstrated neuroprotective properties, its molecular actions against Aβ-related neuronal injury remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of SFN against Aβ-induced neuronal injury and explored the underlying molecular networks associated with its anti-AD activity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Integrated network pharmacology and proteomics approaches were complemented by experimental validation in retinoic acid-differentiated SH-SY5Y cells exposed to Aβ25-35. Cells were pretreated with SFN, which was withdrawn prior to Aβ exposure. Cell viability, apoptosis-related proteins (BAX/BCL-2), and autophagy-associated markers (LC3B and p62) were evaluated. Data-independent acquisition proteomics was performed to characterize global protein alterations. Target prioritization was conducted through integrated bioinformatics analysis and molecular docking, followed by western blot validation. RESULTS: Network pharmacology identified 331 overlapping targets between SFN and AD, mainly enriched in pathways related to apoptosis, autophagy, and oxidative stress. SFN pretreatment significantly attenuated Aβ-induced cytotoxicity and partially normalized apoptosis- and autophagy-related protein alterations, including reduction of the BAX/BCL-2 ratio, recovery of the LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio, and decrease in p62 accumulation. Integrated proteomic and network pharmacology analyses identified 28 candidate targets, among which CTSB, CTSD, CASP6, and IGF1R were validated by molecular docking and western blotting. CONCLUSION: SFN pretreatment protected against Aβ-induced neuronal injury in this in vitro model and was associated with modulation of autophagy-lysosomal and apoptosis-related pathways. The integration of network pharmacology, proteomics, and experimental validation provides a systems-level framework for understanding the multitarget neuroprotective actions of SFN.

best.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

best.title: Two functionally distinct amyloid-β intermediates link aggregation pathways to pathology in Alzheimer's disease.
best.abstract: Neurotoxic intermediates formed during amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation are thought to drive Alzheimer's disease, yet their rarity and transient nature have obscured their identity and formation pathways in the human brain. Here, we combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify Aβ intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them. Applying this framework to recombinant Aβ42, an Alzheimer's knock-in mouse model and human Alzheimer's brain tissue, we find two functionally distinct intermediate populations present across all systems. They form through separate aggregation routes and differ in their neurotoxicity, abundance and susceptibility to inhibition. Both damage neurons and glia, but only one converts into plaques. Suppressing these intermediates pharmacologically in mice reduces plaque burden, attenuates astrogliosis and improves cognition. Our findings connect model systems with human pathology and identify intermediate formation pathways as actionable therapeutic targets across protein-misfolding disorders.
