papers.title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. In this paper, we have measured the Raman spectra of microtubules and their constituent protein tubulin in dry powder form for a range of temperatures, from nitrogen liquid T=77 K up to room and physiological temperature T=310 K, to determine if molecular bond vibrations present potential Fano resonance asymmetry. We have found nontrivial persistence of Fano resonances, q<5, at room and physiological temperatures for some specific vibrational modes.

papers.title: Early Joint Attention Behaviors in Infants at High Familial Risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder: association with cortical development
papers.abstract: Abstract Joint attention is the ability to follow the gaze of others, which allows infants to share a common focus on individuals or objects. Impairments in initiating and responding to joint attention are some of the earliest indicators of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Subcortical brain areas are implicated in joint attention, but less is known about cortical regions and joint attention behaviours in infancy. In this longitudinal study, 101 high-risk infants (64% males) with an older biological sibling with ASD underwent MRI scanning at 4 or 6 months of age and were assessed for joint attention behaviours at 2 years of age. Brain volumes were automatically extracted. High-risk infants with ASD demonstrated atypical initiating and responding joint attention behaviours compared to those who did not. When examining cortical regions in relation to initiating and responding to joint attention behaviours, significant associations were found between the left posterior cingulate gyrus and impaired initiating joint attention in infants who developed ASD. Additionally, the right cuneus was associated with impaired initiating joint attention in this group. Better characterization of the neural mechanisms underlying initiating joint attention can help identify biomarkers to assess the efficacy of therapies to promote improved social and behavioural outcomes.

papers.title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

papers.title: KIF1A-driven entry of degradative lysosomes into the axon is developmentally regulated by the microtubule environment at the axon initial segment.
papers.abstract: Neuronal function requires precise transport of lysosomal vesicles along highly polarized processes, yet how this trafficking is spatially and developmentally regulated remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the neuronally enriched kinesin-3 motor KIF1A is required for dendritic and axonal localization of lysosomal vesicles in both immature and mature rat hippocampal neurons. Remarkably, the specialized microtubule environment of the axon initial segment (AIS) restricts KIF1A-driven transport of degradative, cathepsin D-positive lysosomal vesicles while permitting less degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter axons in mature neurons. Disrupting the AIS microtubule environment or expressing a hereditary spastic paraplegia type 30-associated KIF1A variant with increased affinity for GTP-tubulin bypasses this restriction, enabling degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter mature axons. In human iPSC-derived neurons, KIF1A depletion similarly disrupts axonal lysosomal vesicle transport, causes autophagic vesicle accumulation, and triggers axonal degeneration. Together, our findings reveal a developmentally regulated AIS gate that selectively controls KIF1A-driven lysosomal vesicle transport into axons and link its subversion to KIF1A-associated neurological disease.

papers.title: Parkinson’s disease genetic risk converges on Lewy body pathology-associated microglial states
papers.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) and related α-synucleinopathies are defined by the spread of Lewy body (LB) pathology across vulnerable brain regions, yet how substantia nigra (SN) myeloid cells respond remains unresolved. Using SOX10-based oligodendrocyte depletion and CD11b-based myeloid enrichment, we profiled 169,799 brain myeloid cells and nuclei from 96 donors spanning the LB continuum, including 86,427 from the SN, and integrated them with AMP PD for a total of 298,592 profiles. Across eight conserved states, α-synucleinopathy is associated with a bidirectional signature: upregulated glycolytic and proteostatic-stress programs alongside downregulated lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways. Microglia shift from P2RY12-high sensome cells toward an HSP90AA1-high proteostatic stress state, a transition that intensifies at late Braak LB stages. Immunohistochemistry confirmed that HSP60 + proteostatic microglia state proportions increase with SN neuron loss. A rare NUCKS1-high state (∼1% of myeloid cells), more abundant in late-stage disease, carried the strongest PD polygenic-risk loading. The PD-protective rs3732765-A allele, a microglial cis-eQTL that lowers P2RY12 expression, was nominally associated with a higher proportion of P2RY12-high microglia and higher lysosomal program activity. These findings frame microglial involvement as structured and genetically tractable, nominating the P2RY12 genetic axis and NUCKS1-high microglia for mechanistic studies.

papers.title: A candidate HNRNPU – CHD2 RNA-processing axis in neurodevelopmental disease
papers.abstract: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPU , which encodes a nuclear RNA-binding scaffold protein, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, intellectual disability and brain malformations, but the programs that link HNRNPU dosage to neuronal dysfunction remain poorly defined. We depleted HNRNPU in Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells, profiled gene expression and alternative splicing, intersected the two datasets, and asked which of the resulting genes already carried a neurodevelopmental annotation. Knockdown produced 5,643 differentially expressed genes and 21,728 high-confidence splicing events; 1,222 genes changed at both levels, and two pre-specified neurodevelopmental panel genes were among them: CHD2 and DYRK1A . In K562 eCLIP experiments, 107 reproducible HNRNPU peaks were detected across the CHD2 gene body, and three of the four regulated exons introduce a reading-frame shift whose premature termination codon lies far upstream of the final exon junction, predicting nonsense-mediated decay. Public K562 knockdown data reproduced the rise in CHD2 mRNA and the same skipped-exon change, and CHD2 depletion in the neural line SH-SY5Y altered cell-cycle, DNA-repair and neural gene programs. HNRNPU therefore constrains a frameshift-prone splicing switch in CHD2 , a candidate route from HNRNPU haploinsufficiency to loss of functional CHD2 if these transcripts are degraded. Highlights HNRNPU depletion changes CHD2 expression and exon inclusion in human cells. eCLIP places HNRNPU on CHD2 RNA, consistent with direct control of its splicing. Three CHD2 exons are frameshift-prone, predicting loss of full-length CHD2 .

papers.title: Organotchi: an open-source tool for the automated segmentation, morphological characterization, and longitudinal tracking of organoids
papers.abstract: Neural organoids are three-dimensional stem cell-derived models widely used to study brain development and model disease. Brightfield imaging offers a non-invasive readout of their growth and morphology, and recent advances have made automated organoid segmentation from such images increasingly attainable. Yet existing tools largely leave morphological characterization, quality assessment, and comparisons between conditions to manual or ad hoc analysis. Here we present Organotchi, an open-source tool that integrates automated segmentation with longitudinal morphological analysis of neural organoids. Organotchi quantifies ten morphological features, including area, perimeter, and eccentricity, and tracks cystic structures over time, reports variability within and between batches, and flags outlier organoids and segmentation failures, supporting objective organoid characterization and enhancing downstream analysis. As a proof of concept, we apply Organotchi to disease modelling, pharmacological perturbation, and protocol optimization in neural organoids. One use case assesses drug response in breast cancer spheroids, demonstrating its use beyond its development domain.

papers.title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
papers.abstract: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-μm-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. By shifting optical sectioning from instrumentation to gene expression, SPress makes kilohertz cellular resolution voltage imaging accessible across mesoscopic scales.

papers.title: Donor-Aware Reanalysis of Neuronal Nuclei Supports STMN2 Depletion Associated with Nuclear TDP-43 Loss in FTD and ALS
papers.abstract: Background Nuclear TDP-43 depletion is a central pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), but donor-to-donor variation can obscure transcriptomic associations in small postmortem cohorts. We reanalyzed public RNA-seq data from FACS-isolated NeuN-positive frontal-cortex neuronal nuclei to quantify gene-expression changes associated with nuclear TDP-43 loss while explicitly accounting for donor structure. Methods The supplied GSE126542-derived matrix contained 62,754 genes across 12 libraries from seven donors, including five complete matched pairs. Source labels “TDP-43 positive” and “TDP-43 negative” were harmonized as nuclear TDP-43 retained and lost, respectively. After validation against featureCounts-assigned read counts, 44,225 genes with at least 10 total counts were analyzed using PyDESeq2. The primary model was ∼ donor + nuclear_status; status-only and diagnosis-adjusted models were sensitivity analyses. The contrast was TDP-43 loss minus retained. Results The donor-aware model identified 3,442 genes at false discovery rate (FDR) Conclusions Donor-aware analysis supports a robust association between nuclear TDP-43 loss and STMN2 depletion in this neuronal-nuclei cohort, alongside extensive but model-dependent transcriptomic variation. Whole-gene UNC13A expression cannot be used to infer UNC13A cryptic-exon inclusion or functional UNC13A depletion. No splice-junction, percent-spliced-in, isoform, or protein measurements were available; mechanistic claims therefore require junction-level and experimental validation.

papers.title: Developmental perturbation of Purkinje cell function induces male-biased core and associated autism spectrum disorder–like phenotypes in adulthood
papers.abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition whose etiology remains incompletely understood. Human epidemiological studies have implicated the cerebellum in ASD pathogenesis, and studies in mouse models have provided evidence for a causal contribution of cerebellar dysfunction. However, previous animal studies have largely focused on males and cerebellar manipulations at later developmental stages, with associated features of ASD remaining less explored. To address these gaps, we chemogenetically perturbed Purkinje cell function during early postnatal development in both male and female mice. Developmental Purkinje cell perturbation induced male-biased core ASD-like behavioral phenotypes, including reduced sociability and cognitive inflexibility. Phenotypes related to associated features of ASD, including impaired fine motor learning, altered sensory processing, and sleep abnormalities, were also predominantly observed in males. At the molecular level, bulk RNA sequencing following developmental Purkinje cell perturbation identified candidate sex-dependent transcriptional changes in both the hindbrain and forebrain, suggesting that altered cerebellar activity during development can influence gene expression across distant brain regions. Together, these findings demonstrate that transient early postnatal perturbation of Purkinje cell function can produce diverse core and associated ASD-like phenotypes, predominantly in males, with evidence suggesting transcriptional changes beyond the cerebellum. This study highlights developmental cerebellar dysfunction as a potential contributor to sex differences in ASD vulnerability.

papers.title: Rare protein-disrupting variants in NPY5R, DLGAP1 and MAPK8IP3 segregate with OCD in two multiplex pedigrees.
papers.abstract: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is significantly heritable, but only a fraction of the contributory genetic variation has been identified, and the molecular etiology involved remains obscure. Identifying rare contributory variants of large effect would be an important milestone in helping to elucidate the mechanisms involved. Analysis of densely affected pedigrees is a potentially useful strategy to bypass the sample size challenges of standard case-control approaches. Here we performed whole genome sequencing (WGS) of 25 individuals across two multiplex OCD pedigrees. We prioritised rare variants using a Bayesian inference approach which incorporates variant pathogenicity and co-segregation with OCD. In the first pedigree, we identified a highly deleterious missense variant in NPY5R, carried by the majority of affected individuals. This gene is brain-expressed and has previously been implicated in panic disorder and internet addiction GWAS studies. In the second pedigree, we identified a large deletion of DLGAP1 and a missense variant in MAPK8IP3, that perfectly co-segregated in a specific branch of the family: both genes have previously been implicated in OCD and autism. Both genes contribute to a protein interaction network including ERBB4 and RAPGEF1 which we had previously identified in a large Tourette Syndrome pedigree. Our analysis suggests that both energy homeostasis and downstream signalling from the post-synaptic density may both be important avenues for future research.

papers.title: Anti-Parkinsonian Drugs Rescue Locomotor Deficits in JIP3 Knockout Zebrafish: Implications for Treating Patients with MAPK8IP3 -related Neurodevelopmental Disorders
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT MAPK8IP3- related neurodevelopmental disorders are a spectrum of rare conditions caused by de novo mutations in the MAPK8IP3 gene that encodes the JIP3 protein. These disorders are associated with a spectrum of neurodevelopmental symptoms that manifest in children and cause brain abnormalities, profound intellectual disabilities, movement disorders, and developmental delays. JIP3 is required for axonal transport of proteins and organelles between the soma and the synaptic terminal of neurons, a process critical for normal brain development and function. Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in JIP3 lead to impaired axonal transport and aggregation of cargo, which result in axonal swelling and stunted elongation. Despite these severe outcomes, disease mechanisms are poorly understood, and no current treatments are available. Here we conduct thorough morphological, behavioral, and motility phenotyping in the JIP3 knockout zebrafish and identify locomotor deficits and morphological abnormalities. To identify treatment options, we used insights from expert clinicians and the artificial intelligence tool, mediKanren, to identify drug candidates hypothesized to improve patient symptoms or compensate for the loss of JIP3 at the molecular level. We then prioritized drugs that are FDA-approved, safe for children, and readily available. These collective efforts identified amantadine and levodopa as candidate therapies and rescued motor phenotypes associated with JIP3 loss-of-function in zebrafish.

papers.title: Chronic Sleep Disruption Activates the Transcriptional Unfolded Protein Response and Induces Compartment-Specific Proteomic Changes in Mice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Sleep disruption (SD) is associated with adverse brain health and increased risk of dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the pathological mechanisms underlying this association are not fully understood. Preclinical studies have shown that acute SD impairs cognition by altering vulnerable synapses (molecular composition, ultrastructure, and function). However, the cumulative effects of chronic SD on the adult brain and its vulnerable synapses, that might contribute to AD risk, remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the impact of chronic SD on brain transcriptomic signatures and subcellular compartment-specific proteomic profiles to identify genes, proteins, and signaling pathways that might confer AD risk. Chronic SD induced a modest transcriptional stress response globally, whereas alterations were more pronounced in the synaptosomal (synapse-enriched P2 fractions) and whole-brain proteomes. Remarkably, chronic SD elicited unique proteomic alterations at the synaptic compartment were distinct from whole-brain effects, including increased proteins involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, regulation of dendritic spine morphogenesis, and regulation of long-term synaptic depression, compared to increased proteins involved in immune/inflammatory, glial responses and neuronal function at the whole-brain level. Consistent with the chronic SD-induced molecular signatures, we observed subtle ultrastructural changes in vulnerable CA1 hippocampal synapses, including reduced pre-synapse size and decreased synaptic vesicle density, which suggest that chronic SD modifies synaptic transmission and plasticity. Together, our findings indicate that chronic SD differentially impacts the brain and the synaptic proteome, nominating candidate therapeutic targets and signaling pathways for future mechanistic studies of chronic SD and how SD contributes to increased AD risk. Highlights Brain transcriptomics reveals chronic SD activates the unfolded protein response. Compartment-specific proteomics shows chronic SD drives unique compensatory changes. Chronic SD subtly alters the ultrastructure of vulnerable hippocampal CA1 synapses. We nominate candidate pathways that link effects of chronic SD to AD risk.

papers.title: Autophagy activator AA-20 engages CDK5 to promote lipophagy and improve neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Lipophagy, the selective degradation of lipid droplets (LDs) by autophagy, has the potential to ameliorate neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s (PD) and Alzheimer’s (AD), wherein LD accumulation has been linked to the exacerbation of the proteinopathy component of neurodegeneration. Pharmacological lipophagy inducers remain scarce. We previously identified AA-20 as a novel autophagy activator that acts independently of mTORC1 inhibition, thereby providing a means of stimulating autophagy while avoiding the immunosuppressive side effects associated with direct mTORC1 inhibition. Prior work also showed that AA-20 treatment reduces PolyQ aggregate levels in several C. elegans tissues. Here, we demonstrate that AA-20 enhances LD recruitment to autophagosomes and promotes LD degradation via lysosomal acid lipase activation in murine hippocampal neuronal cells, consistent with lipophagy activation. In human Swedish Amyloid Precursor Protein mutated cerebral organoids, two weeks of AA-20 treatment normalized aberrant lipidomic profiles by selectively reducing various disease-associated lipids, while also correcting the AD-associated electrical hyperexcitability phenotype. Moreover, we identified cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), a neuronal kinase linked to AD hyperexcitability and PD pathology, as a target of AA-20. AA-20-induced autophagy and lipid clearance in HT22 cells require CDK5. In a neuronal seeding model of α-synuclein pathology, AA-20 reduced pS129-α-synuclein levels. Collectively, these findings indicate AA-20 can promote lipophagic clearance of LDs and mitigate multiple cellular phenotypes associated with lipidopathy and proteinopathy in neurodegenerative disease models. SIGNIFICANCE Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are associated with impaired autophagy and abnormal lipid droplet (LD) accumulation. Few small molecules enhance neuronal lipid clearance without inhibiting mTORC1, but chronic blockade of which is associated with immunosuppressive and metabolic side effects. This study shows that AA-20, an mTORC1-independent autophagy activator, promotes lipophagic LD clearance in neuronal cells and reduces selected disease-associated lipids in human Alzheimer’s cerebral organoids in a lysosomal acid lipase-dependent manner. AA-20 binds CDK5 and appears to modulate, rather than classically inhibit, this neuron-enriched kinase. In an exploratory Parkinson’s neuron model, AA-20 also reduced pathological α-synuclein phosphorylation. These findings support further investigation of AA-20 as a tool to probe neuronal lipid clearance and neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes.

papers.title: Automahout: an autonomous image analysis system for cell tracking
papers.abstract: Cell tracking in time-lapse images is complex image analysis that involves detection, linking and proofreading, often requiring the algorithm to be tuned for every new dataset. We present Automahout, an autonomous agent for the Mastodon/ELEPHANT platform that carries out these operations. It looks at the data and tries existing models; where none fits, it annotates reference cells, trains a detector from those sparse annotations, reviews its output against them and feeds the corrections back until its own stopping criteria are met. It then links, checks the lineage and moves on. On three public datasets, a 2D fluorescence culture, a 2D phase-contrast culture and a 3D embryo, it produced lineages without human input and reached TRA scores of 0.95–0.96.

papers.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
papers.abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer’s Disease
papers.abstract: Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5×5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE ε4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 ± 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 ± 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 ± 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Transmural Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics Nominates Candidate Disease Programs in Human Necrotizing Enterocolitis
papers.abstract: Background: & Aims: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a life-threatening disease of premature infants marked by inflammation, ischemia, mucosal injury, and, in advanced cases, necrosis extending into deeper layers of the intestinal wall. Because NEC affects specialized, interacting cells in a developing intestine, we used single-nucleus transcriptomics to build a transmural, cell-type-resolved map and nominate hypothesis-generating disease programs distinct from maturation. Methods: Full-thickness intestinal specimens from fetal/prenatal controls, acute NEC cases, and infant controls were analyzed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Fetal and infant samples served as developmental references. Analyses included cell annotation, NEC-versus-infant differential expression, gene ontology (GO), cross-lineage recurrence, cell death signatures, and developmental maturity. Results: We profiled 53,735 nuclei by snRNA-seq and resolved 34 epithelial, stromal, vascular, immune, neuronal, glial, and smooth muscle populations. We used a morphology-based nuclei scoring system for sample selection that predicted high-quality transcript recovery. NEC nuclei were represented across this cellular landscape, with recurrent gene-expression changes suggesting shared inflammatory recruitment, antimicrobial/redox defense, stress adaptation, complement/vascular activation, reduced homeostatic signaling, and cell death-associated regulation. Developmental maturity analysis identified fetal-like expression levels in subsets of NEC-regulated genes. Proliferative crypt populations retained DNA repair/cell-cycle programs with inflammatory, hypoxic, and ER-stress features, while absorptive enterocytes showed reduced digestive, transport, detoxification, and terminal villus-function programs. Secretory-lineage changes implicated goblet mucus-barrier responses with reduced glycosylation, trafficking, and hydration; enteroendocrine changes in epithelial defense, metabolic stress, and neural signaling; and Paneth cell retention of antimicrobial effector transcripts despite altered ER quality control, autophagy, and granule delivery in NEC. Non-epithelial programs implicated stromal Wnt/BMP niche loss, impaired lymphatic drainage/scavenging, macrophage cytokine activation with reduced clearance machinery, neuroglial circuit defects, and altered smooth muscle contraction-relaxation balance. Conclusions: This single nuclear intestinal cell atlas nominates multicellular programs that may govern NEC initiation, progression toward tissue destruction, and resolution toward functional recovery.

papers.title: Stage–Specific Roles of Plasma GFAP in Linking Amyloid Cascade in Alzheimer Disease
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION Astrocytic reactivity, measured by plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), is robustly elevated across the Alzheimer disease (AD) continuum, yet its relationship with the amyloid cascade remains poorly understood. METHODS We integrated plasma GFAP with multimodal AD biomarkers including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or plasma Aβ (Aβ42/40), Aβ and tau positron emission tomography (PET), structural MRI, and clinical severity, across a discovery cohort (Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center, n=278) and an independent replication cohort (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, n=236). RESULTS In both cohorts, plasma GFAP mediated the association of soluble Aβ42/40 (CSF in the Knight ADRC; plasma in ADNI) with Aβ PET, as well as the association of Aβ PET with tau PET in the overall samples, which remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Among tau-negative individuals, GFAP mediated the association between CSF Aβ42/40 and Aβ PET in Knight ADRC, but this effect did not survive FDR correction with plasma Aβ42/40 in ADNI. In Aβ-positive individuals, GFAP mediated the association between Aβ PET and tau PET burden in both cohorts, but survived correction only in ADNI. Interaction findings were partially replicated across cohorts. Exploratory plasma proteomics further revealed a GFAP-associated protein network enriched for extracellular matrix (ECM)-immune remodeling network. DISCUSSION These findings reveal stage-specific associations of plasma GFAP with the amyloid cascade and implicate an astrocyte-centered ECM–inflammatory axis, which may inform future diagnostic panels or targeted therapies. papers.title: Inflammatory proteostasis reprogramming creates a lysosomal bottleneck for microglial aggregate clearance
papers.abstract: Efficient clearance of extracellular protein aggregates by microglia is essential for maintaining brain homeostasis and limiting the accumulation of pathological proteins during neurodegeneration. However, how inflammatory activation affects the ability of microglia to internalize and degrade these aggregates remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory activation impairs the degradation of extracellularly-acquired α-synuclein (α-Syn) and Tau aggregates while largely preserving their uptake. Mechanistically, Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation induces translational reprogramming and increases intracellular proteostatic demand, while inhibition of protein synthesis restores α-Syn degradation without preventing inflammatory Nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) activation. Despite largely preserved canonical autophagic flux, inflammatory stimulation is associated with reduced expression of lysosomal proteins, including cathepsin D, suggesting insufficient lysosomal adaptation to increased intracellular demand. Consistent with this model, pharmacological activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) restores aggregate degradation, indicating that the impairment can be overcome by enhancing lysosomal function. Supporting its potential relevance to human disease, microglial α-Syn deposits in brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies show limited spatial association with cathepsin D-positive structures. Together, our findings identify a demand-driven lysosomal bottleneck through which inflammatory activation compromises aggregate degradation without substantially affecting uptake, highlighting lysosomal adaptation as a critical determinant of microglial aggregate clearance during neuroinflammation.

papers.title: TMEM55B promotes anterograde transport and distal axonal distribution of LAMP1-positive organelles
papers.abstract: Lysosomal function throughout life is vital for the proper functioning and survival of post-mitotic neurons by mediating cellular signaling, degradation, and recycling processes. Their intracellular transport relies on microtubule-dependent mechanisms involving kinesin and dynein motors. While lysosomes were long thought absent from axons, recent studies have demonstrated the importance of LAMP1-positive endo-/lysosomal organelles in axonal compartments. This study investigates the physiological role of TMEM55B, a lysosomal membrane protein involved in lysosome positioning and motor coupling in neurons. TMEM55B is highly expressed in LAMP1-positive organelles in cortical neurons. We generated viable Tmem55b knockout mice that exhibited altered lysosomal positioning in neurons. Lysosomes clustered abnormally in the pre-axonal exclusion zone and the proximal axon, with many forming elongated tubular structures. Similarly, in primary rat neurons, TMEM55B depletion resulted in lysosomal tubulation and impaired bidirectional lysosomal transport, particularly in distal axon segments, without affecting lysosome velocity in the proximal and mid-axon. These transport defects were consistent with disrupted JIP4 function, a scaffold linking TMEM55B to both dynein and kinesin motors. TMEM55B deficiency did not result in neurodegeneration, behavioral deficits, or reduced lifespan in mice. As an orthogonal approach, we analyzed TMEM55B function in C. elegans . Worms lacking the TMEM55B homolog Y71H2AM.2 showed altered lysosomal dynamics in cholinergic neurons, supporting an evolutionarily conserved role. To test the involvement of TMEM55B’s paralog, TMEM55A, in regulating neuronal lysosome positioning, we generated Tmem55a/b double-knockout mice, which exhibit impaired growth, premature death, and an overall aggravated phenotype. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that both TMEM55B and TMEM55A regulate lysosome distribution in neurons, particularly in axons, by influencing JIP4-dependent retro- and, notably, anterograde motor protein-mediated transport. This function is critical for spatial lysosomal homeostasis. Our study underscores the importance of TMEM55A/TMEM55B in regulating neuronal organelle dynamics and may be a factor considered in neurodegenerative diseases involving lysosomal trafficking defects.

papers.title: Longitudinal single-cell transcriptional profiling identifies dynamic neurodegenerative mechanisms in Christianson Syndrome rat
papers.abstract: Endolysosomal dysfunction is a central feature of many neurodegenerative disorders. Loss-of-function mutations in the endosomal Na+/H+ exchanger NHE6 cause lysosomal dysfunction and the early-onset neurodegenerative disorder Christianson syndrome (CS). CS shares pathological features with more common neurodegenerative diseases; however, the extent of mechanistic overlap remains unclear. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing across the lifespan in a CS rat model, we define the temporal progression of disease at single-cell resolution in the hippocampus. Neurons exhibit early transcriptional signatures of mitochondrial dysfunction. We investigated mitochondrial function in vitro and ex vivo and discover progressive defects in mitochondrial quality control and bioenergetics in NHE6-null tissue. Furthermore, both transcriptomic and proteomic analyses reveal robust activation of innate immunity, including cGAS-STING signaling which localizes to microglia. Therefore, in CS rat brain, early neuronal endosomal and mitochondrial impairments are followed by pronounced microglial and astrocytic activation, as well as age-dependent decline in oligodendrocyte myelinating capacity. Cross species comparison reveals substantial overlap between single-cell analyses in CS rat and in human postmortem Alzheimers disease hippocampus. Together, our findings define the cellular trajectories of neurodegeneration in CS, and identify convergent endolysosomal, mitochondrial, and inflammatory mechanisms that support a broader role for endolysosomal dysfunction in Alzheimers disease pathogenesis.

papers.title: MAST1 is neuron-specific regulator of mitochondrial trafficking and abundance in human brain tissue
papers.abstract: In human neurons, energy-demanding axonal and dendritic development requires sufficient mitochondrial distribution at distal locations, and the responsible mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here, we characterize rare de novo mutations in microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 1 (MAST1) in patients with multiple neurodevelopmental abnormalities, including microcephaly and thin corpus callosum. Experiments using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived telencephalic brain organoids and cortical neurons from patients and unaffected parents, as well as engineered lines demonstrate association of the MAST1 mutations with organoid growth deficits and impaired neurites. Mechanistically, the MAST1 mutations alter its interaction with mitochondria as well as mitochondrial trafficking and abundance, increasing the proportion of hyperactive mitochondria and reactive oxygen species accumulation. Exogenous wild-type MAST1 expression rescues neurite outgrowth in mutant neurons, as does prolonged treatment with creatine or N-acetyl-L-cysteine. This study identifies MAST1 as an important regulator of mitochondrial properties in human neurons and links microcephaly-associated MAST1 mutations to neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired neurites, and neuronal loss.

papers.title: Mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors at mouse brain hippocampal synapses by cryo-ET.
papers.abstract: AMPA and NMDA receptors are fundamental to synaptic transmission through the detection of released neurotransmitter. These ion channels open in response to glutamate binding, resulting in depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and influx of calcium. Receptor localization plays a key role in synaptic strength, and changes in receptor number and location underpin synaptic plasticity, learning and memory. Here we apply receptor subunit-specific antibody fragments and multiplexed gold nanoparticle conjugates, together with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), to elucidate the in-situ molecular organization of AMPA and NMDA receptors at hippocampal synapses in adult mouse brain tissue. AMPA receptors are predominantly found in densely packed liquid-like clusters, with interspersed NMDA receptors and adjacent NMDA receptor clusters. By direct localization of individual receptors, we provide molecular-resolution insight into the distribution of AMPA and NMDA receptors across the synapse, at peri and extrasynaptic sites, and within endocytosed vesicles. Visualization of multiple presynaptic vesicle fusion events suggests that receptors are near, but not always directly adjacent to, transmitter release sites. By mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors, and glutamate release sites, we provide receptor-resolution insight into the structure and function of brain hippocampal synapses.

papers.title: A compact three-way junction oligonucleotide probe for widefield and super-resolution imaging of RNAs and proteins
papers.abstract: Molecular imaging of RNAs and proteins requires methods that preserve nanoscale organization while enabling large-scale tissue analysis. However, weak or low-abundance targets often need signal amplification, which can increase labeling size, background, or signal spread and compromise super-resolution imaging. Here, we report a compact three-way junction (3WJ) oligonucleotide probe platform for multiscale RNA and protein imaging. The design couples paired target recognition with junction assembly and recruitment of preassembled amplifier complexes, while tunable amplification balances signal strength and labeling size. Using DNA origami and single-molecule localization microscopy, we show enhanced signal while retaining the ability to resolve nanoscale target patterns. The platform improves RNA detection and supports simultaneous RNA-protein super-resolution imaging in cells. It also enhances protein detection in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues under low-numerical-aperture, large-field imaging conditions. Together, this programmable 3WJ platform enables sensitive RNA and protein detection across scales, supporting super-resolution analysis of molecular organization and large-field tissue mapping.

papers.title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor Aβ aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including Aβ neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment. MOTIVATION: High-throughput in vitro drug screening using cerebral organoids (COs) has great potential to accelerate drug discovery efforts for treating Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative diseases. However, live fluorescence imaging of COs has proved challenging due to their dense, optically opaque tissue. Furthermore, conventional COs lack microglia which are key immunomodulators of pathogenesis in the AD brain. To address these limitations, we developed and optimized a live organoid imaging approach employing the fluorescent amyloid-binding probe PyrPeg to label amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregates within human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We achieved selective labeling and visualization of Aβ neuropathology in intact live MCOs and observed increased age-associated Aβ accumulation in MCOs derived from donors with trisomy 21 (T21) relative to disomy 21 (D21), consistent with the Down syndrome-associated AD (DS-AD) phenotype in the human brain. This method establishes a platform for high-throughput longitudinal drug screening in immunocompetent human COs that will enable the identification of new therapeutic candidates to modulate Aβ aggregation, glial reactivity, and neurodegeneration. HIGHLIGHTS: A platform was developed for high-resolution in vitro visualization of insoluble Aβ aggregates in live MCOs. The approach enables deep tissue imaging of Aβ pathology in intact 3D MCOs, allowing spatial mapping of Aβ aggregate distribution over time.Differences in Aβ burden and viability of neurons, neural progenitors, and astrocytes were quantified, distinguishing T21 COs from D21 control MCOs.The platform is positioned to support high-throughput longitudinal drug screening, providing a scalable tool to identify novel therapeutics targeting Aβ-mediated neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Aqueous Humor Proteomic Analysis Identifies Diagnostic Biomarkers for Autoimmune Optic Neuritis
papers.abstract: Abstract Autoimmune optic neuritis (AON) is an inflammatory optic neuropathy that commonly presents with acute or subacute visual loss. In the early stage, AON may overlap clinically with other optic neuropathies, particularly non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). Although serum and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers can provide diagnostic assistance, they do not directly reflect the local ocular microenvironment. In this study, aqueous humor (AH) was used as a local liquid biopsy source to identify candidate molecules associated with AON. Data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics was applied to analyze AH proteins obtained from patients with AON, patients with NAION, and presbyopic surgical controls (CTL group) during anterior chamber paracentesis or surgery. Candidate biomarkers were subsequently quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Proteomic analysis identified 4,264 proteins from 18 samples. Gene Ontology annotation and functional analysis showed that AON-related biological processes were mainly associated with immune responses, ganglioside biosynthesis, glycoprotein biosynthesis, lysosomal function, and protein translation. Candidate protein selection integrated fold change, biological module relevance, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network centrality, and ELISA feasibility, leading to the selection of lactoferrin (LTF), ribosomal protein SA (RPSA), and ATPase H+ transporting V1 subunit A (ATP6V1A) for further validation. The results showed that LTF concentration differed significantly between the AON and CTL groups and demonstrated diagnostic utility in receiver operating characteristic analysis, suggesting that LTF may serve as a potential aqueous humor biomarker for AON. In contrast, RPSA and ATP6V1A did not show stable intergroup differences during validation; nevertheless, the protein translation stress and lysosome-related pathways represented by these molecules suggest corresponding functional alterations in the AH microenvironment of AON. Overall, this study provides an initial characterization of the AH proteomic profile in AON and indicates that AH proteomics may offer a new approach for elucidating local pathological mechanisms and identifying fluid-based diagnostic biomarkers for AON.

papers.title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson’s disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell’s proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic. Inclusions took up whole assemblies, with subunits moving together in 421 of 438 complexes, and the V-ATPase alone was enriched in all three systems. Degradation cargo stayed with the receptors that route it, consistent with sequestration and failed degradation acting together. Neuritic and somatic inclusions differed, the former rich in UBQLN2 and the latter in intermediate filaments. In the cell line, phosphorylated α-synuclein was tenfold higher in the inclusion than in the rest of the cell, with about one third of the rise already present before an inclusion was visible. Measured against its host, the composition of an inclusion becomes a readout of how it formed and a source of candidate markers and therapeutic targets.

papers.title: CD40 ligand and IFN-γ induce proinflammatory activity and microglia-mediated neurodegeneration in human stem cell models
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The cluster of differentiation 40 (CD40)/CD40 ligand (CD40L) co-stimulatory pathway plays a critical role in the activation and regulation of immune networks involving both adaptive and innate immune cells. Dysregulation of this pathway has been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration driven by compartmentalized neuroinflammation within the central nervous system (CNS), sustained low-grade T cell infiltration at the blood-brain barrier, and T cell reactivation at CNS border tissues. CD40L-expressing T cells can activate CD40-expressing microglia, which are a critical effector cell that contribute to neurodegeneration in MS. However, the consequence of this functional interaction in the brain remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the combination of CD40L and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), a cytokine produced by activated T cells, induces a robust inflammatory response and cell death in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived microglia. Stimulation with CD40L elicited microglial clustering, morphological transformation, and robust release of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and IL-6. Anti-CD40L antibody treatment reversed both cell death and inflammatory response and partially normalized the associated transcriptional changes. Furthermore, using an hiPSC-derived tri-culture system comprising neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, we demonstrated that CD40L and IFN-γ trigger microglia-dependent neuronal dysregulation and death. Anti-CD40L treatment substantially attenuated neuronal injury. Finally, transcriptomic enrichment analysis identified CD40L-mediated microglial gene expression signatures that correlated with CD40 expression in primary progressive MS brain tissue but not in the normal-appearing white matter of healthy controls. Collectively, these findings support a role for the microglial CD40/T cell CD40L axis in MS pathology and suggest CD40L blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy warranting further investigation.

papers.title: COG5-mediated Golgi organization coordinates neural progenitor fate during human brain development
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Apical radial glial cells (aRGs) are highly polarized epithelial cells that drive human cortical development through tightly regulated lineage progression. A distinctive feature of aRGs is their non-canonical Golgi organization, raising the possibility that specialized intracellular trafficking and secretory processes contribute to progenitor behaviour. However, how Golgi architecture contributes to human corticogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in the context of COG5 deficiency, a rare congenital disorder of glycosylation associated with neurodevelopmental defects, using patient-derived fibroblasts and brain organoids, N-glycomics, glycolipidomics, and single-cell transcriptomics. We show that COG5 deficiency disrupts Golgi organization and impairs Golgi-to-ER retrograde trafficking. At the neurodevelopmental level, COG5-deficient organoids display altered ventricular organization and reduced basal progenitor abundance. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals rewired developmental trajectories characterized by premature differentiation from apical progenitors with activation of neuronal pathways. Despite the absence of major abnormalities in plasma glycoproteins glycosylation, glycolipidomic analysis identified marked defects in glycosphingolipid maturation within patient-derived brain organoids, indicating selective impairment of neural lipid glycosylation. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of developmental pathways, including reduced Notch signalling and altered localization of both cleaved Notch1 and the Golgi-associated protein ACBD3. Consistent with impaired progenitor maintenance, COG5-deficient organoids displayed altered cleavage plane orientation in apical progenitors. Together, our findings suggest a link between Golgi organization, intracellular trafficking, membrane glycosylation, and lineage progression in human neural progenitors, identifying Golgi architecture as an important regulator of apical radial glial cell biology and cortical development.

papers.title: Matrix stiffness-related transcriptomic signatures reveal astrocyte-centered neuroimmune alterations in Alzheimer’s disease
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Extracellular matrix remodeling and altered tissue mechanics are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but links between matrix stiffness and AD pathology remain unclear. Objective To identify matrix stiffness-related transcriptomic signatures in AD and characterize their diagnostic potential, functions, cell-type specificity, and intercellular communication patterns. Methods Bulk transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus were integrated with literature-derived matrix stiffness-related genes. Differential expression analysis, three machine-learning algorithms, and cross-dataset validation were used to identify candidate genes and construct a multigene classification model. Functional enrichment and immune-cell deconvolution analyses were performed. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed to assess cell-type-specific expression, inferred astrocyte trajectories, and predicted cell–cell communication. Results Eighty-one differentially expressed matrix stiffness-related genes were identified in AD brain tissue. FREM3, DUSP4, and FAM107A were selected and showed concordant differential expression across discovery and validation datasets. The three-gene model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.963 in the discovery cohort. Gene set enrichment analysis linked all three genes to oxidative phosphorylation, although FAM107A showed an enrichment direction opposite to DUSP4 and FREM3. Immune deconvolution suggested associations with immune-cell signatures. Single-cell analysis identified astrocytes as a major population expressing the three-gene signature. AD astrocytes showed altered pseudotime distributions and stronger predicted communication with immune cells, particularly T cells and macrophages. Conclusions FREM3, DUSP4, and FAM107A are candidate matrix stiffness-related transcriptomic signatures in AD and may connect extracellular matrix remodeling with mitochondrial metabolism, immune dysregulation, and astrocyte-associated changes. Independent clinical validation and experimental confirmation are required.

papers.title: Critical regions for human brain development include SON and ITSN1 defined by a panel with chromosome 21 interstitial deletions.
papers.abstract: Abstract Aneuploidies of chromosome 21 (CHR21), including Down syndrome and partial monosomy 21, are major causes of mental retardation and provide unique opportunities to identify candidate genes regulating human brain development. We identified 10 individuals with partial CHR21 deletions and defined molecular breakpoints with high resolution genomic arrays, FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) and quantitative Southern blots. Patient records and neuroimaging generated by the authors or by referring physicians were reviewed. We defined regions from proximal to distal on CHR21, a region consistent with a normal range of cognition, a region associated with microcephaly, and a third region associated with polymicrogyria and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. Three individuals with severe cortical dysgenesis including polymicrogyria (PMG) with callosal hypoplasia or agenesis shared a ~649 kb minimal region at 21q22.11-22.2 whose distal border lies within ITSN1 and contains SON. Seven individuals with large proximal deletions outside this interval, had mild cognitive deficits and did not share this phenotype. Comparison of the human phenotypes with those seen with loss-of function mutations in SON or ITSN1 indicate that the 649kb deleted region disturbs vertebrate brain development with components likely attributable to ITSN1 and SON.

papers.title: Generation of human iPSC-derived motor neurons with defined regional identities across the rostrocaudal axis
papers.abstract: This study establishes a unified pipeline for generating human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (iMNs) with defined hindbrain, cervical, and lumbar identities to support anatomically resolved studies of motor neuron development and degeneration. Conventional differentiation methods can efficiently produce iMNs but provide limited control over rostrocaudal identity and frequently generate populations with heterogeneous HOX profiles. We addressed this limitation by optimizing developmental morphogen combinations and treatment windows, establishing three complementary protocols that reproducibly generated hindbrain/rhombomere-associated motor neurons (RiMNs), cervical motor neurons (CiMNs), and lumbar motor neurons (LiMNs) across iPSC lines from six non-diseased donors balanced by sex. Transcriptomic and protein analyses demonstrated graded rostrocaudal specification from RiMNs through CiMNs to LiMNs, together with region-appropriate motor neuron subtype features. These identities showed the expected relationships to human week 9 fetal rostrocaudal HOX programs. High-density multielectrode array analysis further revealed synchronized network firing, electrically active neurite networks, and enhanced axonal signal propagation in the regional iMN populations compared with conventionally differentiated iMNs. Spike-sorted recordings additionally revealed protocol-associated differences in single-neuron electrophysiological profiles. Together, this three-protocol pipeline enables the reproducible generation and comparative analysis of anatomically defined human motor neuron populations and provides region-matched cellular models for investigating motor neuron development, selective degeneration, and therapeutic responses.

papers.title: TMEM55B downregulation promotes neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease models.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Lysosomal distribution is critical for numerous biological functions within the cell, including protein degradation in autophagosomes, cholesterol homeostasis, and cell invasion. Changes in the positioning of lysosomes and dysregulation of lysosomal trafficking are known to contribute to different human pathologies, such as lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer. Here we report the critical role of the lysosomal T ransmembrane P rotein 55B (TMEM55B) in mediating neurodegeneration. Using human clinical-pathological datasets, transgenic flies and iPSC-derived neurons, we demonstrate that loss of function of dTMEM55 potentiates neuronal degeneration. We found that TMEM55B levels are lowered in severe Alzheimer's Disease (AD) cases, validated from microarray, single neuron and total RNA Seq datasets from brain sections of the ROSMAP cohort. Our results demonstrates that loss of function of dTMEM55 results in accumulation of lysosomes in the fly's larval neuronal axons, enhances Tau-mediated retinal degeneration, locomotory dysfunction, lethality, and cell death in the fly AD model. The iPSC-derived AD neurons exhibit reduced TMEM55B levels, autophagic flux defects and increased accumulation of phosphorylated Tau in the lysosomes, confirming the observations in the fly. Overall, our findings indicate that TMEM55B downregulation could contribute to neurodegeneration through defects in lysosomal transport, potentially hindering autophagic clearance of Tau. Our findings have significant relevance in validating the role of lysosomal proteins in normal lysosomal function and maintaining healthy neurons. This work supports continued research into lysosome-mediated neurodegeneration and may provide a basis for exploring potential therapeutic approaches for lysosome-associated neuronal disorders. HIGHLIGHTS: TMEM55B expression is significantly reduced in postmortem brain tissues of patients with severe AD. Genetic loss of TMEM55B enhances Tau-mediated neurodegeneration in Drosophila , indicating a conserved neuroprotective function. TMEM55B regulates neuronal lysosomal positioning across species, and its loss disrupts lysosomal transport.iPSC-derived Alzheimer's disease neurons exhibit late-stage TMEM55B downregulation concomitant with increased accumulation of pathological phosphorylated Tau.Impaired lysosomal trafficking provides a mechanistic link between TMEM55B loss and progressive neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Exploratory Proteomics of Brain Extracellular Vesicle Enriched Preparations After LPS Challenge and miRNA Associated Vesicle Administration
papers.abstract: We used brain extracellular vesicle (EV) proteomics to identify protein responses to acute neuroinflammation and an EV-based microRNA intervention. Rats received vehicle, intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or LPS followed by an intravenous EV formulation containing anti-inflammatory microRNAs (miRNAs). Brains were collected 24 h after LPS or vehicle administration, and three independently processed animal-derived EV-enriched preparations per group were analyzed by label-free proteomics. Across all nine samples, 953 protein groups had complete normalized abundance measurements. Compared with vehicle controls, LPS exposure was associated with 227 exploratory protein changes, comprising 95 increases and 132 decreases at nominal P < 0.05 and an absolute log 2 fold change ≥ log 2 (1.5). Increased proteins were enriched for translation-related annotations, whereas decreased proteins were enriched for plasma-membrane annotations. These LPS-associated changes did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of q < 0.05. Following treatment, 119 of the 227 candidates were closer to control abundance on the log 2 scale; 23 candidates also showed nominal treatment-versus-LPS differences. Lamb2 and Ptgfrn were the two proteins that differed significantly between treated and LPS-only animals after FDR correction, identifying them as priorities for further validation. Nevertheless, 174 proteins differed significantly between treated animals and vehicle controls, and analysis across the measured proteins did not demonstrate an overall shift toward control values. Thus, the intervention was associated with specific protein responses, but treated animals retained substantial differences from controls. This study identifies candidate markers for investigating treatment responses in brain EV-enriched preparations and demonstrates the value of examining individual proteins alongside broader proteomic changes. Independent validation is needed to determine their functional relevance and distinguish miRNA-specific effects from contributions of the administered EV carrier.

papers.title: JIP4 deficiency causes a lysosomal storage disease arising from impaired cystine efflux.
papers.abstract: Lysosomes break down macromolecules, clear cellular waste and recycle nutrients such as cystine. We describe a novel mechanism whereby JIP4 regulates lysosomal cystine storage by controlling the abundance of cystinosin (CTNS), the transporter responsible for lysosomal cystine efflux. To this end, JIP4, previously characterized as a motor adaptor and kinase signaling scaffold, suppresses TMEM55B-dependent ubiquitylation of CTNS. Loss of JIP4 reduces CTNS protein levels, leading to lysosomal cystine accumulation and lysosomal storage defects that phenocopy loss of CTNS in both human cells and the renal proximal tubules of JIP4 knockout mice. These phenotypes mirror cystinosis, the lysosomal storage disease caused by CTNS loss-of-function. Our findings thus reveal a fundamental process that controls the efflux of lysosomal cystine and has relevance to understanding human disease arising from JIP4 mutations.

papers.title: Network analysis of mouse brain proteomes resolves molecular and cellular endophenotypes of aging and Aβ pathology
papers.abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology exert both shared and distinct effects on the brain, yet their relative contributions to molecular alterations remain poorly defined. Here we performed tandem mass tag proteomics across the lifespan in wild-type and 5xFAD mice and integrated these data with human brain proteomic networks to resolve aging- and amyloid-beta (Aβ-associated molecular programs. We quantified 8,535 proteins and identified 51 co-expression modules representing neuronal, mitochondrial, glial, vascular and proteostatic pathways. Aging emerged as the predominant driver of proteomic remodeling, with widespread alterations in RNA metabolism, protein translation, and neuronal pathways occurring independently of Aβ pathology. In contrast, Aβ selectively modified a subset of age-dependent processes, including suppression of mitochondrial ATP biosynthetic machinery and amplification of astrocytic and microglial activation states. These key aging and disease-related molecular signatures were highly conserved in human AD brain proteomes. Together, our findings establish aging as the primary determinant of brain proteome organization while revealing specific mechanisms through which Aβ pathology reshapes age-associated biological processes. Our results also highlight molecular mechanisms of human aging and AD pathology that can be modeled in mouse models.

papers.title: SNX13 and SNX14 interorganelle tethers suppress lysosome membrane damage and neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Lysosome membrane permeabilization (LMP) is an emerging signature of neurodegenerative diseases, yet the mechanisms that enable an effective repair are largely undefined, particularly in neurons. Here, we reveal sorting nexin (SNX) proteins SNX13 and SNX14 maintain lysosome membrane lipid composition to support efficient LMP repair and neuronal survival. We identify loss of function mutations in SNX13 in children manifesting a previously unrecognized cerebellar neurodegenerative disorder. Consistently, Snx13 ablation in mice causes cerebellar Purkinje cell death and signatures of ataxia-like motor deficits. We show loss of SNX13 or its ataxia-linked paralog SNX14 perturbs lysosome morphology, positioning, and acidity and causes increased susceptibility to lysosome damage. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation and proteomics, we comprehensively map lysosome proteome remodeling during membrane damage and repair, finding that SNX13 or SNX14 deficiency blunts recruitment of repair machinery, including ESCRTs and PITT pathway proteins, to damaged lysosomes. Mechanistically, we determine SNX13 and SNX14 support lysosome integrity through interorganelle lipid crosstalk. We define SNX13 and SNX14 as lipid binding proteins that localize to ER-lysosome junctions, where they support lysosomal phosphoinositide levels in response to membrane damage. In line with this, loss of SNX13 or SNX14 impairs lysosome PtdIns4P signaling. Altogether, our work reveals a conserved mechanism of interorganelle lipid crosstalk by SNX13/14 family proteins that safeguards lysosome membranes, maintaining them competent for repair, and is defective in cerebellar neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Apolipoprotein E4 Exacerbates Aβ Oligomer-Induced Synaptotoxicity through Promoting Autophagic Degradation of Glutathione Peroxidase 4
papers.abstract: Extensive synaptic loss and progressive neurodegeneration are defining pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), primarily driven by soluble Aβ oligomers (AβO) and neurofibrillary tangles. The apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) isoform further aggravates these pathological cascades, yet the precise molecular mechanisms underlying AD pathogenesis remain poorly elucidated. Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) deficiency in neurons has been proven to exert detrimental effect on dendritic spine integrity and function. Herein, we investigated whether SOCE dysregulation contributes to AβO-induced synaptotoxicity and how APOE4 modulates this pathological process. In primary neuronal cultures, co-treatment with AβO and APOE4 markedly reduced synapse density and impaired dendritic arbor complexity, compared with AβO treatments combined with APOE3 or APOE2 isoforms. Consistently, neurons exposed to AβO plus APOE4 exhibited significantly lower SOCE amplitudes than those treated with AβO and APOE3. In line with SOCE suppression, the AβO/APOE4 combination specifically downregulated stromal interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) protein expression, with no observable change in STIM2 levels. Mechanistically, AβO/APOE4-mediated STIM1 reduction was dependent on p62-selective autophagic degradation. Notably, exogenous STIM1 overexpression effectively rescued the deficits in dendritic arbor complexity. Furthermore, STIM1 downregulation induced by AβO and APOE4 initiated the autophagic degradation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4). This autophagy activation was attributed to decreased Bcl2 expression and occurs independently of STING accumulation. Subsequent Gpx4 insufficiency further triggered excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species and disrupted mitochondrial cristae morphology in neurons. Collectively, our findings uncover a previous unrecognized mechanism whereby APOE4 exacerbates AβO-induced synaptotoxicity. Specifically, the combination facilitates p62-mediated selective autophagic degradation of STIM1, which suppresses Bcl2 expression and ultimately promotes robust Gpx4 autophagic degradation, driving neuronal synaptic damage. Graphic abstract Schematic overview of this study Aβ oligomers (Aβo), together with APOE4, suppress store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) via STIM1 protein downregulation, which reduces dendritic arbor complexity and compromises synaptic integrity. STIM1 depletion is mediated through the p62-dependent selective autophagy pathway. Deficient SOCE further lowers Bcl2 expression, thereby inducing bulk autophagy-dependent degradation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) — a critical antioxidant enzyme. This cascade drives reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and disrupts mitochondrial cristae architecture.

papers.title: Multiscale Transcriptomic Architecture of the ALS Motor Cortex
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibits marked clinical and molecular heterogeneity, but how this heterogeneity is organized within disease-relevant central nervous system regions remains incompletely understood. Because pooled cross-region analyses may confound regional variation with subtype structure, we focused on the motor cortex, a key site of ALS pathology, to resolve its internal transcriptomic organization. Using approximately 600 postmortem motor cortex transcriptomes from the Target ALS resource, we applied gene set variation analysis to generate sample-level pathway activity profiles and performed consensus clustering in pathway space. We identified seven reproducible ALS motor cortex subtypes characterized by distinct inflammatory, damage-response, metabolic, glial, and neuronal/synaptic programs. Donor-held-out projection recovered the seven subtype assignments with a mean balanced accuracy of 0.939, supporting the reproducibility of the pathway-defined subtype structure in unseen donors. Mapping these bulk-defined programs to an independent motor-cortex single-nucleus RNA-seq dataset revealed distinct cellular contexts, while cell-type marker adjustment showed that cellular differences contributed to, but did not fully account for, subtype-associated pathway variation. The seven subtypes also recapitulated major molecular programs reported in previous ALS subtype frameworks while resolving them into finer motor-cortex- specific states. Rather than forming isolated molecular classes, these subtypes occupied a structured pathway-space landscape with both discrete subtype-centered peaks and continuous biological gradients. Principal component analysis and representative pathway overlays defined a major axis from an upper inflammatory/damage region to a lower neuronal/metabolic/remodeling region, with C7 forming a neuronal/synaptic connector within the lower landscape. Co-expression network analysis further supported this multiscale organization, revealing family-level network backbones, subtype- specific modular refinements, and bridge-like rewiring. Metadata-informed analyses showed that this molecular architecture was not primarily organized by disease duration. Instead, the landscape was more clearly associated with clinical and genetic-background variables, including ALS/FTD family history and mutation-related signals. In particular, family-history-positive and C9orf72 repeat expansion-positive samples were more represented in the lower neuronal/metabolic/remodeling region, whereas family-history-negative samples and C9orf72-negative cases were more represented in the upper inflammatory/damage region. These findings support a model in which ALS motor cortex heterogeneity is organized as a multiscale transcriptomic architecture more closely associated with genetic-background variables than with disease duration. This framework provides a basis for subtype- aware biological comparison, future patient-stratification, biomarker, or therapeutic target- prioritization studies.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation is an early pathological process in a mouse model of prodromal Parkinson’s disease
papers.abstract: Approximately 90% of Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients exhibit olfactory deficits, which often precedes motor symptoms by years, and are a robust predictor for PD and subsequent cognitive decline. Pathological changes in the PD olfactory system, particularly α-synuclein (αSyn) pathology in the olfactory bulb (OB) and severe involvement of the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), are distinct from normal aging. However, the causal link between αSyn aggregation and functional impairment, potentially involving cytotoxicity and neuroinflammation, remains elusive. To investigate these early pathological events, we utilized a prodromal PD model that we have previously characterized, involving the unilateral OB injection of αSyn pre-formed fibrils (PFF) in wild-type mice. This triggers the transneuronal spread of pathogenic αSyn, and olfactory dysfunction starting at 1-month post-injections. Here we report on neuropathological and inflammatory events 1–3 month following injection of PFFs into the OB. Following PFF injection, αSyn pSer129 pathology progressively accumulated bilaterally in the AON and ipsilateral in the piriform cortex (PCX) over three months. Stereological quantification revealed no significant neuronal loss in the AON or PCX during this 1–3 month interval, indicating that olfactory impairment precedes overt neurodegeneration. Instead, we identified the upregulation of pro-inflammatory genes ( Il- 1β and Il-6 ), significant microglial reactivity, and sustained astrogliosis within olfactory structures. These findings identify neuroinflammation as a key early mediator linking αSyn pathology to olfactory dysfunction in the absence of neuronal loss. This suggests a critical window for therapeutic intervention and highlights neuroinflammatory markers as potential biomarkers for the prodromal phase of PD. Highlights Neuroinflammation Precedes Neuron Loss. Inflammation is an early pathological process that is detected before any significant loss of NeuN-positive neurons in olfactory structures. Progressive αSyn pSer129 spreading. Pathological αSyn pSer129 progressively spreads transneuronally from the injection site in the OB to secondary olfactory structures (AON and PCX) within 1 to 3 months. Early Microglial Reactivity. The spreading of αSyn pSer129 pathology rapidly induces microglial reactivity, which is prominent at the 1- and 2-month time points. Persistent Astrogliosis. Astrogliosis is also an early and persistent component of the neuroinflammatory response, starting at 1 month and remaining detectable through 3 months, suggesting a sustained inflammatory environment.

papers.title: STING activation drives pericentrosomal positioning of acidic organelles via the VAIL-LRRK2-Rab35 pathway
papers.abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is an innate immune system that responds to cytoplasmic double-stranded DNA, but recent studies have highlighted its noncanonical role in facilitating lysosomal stress responses. Specifically, STING activation has been shown to trigger V-ATPase-ATG16L1-induced LC3 lipidation (VAIL) and to activate LRRK2, a Parkinson disease-associated kinase, but the detailed molecular mechanism and the physiological roles of the activation have remained unclear. Here, we found that STING activation in microglia induces the translocation of LRRK2 to the pericentrosomal area, where lysosomes and recycling endosomes (REs) concentrate. This process was VAIL-dependent, and LRRK2 was found to be localized to the organelles. The translocation of LRRK2 required intact microtubule structures and was mediated by LRRK2 kinase activity, its substrate Rab35 and the motor adaptor proteins including JIP4. All these proteins were concentrated at the pericentrosomal area upon STING stimulation. The hyperactivating G2019S mutation of LRRK2 promoted the pericentrosomal translocation of these proteins. Overall, we propose a novel STING-induced noncanonical pathway that involves LRRK2 to facilitate pericentrosomal organelle positioning.

papers.title: Trisomy 21 Perturbs Oligodendrocyte Developmental States and Oligo–Neuron Communication in Human Forebrain Assembloids
papers.abstract: Intellectual disability is a hallmark of Down syndrome (DS), caused by the triplication of human chromosome 21. Abnormal neuronal connectivity and impaired myelination are consistently observed in DS, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we used DS-derived isogenic induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain assembloids (FAs) to investigate oligodendrocyte lineage cell (OLLC) development and neuron–glia interactions. Trisomic FAs exhibited an expansion of BCAS1+ pre-myelinating OLLCs, without a corresponding increase in myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. Transcriptomic analyses identified a euploid-enriched, trophic and maturation-supportive state (OLLC_2-TMS) and a trisomy-enriched synaptic interactions and differentiation state (OLLC_3-SID), lacking coordinated enrichment in myelination-promoting programs. Corresponding transcriptional signatures were identified in OLLCs from early postnatal human cortex. Increased excitatory neuronal contacts with pre-myelinating OLLCs accompanied ultrastructural myelin abnormalities in trisomic assembloids. Our findings suggest that trisomy redirects OLLC development toward a pre-myelinating state, uncoupling oligodendrocyte differentiation from productive myelination.
